# Apache Iceberg

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.12.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-09-29</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java (reference implementation)</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[iceberg.apache.org](https://iceberg.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/iceberg](https://github.com/apache/iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg releases page (1.12.0), the Iceberg table spec and the ASF incubator record</Verified>

**Apache Iceberg** is an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) for large analytic tables stored as files in a distributed file system or object store. The Iceberg specification describes how a table's schema, partitioning and data files are tracked in metadata files, so that several engines can read and write the same table with transactional guarantees.[^spec] Iceberg is a common table layer in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), where data stays in open file formats such as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and is shared between engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB).

## How it works

Apache Iceberg tracks individual data files instead of directories. Table state is held in a metadata file that records the schema, partition configuration, properties and snapshots. Each snapshot points to manifest files, and each manifest lists data files together with their partition values and column statistics.[^spec]

Every change to an Iceberg table writes a new metadata file and replaces the old one with an atomic swap. Writers work optimistically: a writer prepares its change, then commits by swapping the table's metadata pointer from the version it started from to the new version. If another commit happened first, the writer must retry against the new current version. Readers use the snapshot that was current when they loaded the table and do not take locks.[^spec]

The atomic swap of the metadata pointer is performed by a catalog. Catalog types supported by the Iceberg Spark integration include a REST catalog, the Hive Metastore and a directory-based Hadoop catalog,[^sparkconf] and Iceberg also provides a JDBC catalog.[^n1] The REST catalog is an HTTP protocol defined by the Iceberg project,[^rest] described further in [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog). Catalog services such as [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) and [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) are covered in their own articles.

## Features

### Snapshots and time travel

Each write to an Apache Iceberg table creates a new snapshot. Snapshots are the basis for reader isolation, time travel queries and rollback. Branches and tags are named references to snapshots, each with its own retention policy.[^branching]

In Spark SQL, Iceberg supports time travel with the `TIMESTAMP AS OF` and `VERSION AS OF` clauses. `VERSION AS OF` accepts a snapshot ID or a branch or tag name.[^sparkq]

```sql
-- Iceberg 1.12.0 with Spark SQL
SELECT * FROM prod.db.events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-11-01 00:00:00';
SELECT * FROM prod.db.events VERSION AS OF 10963874102873;
SELECT * FROM prod.db.events VERSION AS OF 'audit-branch';
```

### Hidden partitioning

Apache Iceberg produces partition values from column values, for example the day of a timestamp column, and records the relationship in table metadata. Queries filter on the source column and Iceberg skips files that cannot match. Users do not need to know how the table is partitioned or add a separate partition filter, as they would with a Hive-style partition column.[^partitioning]

### Schema and partition evolution

Apache Iceberg supports adding, dropping, renaming, reordering and widening columns, including fields in nested structures. Schema changes are metadata changes and do not rewrite data files. Columns are tracked by unique IDs, so a change to one column does not change the values read from another.[^evolution] The partition layout of a table can also change in place, for example from daily to hourly partitions, without creating a new table.[^evolution]

### Format versions

The Iceberg specification is versioned. The format version increases when a feature breaks forward compatibility, meaning older readers would not read the newer table correctly. Versions 1, 2 and 3 are complete and adopted; version 4 is under development and not formally adopted.[^spec]

| Format version | Main additions (per the spec) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Analytic tables built on immutable Parquet, Avro and ORC files |
| 2 | Row-level deletes through delete files; stricter writer requirements |
| 3 | New types (nanosecond timestamps, variant, geometry, geography, unknown), column default values, multi-argument transforms, row lineage, binary deletion vectors, table encryption keys |
| 4 (in development) | Restructured metadata tree, combined data file and deletion vector entries, relative locations, table constraints; new equality deletes no longer allowed |

## History

Iceberg was developed at Netflix. The proposal to the Apache Incubator described it as a table format designed to improve on the Hive table layout, and stated that it was under active development at Netflix.[^proposal] The project entered the Apache Incubator on 16 November 2018 and graduated to a top-level Apache project on 20 May 2020.[^incubator]

Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 was released on 29 September 2026. That release removed Spark 3.4 support.[^releases]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Apache Iceberg tables sit on object storage, and a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) holds the pointer to each table's current metadata file. Because the table state is defined by the specification and not by one engine, a table written by one engine can be read by another that implements the same format version. Pipelines that move data through layers, such as the [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture), can use Iceberg tables at each layer.

## Engine support

Connectors for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Apache Flink and Apache Hive are maintained in the main Iceberg repository, with a separate runtime artifact for each supported engine version.[^multiengine] [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) reads and writes Iceberg tables through its Iceberg connector,[^n2] and [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) reads them through its iceberg extension.[^n3] The Iceberg project also maintains implementations in Python (PyIceberg), Rust and Go in separate repositories.[^n4][^n5][^n6]

## Limitations

Apache Iceberg tables need regular maintenance. Snapshots accumulate until they are expired, and data files are not deleted while any retained snapshot still references them. Each commit also writes a new metadata file, so tables with frequent commits, such as streaming tables, may need old metadata files cleaned up.[^maintenance]

Support for newer features depends on the engine. A table can be kept on an older format version so that engines without support for newer features can still use it.[^spec]

[^n5]: [apache/iceberg-rust](https://github.com/apache/iceberg-rust). *GitHub*. Retrieved 2026-11-22.

# Apache Mesos support in Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark on Mesos, Mesos cluster manager</Field>
  <Field name="field">Cluster resource management</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Before Spark 1.0; Spark was first built on Mesos</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`mesos://` master URLs, coarse-grained and fine-grained modes, `MesosClusterDispatcher`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 3.5 and earlier</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN), [Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v3.1.1, v3.2.0, v3.5.0 and v4.0.0 tags of apache/spark (docs/running-on-mesos.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md, resource-managers/), SPARK-35050, SPARK-44442, the Spark 4.0.0 release notes, the Apache Attic page for Mesos and the ASF board minutes</Verified>

<Status level="removed" since="Apache Spark 3.2.0">Removed in Apache Spark 4.0.0. Use [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN) or the standalone cluster manager instead. Deprecated by SPARK-35050 and removed by SPARK-44442.[^jira44442]</Status>

**Apache Mesos support in Spark** was the integration that let [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) use Apache Mesos as its cluster manager: a Spark application pointed at a `mesos://` master URL received resources from Mesos and ran its [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) as Mesos tasks.[^mesos35] Spark itself was first written as a Mesos framework. Spark deprecated Mesos support in 3.2.0 and removed it in 4.0.0, so Spark 3.5 is the last release line that can run on Mesos.[^mig400][^jira44442]

## Status

Mesos support was deprecated in one minor release and removed in the next major release.

- **Deprecated in Spark 3.2.0.** SPARK-35050, "Deprecate Apache Mesos as resource manager", has fix version 3.2.0. Its description gives the reason: a thread on the Mesos dev list said that Mesos was moving to the Apache Attic and ceasing development.[^jira35050] From 3.2.0 the Mesos page of the Spark documentation opens with the note that Mesos support "is deprecated as of Apache Spark 3.2.0" and "will be removed in a future version", and the core migration guide says the same.[^mesos35][^mig400]
- **Removed in Spark 4.0.0.** SPARK-44442, "Drop mesos support", has fix version 4.0.0. The `resource-managers/mesos` module is present at the v3.5.0 tag and absent at the v4.0.0 tag. The Spark 4.0.0 core migration guide states: "In Spark 4.0, support for Apache Mesos as a resource manager was removed."[^jira44442][^mig400] The 4.0.0 release notes list SPARK-44442 and show the `mesos` library dependency (1.4.3) as removed.[^r400]
- **Fine-grained mode** was deprecated earlier, in Spark 2.0.0, as the Mesos documentation noted until support ended.[^mesos311]

The Mesos project itself is also gone. The ASF board approved a resolution to terminate the Apache Mesos project on 20 August 2025, and the Apache Attic records that Mesos retired in August 2025 and that its move to the Attic was completed in October 2025.[^board][^attic]

## History

Spark began at UC Berkeley as an application of Mesos. The 2010 HotCloud paper that introduced Spark says that "Spark is built on top of Mesos", a "cluster operating system" that lets several parallel applications share a cluster, and that building on Mesos reduced the programming effort Spark needed.[^paper] Spark later supported other cluster managers as well (its own standalone manager, Hadoop YARN and Kubernetes), and Mesos became one option among several.

When the Mesos community discussed moving the project to the Attic, Spark deprecated its integration (SPARK-35050, April 2021).[^jira35050] The Mesos board reports record attic discussions again in 2023 and a request in February 2024 to hold off, before the board terminated the project in 2025.[^board] By then Spark had already removed the integration from its main branch in September 2023, in the work that became Spark 4.0.0.[^jira44442]

## How it worked

A Spark application used Mesos by setting its master URL to `mesos://host:5050`, or to `mesos://zk://host1:2181,host2:2181/mesos` for a Mesos cluster with several masters coordinated through ZooKeeper.[^mesos35] The Spark 3.5 documentation describes two scheduling modes, chosen with `spark.mesos.coarse`:[^mesos35]

- **Coarse-grained mode** (default, `spark.mesos.coarse=true`): Spark acquired one long-lived Mesos task per machine and ran an executor in it, much like executors on other cluster managers.
- **Fine-grained mode** (`spark.mesos.coarse=false`, deprecated since 2.0.0): Spark created one Mesos task for each Spark task, so cores moved between applications as tasks finished, at the cost of higher task launch overhead.

For cluster deploy mode, operators ran the `MesosClusterDispatcher` (started with `sbin/start-mesos-dispatcher.sh`) and submitted applications to its URL. The documentation warned that the dispatcher had no authentication.[^mesos35]

```bash
# Spark 3.5 and earlier only; in Spark 4.0 spark-submit accepts only yarn, spark://, k8s:// and local masters
./bin/spark-shell --master mesos://host:5050
```

## Migrating off Mesos

Applications that ran on Mesos need another cluster manager to move to Spark 4. Spark 4.0 documents three: the standalone cluster manager, Hadoop YARN and Kubernetes.[^n1] Kubernetes is the closest match for a shared, multi-tenant cluster: each executor runs in its own pod, as each coarse-grained executor ran in its own Mesos task. All `spark.mesos.*` settings stop having any effect and should be removed from configuration files. See [Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration) for the other changes in the same release.

- [Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration)

# Apache Parquet

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) (originally Twitter and Cloudera)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">parquet-format 2.14.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-09-11</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Thrift (format definition); Java (parquet-java)</Field>
  <Field name="type">Columnar data file format</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[parquet.apache.org](https://parquet.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/parquet-format](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the parquet-format 2.14.0 release announcement, the Parquet file format documentation and the ASF incubator record</Verified>

**Apache Parquet** is an open source, column-oriented data file format for efficient storage and retrieval of analytic data. Parquet stores the values of each column together and supports per-column compression and encoding, and it is implemented in many programming languages and analytics tools.[^overview] In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Parquet files commonly hold the table data, and [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) add table metadata and transactions on top of Parquet files.

## Specification and implementations

The Apache Parquet project separates the format from its libraries. The parquet-format repository holds the official specification and the Thrift definitions of the file metadata (`parquet.thrift`); it contains no code for reading or writing files. The parquet-java repository, formerly named parquet-mr, holds the Java libraries and tools.[^overview] Other implementations include Apache Arrow (C++, Go and Rust), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), ClickHouse, cuDF and Polars, and the project publishes a table of which format features each one supports.[^impl]

## How it works

### File layout

An Apache Parquet file begins and ends with the 4-byte magic number `PAR1`. Between them come the column chunks, then the file metadata, then a 4-byte little-endian length of the metadata. The metadata records where every column chunk starts. Because it is written after the data, a writer can produce a file in a single pass; a reader first reads the footer, then reads only the column chunks it needs.[^fileformat]

### Row groups, column chunks and pages

A Parquet file contains one or more row groups, each a horizontal slice of the rows. A row group holds exactly one column chunk per column, and each column chunk is stored contiguously in the file. Column chunks are divided into pages, the smallest unit of encoding and compression.[^concepts]

| Level | Contains | Unit of |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File | One or more row groups and the footer metadata | Whole-file reads |
| Row group | One column chunk per column | Parallel processing of a file |
| Column chunk | One or more pages for one column | Column input and output |
| Page | Encoded, optionally compressed values | Encoding and compression |

### Nested data

Apache Parquet was designed for nested data from the start. It uses the record shredding and assembly algorithm from Google's Dremel paper, encoding nested structure with definition and repetition levels instead of flattening nested names.[^motivation][^readme] Null values are not stored in the data; nullness is recorded in the run-length encoded definition levels.[^n1]

## Features

### Types

Apache Parquet keeps a small set of physical types (such as INT32, INT64, DOUBLE and BYTE_ARRAY) and uses logical type annotations to say how to interpret them. For example, a string is a BYTE_ARRAY with a STRING annotation.[^logical] The specification also defines a Variant type for semi-structured data such as JSON, encoded as a value and a metadata binary so that nested fields can be read by path.[^n2]

### Encodings and compression

Parquet defines encodings including plain, dictionary, run-length/bit-packing hybrid, several delta encodings, byte stream split and ALP (adaptive lossless floating-point).[^encodings] Data and dictionary pages can be compressed with one of several codecs, and the codec can be chosen per column.[^n3][^motivation]

### Statistics, page index and Bloom filters

Readers can skip data using metadata stored in the file. Column statistics hold minimum and maximum values, and dictionaries let readers rule out values inside that range. An optional Bloom filter answers "definitely not present" or "probably present" for a value, which helps on high-cardinality columns.[^n4] The optional page index stores per-page statistics so that a reader can skip individual pages without reading every page header.[^n5]

## History

Parquet originated as a joint effort of Twitter and Cloudera; the parquet-format README carries the notice "Copyright 2013 Twitter, Cloudera and other contributors".[^readme] The project's stated aim was to make compressed, efficient columnar storage available to any project in the Apache Hadoop ecosystem without favouring one processing framework.[^motivation]

Parquet entered the Apache Incubator on 20 May 2014 and graduated on 22 April 2015.[^incubator] The Apache Software Foundation announced Parquet as a top-level project on 27 April 2015.[^n6]

parquet-format 2.14.0 was released on 11 September 2026. It added chronological ordering of INT96 timestamps, a FILE logical type and the ALP encoding.[^release]

## Use in an open lakehouse

Apache Parquet defines single files, organised internally into row groups, column chunks and pages.[^concepts] Grouping many files into one table, with commits and snapshots, is the job of an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format). The [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) specification lists Parquet as one of its data file formats, alongside Avro and ORC.[^n7] [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), Iceberg and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) all store Parquet data files, which is what allows Delta Lake's UniForm feature to expose one copy of the data through several table formats.[^n8]

## Engine support

[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) reads and writes Parquet through a built-in data source.[^n9] [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) reads and writes Parquet files directly.[^n10] The Parquet implementation status page lists feature support for Arrow C++, parquet-java, Arrow Go, Arrow Rust, ClickHouse, cuDF, hyparquet, DuckDB, Polars and DataHaskell.[^impl]

## Limitations

Apache Parquet implementations do not all support the same features of the format, so a file that uses a newer encoding or logical type may not be readable by every tool.[^overview][^impl] The specification keeps older representations for compatibility: the ConvertedType annotation is deprecated, but writers must still write it next to LogicalType so that old readers work.[^logical] The INT96 timestamp type is deprecated, yet the project notes it was still common in files produced as of 2024.[^impl]

# Apache Polaris

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2025 (0.9.0-incubating)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.9.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-14</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) server</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[polaris.apache.org](https://polaris.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/polaris](https://github.com/apache/polaris)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Polaris download page, the 1.9.0 documentation and the Apache Incubator status page</Verified>

**Apache Polaris** is an open source catalog for [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables that implements the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) API, so that several query engines can read and write the same tables through one catalog.[^incubator][^docs] Polaris adds role-based access control and credential vending on top of the REST protocol.[^docs] It is a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation (ASF).[^grad]

## History

The Polaris incubation proposal states that the project was first developed from ideas of many employees within Snowflake, that most core developers came from Snowflake and Dremio, and that the code was licensed under the Apache License 2.0.[^proposal]

Polaris entered the Apache Incubator on 9 August 2024.[^incubator] The first release listed on the project's download page is 0.9.0, dated 11 March 2025, and version 1.0.0 followed on 9 July 2025.[^downloads]

Polaris graduated from the Incubator to become an ASF top-level project in February 2026. The project announced the graduation on 19 February 2026, and the ASF announced it publicly on 5 March 2026.[^grad][^n1]

## How it works

Polaris exposes the Iceberg REST API, so any engine with an Iceberg REST client can connect to it. The project site lists engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Apache Flink, Apache Doris, Dremio OSS, StarRocks and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino).[^home]

A Polaris server holds one or more catalogs. An internal catalog is managed by Polaris and supports reads and writes. An external catalog is managed by another provider, is synced into Polaris, and is read-only. Each catalog has a storage configuration for Amazon S3, Azure or Google Cloud Storage. Inside a catalog, namespaces group tables and can be nested.[^docs]

## Access control

Polaris uses role-based access control (RBAC) in three layers. Privileges are granted to catalog roles, catalog roles are granted to principal roles, and principal roles are assigned to principals. A catalog role belongs to one catalog, and the relationship between principals and principal roles is many-to-many.[^rbac]

Privileges in Polaris are grouped by securable object: catalog, namespace, table, view, policy and semantic model. Examples are `TABLE_READ_DATA` and `NAMESPACE_LIST`.[^rbac]

## Credential vending

Polaris vends temporary storage credentials to query engines during query execution, so the engines do not need their own long-lived access to cloud storage.[^docs] The [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification defines this mechanism, under the name vended credentials, as a way for a catalog to return storage credentials together with a loaded table.[^n2]

## Other features

**Generic tables** let Polaris register tables that are not Iceberg tables, defined by a name, a format (for example `delta` or `csv`) and an optional base location. They share namespaces with Iceberg tables. The documentation marks generic tables as beta.[^n3]

**Catalog federation** connects Polaris to existing metadata services. The namespaces, tables and views of a federated catalog stay in the remote system. The 1.9.0 documentation has integration guides for Iceberg REST, Hive Metastore, Hadoop catalog and BigQuery Metastore, and federation is disabled by default.[^n4]

**Policies** are catalog entities that define rules for actions on catalogs, namespaces, tables or views. The predefined types cover data compaction, metadata compaction, orphan file removal and snapshot expiry. Polaris stores and resolves policies but does not run the maintenance work itself; external engines do that.[^n5]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Apache Polaris serves as the shared catalog for Iceberg tables. Because Polaris speaks the standard Iceberg REST protocol, engines connect with their existing Iceberg REST clients instead of a Polaris-specific connector, and access rules defined once in Polaris apply to every engine that uses it.[^home][^rbac]

## See also

- [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)
- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)
- [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)
- [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)
- [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)

# Apache Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2010 (open sourced)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Java, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Distributed data processing engine</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[spark.apache.org](https://spark.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark](https://github.com/apache/spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the spark.apache.org news page and release notes (latest release 4.3.0), the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark and its documentation</Verified>

**Apache Spark** is an open source, distributed engine for large-scale data processing, with high-level APIs in Java, Scala, Python and R and an optimized engine that runs general execution graphs.[^docs-index] Spark runs batch queries, SQL, stream processing and machine learning on one engine, on a single machine or on a cluster. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Spark is one of the engines that reads and writes [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) through a shared [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog).

## Architecture

A Spark application runs as a set of independent processes on a cluster. The **driver** program holds the `SparkContext` (wrapped by `SparkSession` in the DataFrame API) and plans the work. The driver connects to a **cluster manager**, which allocates resources, and then obtains **executors**: processes on worker nodes that run computations and store data for the application. The driver sends application code and then **tasks** to the executors.[^cluster]

Each Spark application gets its own executor processes, which stay up for the whole application. This isolates applications from one another, but it also means two Spark applications cannot share in-memory data without writing it to external storage.[^cluster]

### Execution model

Spark evaluates transformations lazily. A transformation such as a filter or a join only records how a dataset is derived; Spark computes it when an **action**, such as `collect` or a write, needs a result. The Spark documentation explains that this lets Spark run more efficiently, for example by returning only the result of a final aggregation to the driver instead of a large intermediate dataset.[^n1]

A Spark **job** is a parallel computation that Spark starts in response to an action. Spark divides each job into **stages**, sets of tasks that depend on one another in a similar way to the map and reduce stages of MapReduce, and sends each **task** to one executor.[^cluster]

The **deploy mode** sets where the driver runs. In cluster mode, the driver is launched inside the cluster; in client mode, the process that submits the application runs the driver outside the cluster.[^cluster]

### Cluster managers

Spark 4.3 supports three cluster managers: Spark's own **standalone** manager, **Hadoop YARN** and **Kubernetes**. Applications are submitted to any of them with the `spark-submit` script. Each driver also serves a web UI, by default on port 4040.[^cluster] The project also maintains a separate Spark Kubernetes Operator for running Spark applications and clusters through Kubernetes custom resources.[^docs-index]

## APIs and libraries

Spark exposes several libraries on top of its core engine:[^docs-index]

- **Spark SQL and DataFrames**: structured data processing through SQL or the DataFrame and Dataset APIs, optimized by the Catalyst query optimizer.[^r200][^n2]
- **[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)**: stream processing built on the Spark SQL engine, using the same DataFrame operations as batch queries.
- **MLlib**: a library of machine learning algorithms and pipelines.[^n3]
- **pandas API on Spark**: a pandas-compatible API that runs on Spark. It was added in Spark 3.2.0.[^r320]
- **GraphX**: graph processing.[^docs-index]

The R API (SparkR) is marked as deprecated in the Spark 4.3 documentation. Spark 4.3 runs on Java 17, 21 or 25, Scala 2.13 and Python 3.11 or later.[^docs-index]

A short PySpark example that reads a table and aggregates it:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("example").getOrCreate()

orders = spark.read.table("sales.orders")
daily = orders.groupBy("order_date").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
daily.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("sales.daily_revenue")
```

## Spark Connect

<Hatnote>Main article: [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Hatnote>

Spark Connect is a client-server protocol, introduced in Spark 3.4, in which a thin client sends unresolved logical plans to a Spark server over gRPC and receives results as Apache Arrow batches.[^connect] The client does not run inside the driver process, so applications can run in IDEs, notebooks and services away from the cluster. Besides the Python and Scala clients in the main repository, the Spark project maintains separate Spark Connect clients for Go, Rust and Swift.[^n4][^n5][^n6] Spark 4.0 added a lightweight Python client package (`pyspark-client`) and the `spark.api.mode` setting, which lets a classic application switch to Spark Connect.[^r400]

## Spark Declarative Pipelines

<Hatnote>Main article: [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Hatnote>

Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP), added in Spark 4.1.0, is a framework in which a user declares datasets (streaming tables, materialized views and temporary views) and the flows that fill them, and Spark works out the dependency order, parallelism, checkpoints and retries.[^r410] Pipelines are run with the `spark-pipelines` command line tool.[^n7]

## History

Spark started in 2009 as a research project at the AMPLab of the University of California, Berkeley, and was open sourced in early 2010. The project moved to the Apache Software Foundation in 2013.[^history] The ASF announced on 27 February 2014 that Spark had graduated from the Apache Incubator to become a top-level project.[^n8]

| Version | Announced | Selected changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.0.0 | 2014-05-30 | First release of the 1.x line[^news] |
| 2.0.0 | 2016-07-26 | First, experimental release of Structured Streaming[^news][^r200] |
| 3.0.0 | 2020-06-18 | First release of the 3.x line; adaptive query execution, dynamic partition pruning[^news][^n9] |
| 3.4.0 | 2023-04-13 | Python client for Spark Connect[^news][^n10] |
| 4.0.0 | 2025-05-23 | First release of the 4.x line; VARIANT type, SQL user-defined functions, pipe syntax, Arbitrary State API v2 (`transformWithState`)[^news][^r400] |
| 4.1.0 | 2025-12-16 | Spark Declarative Pipelines; Real-time Mode in Structured Streaming; SQL scripting and VARIANT enabled by default[^news][^r410] |
| 4.2.0 | 2026-07-14 | SQL `CHANGES` clause for change data capture; Auto CDC in Declarative Pipelines[^news][^r420] |
| 4.3.0 | 2026-10-30 | Stateful queries in Real-time Mode; SCD Type 2 Auto CDC; start of a quarterly feature-release cadence[^news][^r430] |

Older release lines continue to receive maintenance releases; Spark 4.2.1, 4.1.4 and 4.0.5 were announced on 27 October 2026, three days before 4.3.0.[^n11]

## Use in an open lakehouse

Spark reads and writes lakehouse tables through table format connectors and its catalog plugin API. A catalog is registered by setting Spark properties under `spark.sql.catalog.<name>`; the [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) documentation, for example, shows a catalog of type `rest` that talks to an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog).[^n12] [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) is enabled with the `io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension` SQL extension and the `DeltaCatalog` session catalog.[^n13]

Because the table data sits in open formats such as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and the metadata sits in a catalog such as [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) or [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), the same tables Spark writes can be queried by other engines, for example [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) or [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB). Spark is commonly used for the ingestion and transformation layers of a [medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture), with [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow) or Spark Declarative Pipelines deciding when each step runs.

# Business Source License

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Business_Source_License

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">BSL, BUSL, BSL 1.1</Field>
  <Field name="field">Software licensing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Licensor, Licensed Work, Additional Use Grant, Change Date, Change License</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">Terraform (1.6.0 and later), Materialize, CockroachDB (19.2 to 24.2)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[MinIO](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MinIO), [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the BSL 1.1 text published by MariaDB, the LICENSE files of hashicorp/terraform, MaterializeInc/materialize and cockroachdb/cockroach (v19.1.0, v19.2.0 and current), the HashiCorp and Cockroach Labs announcements and the Linux Foundation OpenTofu announcement</Verified>

The **Business Source License** (BSL, also written BUSL) is a source-available software license, published by MariaDB, under which the source code can be read, changed and redistributed, but production use is allowed only as far as the licensor's **Additional Use Grant** permits, until each version converts to an open source license on its **Change Date**.[^bsl] The license text itself says it "is not an Open Source license".[^bsl] In data infrastructure the BSL is best known from vendors that moved projects off open source licenses to stop competitors from selling hosted versions; the move of HashiCorp's Terraform in 2023 led to the OpenTofu fork.

## How it works

The BSL is a template. A licensor fills in a short parameter block at the top, and the fixed license text below it applies to those values:[^bsl]

| Parameter | What it sets |
| --- | --- |
| Licensor | Who grants the license. |
| Licensed Work | The software and version covered. |
| Additional Use Grant | Which production use is allowed before the Change Date. Without a grant, only non-production use is allowed. |
| Change Date | When the version converts. The conversion happens on the Change Date or on the fourth anniversary of the version's first public release, whichever comes first. |
| Change License | The license the version converts to. It must be GPL version 2.0 or later, or a license compatible with it. |

Without an Additional Use Grant, the BSL lets anyone copy, modify, create derivative works of and redistribute the code, and make non-production use of it.[^bsl] Each version has its own clock: a newer release starts a new period, so the latest code is always under the restrictive terms while versions older than the change period become open source.[^bsl]

## Is the BSL open source?

No. The BSL text states that it is not an Open Source license, and that the Licensed Work will eventually be made available under one, namely the Change License.[^bsl] Code under the BSL is often called *source available*: anyone can read it, but the restriction on production use conflicts with the Open Source Definition's rule that a license must not restrict anyone from using the program in a specific field of endeavor.[^n1] A version becomes open source only when it reaches its Change Date.

## Use in data tools

The parameters vary a great deal between projects, so "under the BSL" says little until the parameter block is read.

| Project | Previous license | First BSL version | Additional Use Grant (summary) | Change period | Change License |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Terraform (HashiCorp, now IBM) | Mozilla Public License 2.0[^hashi] | 1.6.0[^tf] | Production use allowed, except offering it to third parties on a hosted or embedded basis to compete with the licensor's paid versions[^tf] | Four years from publication[^tf] | MPL 2.0[^tf] |
| Materialize | Not covered here | Each release; the current LICENSE names a dated version[^mz] | Production use within memory and disk limits per installation, and no commercial database service that lets third parties define views[^mz] | Four years (the current LICENSE has a Change Date of 23 November 2030)[^mz] | Apache License 2.0[^mz] |
| CockroachDB (Cockroach Labs) | Apache License 2.0 (core, up to 19.1)[^crdb191] | 19.2[^crdb192] | Use allowed, except a commercial database service that lets third parties create tables[^crdb192] | Change Date 1 October 2022 for 19.2[^crdb192] | Apache License 2.0[^crdb192] |

HashiCorp announced on 10 August 2023 that future releases of its products would move from the MPL 2.0 to the BSL 1.1, while its APIs, SDKs and almost all other libraries would stay under the MPL 2.0.[^hashi] On 20 September 2023 the Linux Foundation announced OpenTofu, which it described as an open source successor to the MPLv2-licensed Terraform.[^n2]

The BSL is not always the last step. Cockroach Labs used it for the CockroachDB core from 19.2, then announced in August 2024 that from version 24.3 it would retire its Core offering and consolidate on a single enterprise license, with free tiers for individuals and smaller companies; the code remains source available.[^n3] The repository's current `LICENSE` file is the CockroachDB Software License, not the BSL.[^n4]

## What the BSL is not

- **Not a single set of terms.** Two BSL projects can have opposite production rules, because the Additional Use Grant is written by each licensor.
- **Not the same as the AGPL.** The GNU AGPLv3 is an open source license that allows any use but requires source code for network-served modifications; [MinIO](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MinIO) used it for its community edition and never moved to the BSL.[^n5]
- **Not retroactive.** A license change applies to new versions. Releases published under an earlier open source license stay available under it, which is what makes forks such as OpenTofu possible.[^hashi]

## Use in an open lakehouse

The core open lakehouse projects (for example [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)) are under the Apache License 2.0. The BSL matters at the edges of a stack: infrastructure as code, databases and streaming tools that a team runs next to the lakehouse. For each such tool the questions are the same: what the Additional Use Grant forbids, whether the planned use is production use, and which version converts to which license on which date.

# Copy-on-write and merge-on-read

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">CoW and MoR; write modes for row-level operations</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Rewritten data files (copy-on-write); delete files, deletion vectors or log files merged at read time (merge-on-read)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Deletion vector](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg table spec and configuration documentation (1.12.0), the Delta Lake deletion vectors documentation and PROTOCOL.md at v4.4.1, and the Apache Hudi table types documentation (version 1.2.1)</Verified>

**Copy-on-write** and **merge-on-read** are the two strategies an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) can use to apply row-level updates and deletes to data stored in immutable files. With copy-on-write, the writer rewrites every data file that contains a changed row, so readers only read data files. With merge-on-read, the writer records the change separately (as delete files, [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) or log files) and readers combine those records with the original data files at query time.[^hudi-types] The choice moves cost between writes and reads. [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) all support both approaches, with different names and defaults.

## Why the choice exists

Lakehouse data files, usually [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), are written once and never changed in place. The Iceberg specification requires that files are not moved or altered once they are written, and states that data and metadata files are immutable until they are deleted.[^icespec] A `DELETE`, `UPDATE` or `MERGE` that touches one row must therefore either produce a new copy of the file without that row, or leave the file alone and write a note saying the row is gone.

The Delta Lake documentation states the copy-on-write cost directly: by default, deleting a single row means rewriting the entire Parquet file that contains it.[^delta-dv]

## Copy-on-write

In copy-on-write, a row-level operation reads each affected data file, writes a new file with the changes applied, and commits a snapshot that replaces the old file with the new one. Readers see only complete data files and do no merging. The cost is write amplification: the whole file is rewritten even when a small fraction of its rows changed.[^hudi-types]

Iceberg's Spark integration reports this cost as a metric: `spark.delete.num-copied-rows` counts unmodified rows that were rewritten in copy-on-write mode and is zero in merge-on-read.[^ice-writes]

## Merge-on-read

In merge-on-read, the writer adds a small record of the change and leaves existing data files untouched. Each project encodes the record differently:

- **Apache Iceberg** (format version 2 and later) writes delete files. Position deletes mark a row by data file and row position; equality deletes mark rows by column values, such as `id = 5`. In format version 3, position deletes are stored as deletion vectors in Puffin files, and position delete files are deprecated.[^icespec]
- **Delta Lake** attaches a deletion vector to the data file's entry in the transaction log, marking rows as logically deleted while they stay physically in the file. Readers must skip those rows.[^delta-proto]
- **Apache Hudi** merge-on-read tables write updates and deletes to log files next to a columnar base file, and a periodic compaction merges the log files into a new base file. Queries on such tables can be snapshot queries, which merge the logs for the freshest data, or read-optimized queries, which read only the compacted base files.[^hudi-types]

Merge-on-read makes writes cheaper but adds work to every read until the changes are compacted into rewritten data files. Hudi's documentation notes that merge-on-read query performance depends on whether the log files have been compacted.[^hudi-types]

## Comparison

|  | [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) | [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) | [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How the strategy is chosen | Per operation, with table properties `write.delete.mode`, `write.update.mode` and `write.merge.mode`[^ice-conf] | Table property `delta.enableDeletionVectors`[^delta-dv] | Table type, fixed when the table is created: `hoodie.datasource.write.table.type` or `hoodie.table.type`, values `COPY_ON_WRITE` or `MERGE_ON_READ`[^hudi-conf] |
| Default | `copy-on-write` for all three properties[^ice-conf] | Files are rewritten unless deletion vectors are enabled on the table[^delta-dv] | `COPY_ON_WRITE`[^hudi-conf] |
| Merge-on-read record | Position delete files (v2), equality delete files, deletion vectors (v3)[^icespec] | Deletion vectors stored in files or inline in the log[^delta-proto] | Log files attached to a base file[^hudi-types] |
| Requirements | Merge-on-read requires format version 2 or later[^ice-conf] | Reader version 3 and writer version 7 with the `deletionVectors` table feature[^delta-proto] | The table type cannot change between writes[^hudi-conf] |
| Folding changes back into data files | Data file compaction with `rewrite_data_files`, which can select files by delete count or delete ratio[^ice-proc] | `OPTIMIZE`, DML with deletion vectors disabled, or `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)`[^delta-dv] | Compaction of merge-on-read file groups[^hudi-types] |

## Example

In Iceberg the mode is a table property, so one table can use merge-on-read for deletes and copy-on-write for merges.[^ice-conf]

```sql
-- Apache Iceberg (Spark SQL): merge-on-read for DELETE and UPDATE, copy-on-write for MERGE
ALTER TABLE db.events SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.merge.mode'  = 'copy-on-write'
);
```

The Delta Lake equivalent enables deletion vectors on the table: `ALTER TABLE t SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = true)`. Doing so upgrades the table protocol, and clients that do not support deletion vectors can no longer read the table.[^delta-dv]

## Choosing a strategy

The projects document the tradeoff in general terms rather than with a fixed rule.

Apache Hudi gives the most explicit guidance. Its documentation describes copy-on-write as suited to read-heavy workloads, batch ETL, data warehousing on data lakes and slowly changing reference data, and merge-on-read as suited to change data capture pipelines, streaming ingestion, hybrid batch and streaming workloads, and tables with frequent updates and deletes. Its comparison lists copy-on-write as having higher write latency and update cost and lower query latency, and merge-on-read the reverse.[^hudi-types]

Delta Lake describes deletion vectors as a storage optimization that avoids rewriting Parquet files for some operations, with reads applying the recorded deletions. Its documentation adds that `UPDATE`, `MERGE` and `OPTIMIZE` do not guarantee that all recorded deletions get applied, so `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` is the command that rewrites every affected file.[^delta-dv]

Apache Iceberg documents the properties and their defaults, and documents compaction as the way to rewrite files with many deletes, but its configuration page does not recommend one mode over the other.[^ice-conf][^ice-proc]

# Data catalog

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Lakehouse catalog, metastore</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data management, data governance</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Namespaces, table metadata pointers, commit coordination, access control, credential vending</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), Lakekeeper, any [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Iceberg REST catalog specification and OpenAPI file, the Apache Polaris documentation, the Unity Catalog OSS documentation, the Delta transaction log protocol and the Lakekeeper site</Verified>

A **data catalog**, in a lakehouse, is the service that names tables and other data assets, records where each table's current metadata lives, coordinates commits, and decides who may read or write each asset. Engines ask the catalog which files make up a table and whether the current user may access them before they read any data. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), the catalog is reached through an open API, so that several engines share one view of the same tables. Open source examples include [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) and other implementations of the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification.

## Role in a lakehouse

An [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) describes how one table is stored, but it does not say how a table is found by name or how concurrent writers agree on its current version. The catalog fills both gaps.

The Unity Catalog OSS documentation summarizes the catalog's job as answering three questions for an engine before it reads data: which files hold the table's data, whether the user may read them, and what the table's schema is.[^ucwhat]

For [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables, the Apache Polaris documentation states that a catalog must store the current metadata pointer for each table (a mapping from table name to the location of its current metadata file) and must update that pointer atomically when a new table version is committed.[^polaris-docs] This atomic swap is the basis of Iceberg's serializable isolation.[^icespec]

For [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) tables, the transaction log is stored alongside the data, so a table can be read without a separate metastore.[^deltaproto] The Delta protocol also defines catalog-managed tables, in which the managing catalog becomes the source of truth for whether a commit succeeded.[^deltaproto]

## Functions

A lakehouse catalog typically provides the following functions.

- **Namespace.** Assets are organized in a hierarchy. Unity Catalog uses a three-level namespace, `catalog.schema.asset`.[^ucwhat] The Iceberg REST catalog API organizes tables into namespaces.[^restyaml]
- **Metadata pointer and commits.** The catalog records each table's current version and accepts or rejects commits from writers.[^polaris-docs]
- **Access control.** With authentication and authorization enabled, Unity Catalog OSS checks ownership and privileges such as `USE_CATALOG`, `SELECT` and `MODIFY` on every request.[^ucwhat]
- **Credential vending.** The catalog issues short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table or volume, so that an engine can read or write only the data the user is allowed to access.[^ucwhat]
- **Discovery.** Because namespaces, tables and schemas are available over an API, engines and AI agents can list what exists instead of inferring it from storage paths.[^olio-agentic]

## The Iceberg REST catalog specification

<Hatnote>Main article: [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Hatnote>

The Iceberg REST catalog specification is an OpenAPI definition of a catalog API for Iceberg tables. The Iceberg project created it because pluggable catalogs had to be implemented separately in every language, which made it hard for engines and commercial offerings to support many catalogs. With the REST protocol, a new language or engine needs only one client implementation to work with any compliant catalog.[^icerest]

The Iceberg documentation lists further benefits of the REST protocol: change-based commits that let the server resolve conflicts and retry, root metadata written by the catalog service, multi-table commits, lazy snapshot loading, and secure table sharing through credential vending or remote signing.[^icerest] The Iceberg documentation compares the role of the REST protocol to that of Hive's Thrift protocol for the Hive Metastore.[^icerest]

A client signals delegated storage access with the `X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation` request header. The defined values are `vended-credentials`, `remote-signing` and `none`, and the server may honor any or none of the requested mechanisms.[^restyaml]

## Open source catalogs

| Catalog | Description | Table formats and APIs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) | A catalog for tables, volumes, functions and models; an LF AI & Data project. Databricks created it and open sourced it in 2024.[^ucwhat][^uc-home] | Delta Lake and Iceberg; Unity Catalog REST API, UC Delta API and Iceberg REST catalog API[^uc-home] |
| [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) | An Apache Software Foundation catalog for Apache Iceberg[^polaris] | Iceberg; implements the Iceberg REST API[^polaris] |
| Lakekeeper | An Iceberg REST catalog written in Rust, under the Apache License[^lakekeeper] | Iceberg; Iceberg REST catalog API[^lakekeeper] |

Apache Polaris lists Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Trino, Apache Doris, Dremio OSS and StarRocks among the engines that work with it through the Iceberg REST API.[^polaris] Unity Catalog lists Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Daft among the clients with governed access.[^uc-home]

## Catalogs and AI agents

In an [agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse), the catalog is the main control point for AI agents. It tells an agent which tables exist and which it may touch, and it vends storage credentials scoped to the agent's identity, so that an agent can be limited to writing in its own sandbox namespace.[^olio-agentic]

## Limitations

A catalog governs only access that passes through it. The Unity Catalog OSS documentation warns that anyone holding direct storage credentials can bypass the catalog's checks, so the storage must also be locked down as part of a secure deployment.[^ucwhat]

# Deletion vector

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">DV</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Delta Lake 2.3.0 (reads); Apache Iceberg format version 3</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Bitmap of deleted row positions (64-bit Roaring bitmap), reference to one data file, cardinality</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">Delta Lake PROTOCOL.md at tag v4.4.1 and the Delta Lake deletion vectors documentation, the Apache Iceberg table spec and Puffin spec at tag apache-iceberg-1.12.0, and the Iceberg maintenance documentation</Verified>

A **deletion vector** (DV) is a compact bitmap, stored outside a data file, that marks which rows of that data file are deleted. Readers skip the marked rows, so a table can delete or update individual rows without rewriting the immutable data file that holds them.[^deltaproto][^icespec] Deletion vectors are one way of implementing the merge-on-read strategy for row-level changes. [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (from format version 3) both define them, and the two encodings are closely related.

## How it works

A deletion vector is a set of row positions in one data file, counting from zero. In both formats the set is a 64-bit Roaring bitmap: each 64-bit position is split into a 32-bit key (the high bytes) and a 32-bit sub-position, and each key points to a 32-bit Roaring bitmap of sub-positions.[^deltaproto][^puffin] Roaring bitmaps switch between an integer array, a bitmap and run-length encoding per block of values, which keeps both sparse and dense deletes small.[^deltaproto]

A row is deleted if its position is set in the deletion vector that applies to its data file. The table metadata records which data file a deletion vector belongs to and how many rows it removes (its cardinality).[^deltaproto][^icespec]

| Approach | What is written for a one-row delete | What a reader does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copy-on-write | A new copy of the whole data file without the row | Reads the new data file |
| Position delete file (Iceberg v2) | A file listing (data file path, row position) pairs | Treats a row as deleted if a delete file has an entry for its file and position |
| Deletion vector | A bitmap for that single data file | Skips the set positions while reading the data file |

The rows of this table are drawn from the Iceberg delete format definitions and the Delta Lake deletion vector documentation.[^icespec][^deltadoc]

## Delta Lake

In the Delta transaction log protocol, deletion vectors are a table feature. A table must use reader version 3 and writer version 7 and list `deletionVectors` in both its reader and writer features. Writers may only create new deletion vectors when the table property `delta.enableDeletionVectors` is true, but readers must honour existing deletion vectors whether or not the property is set.[^deltaproto]

A deletion vector is attached to a file's `add` or `remove` action through a descriptor with a `storageType`: `u` for a file whose path is derived from a UUID relative to the table, `p` for an absolute path, or `i` for a bitmap stored inline in the log, base85-encoded. The descriptor also holds the offset, size in bytes and cardinality. Deletion vector files live in the table root and can hold vectors for data files in several partitions.[^deltaproto]

The protocol's reader requirement is that rows invalidated by a deletion vector must not be returned. Its writer requirement is that a file added with a deletion vector must carry a correct `numRecords` statistic.[^deltaproto]

Support arrived across several releases. According to the Delta Lake documentation, scans with deletion vectors are available from 2.3.0, `DELETE` from 2.4.0, `UPDATE` from 3.0.0 and `MERGE` from 3.1.0. The same page marks the feature as being in experimental support mode.[^deltadoc]

```sql
-- Delta Lake: enable deletion vectors (upgrades the table protocol)
ALTER TABLE events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = true);

-- Later: rewrite every file that has soft-deleted rows
REORG TABLE events APPLY (PURGE);
```

Enabling deletion vectors upgrades the table protocol, after which clients without deletion vector support cannot read the table. From Delta Lake 3.0 the table feature can be dropped again to restore compatibility.[^deltadoc]

## Apache Iceberg

Format version 3 of the Iceberg spec adds binary deletion vectors. They are stored as the `deletion-vector-v1` blob type in Puffin files and tracked in delete manifests by file location, blob offset (`content_offset`) and length (`content_size_in_bytes`), together with the referenced data file.[^icespec] One Puffin file can hold deletion vectors for many data files.[^icespec]

Deletion vectors replace position delete files in version 3. Position delete files are deprecated, must not be added to v3 tables, and existing ones stay valid until the deletes for that data file are next updated, at which point they must be written into a deletion vector.[^icespec] Equality delete files are unaffected and remain the way to delete rows by column value.[^icespec]

The spec allows at most one deletion vector per data file in a snapshot. Writers must merge new deletes with the existing vector or position delete files, so when a deletion vector is present, readers can ignore matching position delete files.[^icespec] At read time, a deletion vector applies to a data file when the paths match, the data file's sequence number is less than or equal to the vector's, and the partitions are equal.[^icespec]

The Puffin blob wraps the bitmap with a length, the magic bytes `D1 D3 39 64` and a CRC-32 checksum. The Puffin spec says its big-endian length and checksum fields were chosen for compatibility with existing deletion vectors in Delta tables.[^puffin]

## Compaction and purge

A deletion vector hides rows but does not remove their bytes, so both projects provide ways to rewrite data files and drop the deleted rows physically.

In Delta Lake, changes recorded in deletion vectors are applied when files are rewritten: by DML run with deletion vectors disabled, by `OPTIMIZE`, or by `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)`. Only the last guarantees that every file with soft-deleted rows is rewritten. The old files remain until `VACUUM` removes them.[^deltadoc]

In Iceberg, the spec requires that when a data file is removed, any deletion vector for it is removed from the delete manifests, though the Puffin file holding it need not be rewritten.[^icespec] The `rewrite_data_files` procedure can select data files for rewriting by the number of deletes or the ratio of deleted rows, and the `removeDanglingDeleteFiles` action drops deletion vectors whose data file is no longer live.[^iceproc][^icemaint]

## Not to be confused with

- **Position delete files** in Iceberg v2 also mark rows by position, but as rows in a separate data file that can reference many data files, rather than one bitmap per data file.[^icespec]
- **Merge-on-read log files** in [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) record updates and deletes for a file group in log files that compaction merges into a new base file; Hudi's documentation describes them as log files, not deletion vectors.[^huditypes]

- [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)
- [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)
- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)

[^icespec]: [Iceberg Table Spec (format/spec.md at apache-iceberg-1.12.0)](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/apache-iceberg-1.12.0/format/spec.md). *Apache Software Foundation*. Retrieved 2026-11-22.

# Delta Lake

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Delta Lake project, a [Linux Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Linux_Foundation) project (created by [Databricks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Databricks))</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2019 (open source)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">4.4.1</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-05</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Java (Delta Spark); Rust (delta-rs)</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[delta.io](https://delta.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/delta-io/delta](https://github.com/delta-io/delta)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Delta Lake 4.4.1 GitHub release and the Delta Transaction Log Protocol (PROTOCOL.md)</Verified>

**Delta Lake** is an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) and storage framework that adds ACID transactions to tables stored as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) files in a distributed file system or object store. A Delta table records every change in a transaction log kept next to the data, and the Delta Transaction Log Protocol specifies how readers and writers use that log.[^protocol] Delta Lake is one of the table formats used in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), with connectors for engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and Apache Flink.[^readme]

## How it works

A Delta Lake table is a directory that holds data files and a `_delta_log` subdirectory. The log contains JSON files named by table version, zero-padded to 20 digits. Each JSON file holds an atomic set of actions, such as adding or removing a data file or changing table metadata, that turns the previous version of the table into the next one.[^protocol]

Delta Lake writers work in two phases. They first write new data files optimistically, then commit by adding the next numbered entry to the log. The table therefore has a single serial history of versions. Readers use the log to choose which data files make up a consistent snapshot, so they are isolated from concurrent writes.[^protocol] The project states that Delta Lake provides serializability for concurrent reads and writes.[^readme]

Checkpoints, also stored in `_delta_log`, contain the full replayed state of the table at one version. Readers start from the newest suitable checkpoint so that they do not need to replay every JSON entry.[^protocol]

Because all metadata is stored with the data, a Delta table does not need a separate metastore to be read, and a static table can be copied with ordinary file system tools.[^protocol] The protocol also defines catalog-managed tables, in which a catalog ratifies commits and clients must contact that catalog to find the latest ones.[^protocol]

## Features

### Time travel

The Delta Lake log keeps older table versions readable, so a reader can query the table as of an earlier version. For time travel, the checkpoint used to rebuild the state must not be newer than the requested version.[^protocol] Data files that are no longer in the latest version can be removed by the vacuum command after a retention period, which defaults to 7 days.[^protocol]

### Protocol versions and table features

Each Delta table declares a minimum reader version and a minimum writer version. The protocol version increases when a change to the specification is not forward compatible, so that older clients refuse tables they cannot interpret correctly. From reader version 3 and writer version 7, a table instead lists named table features, and a client must support every listed feature to read or write the table.[^protocol]

### Other features in the protocol

The Delta protocol specification defines, among others:[^protocol]
- **Deletion vectors**, which mark rows in a data file as deleted without rewriting the file.
- **Change data files**, which record row-level changes for readers of a change feed.
- **Column mapping**, which maps logical column names to physical names.
- **Row tracking**, **in-commit timestamps**, **type widening** and the **variant** data type.
- **Iceberg compatibility** table features, which constrain writers so that Iceberg metadata can be produced for the table.

### UniForm

Delta Universal Format (UniForm) lets Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi clients read Delta tables. UniForm generates Iceberg or Hudi metadata asynchronously after Delta commits, over the same Parquet data files. Iceberg and Hudi clients can only read such tables; Hudi support is in preview.[^uniform]

## History

Delta Lake was created by [Databricks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Databricks). Databricks announced the open sourcing of the Delta Lake project under the Apache License 2.0 on 24 April 2019.[^opensource] On 16 October 2019 the Linux Foundation announced that it would host Delta Lake under an open governance model.[^lf]

Delta Lake 4.4.1, a patch release on top of 4.4.0, was published on 5 October 2026. Its Delta Spark artifacts are built for Apache Spark 4.2.0, 4.1.0 and 4.0.1, with Scala 2.13.[^release]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Delta Lake tables live on object storage in Parquet, and engines read the transaction log to find the current files. With catalog-managed tables, a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) takes part in each commit and is the source of truth for the latest versions.[^protocol] UniForm allows the same table to be read by Iceberg clients without copying the data.[^uniform]

## Engine support

The Delta Lake project lists connectors for Apache Spark (read and write), Trino (read and write), Apache Flink (write, preview), PrestoDB (read) and Apache Hive (read). The delta-rs library gives Rust code, with Python bindings, direct access to Delta tables.[^readme] [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) reads Delta tables through its delta extension.[^n1] Delta Spark also ships [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client and server artifacts.[^release]

## Limitations

Delta Lake's ACID guarantees depend on the storage system. The project requires atomic visibility of files, mutual exclusion so that only one writer can create a given log file, and consistent directory listing.[^readme] On Amazon S3, for example, writes from multiple clusters must be enabled explicitly by configuring a LogStore implementation (such as one backed by DynamoDB) that supplies the mutual exclusion S3 lacks.[^n2]

Delta Lake keeps backward compatibility, so newer versions read tables written by older versions, but forward compatibility can break: an older client may not read a table that uses newer protocol features.[^readme] UniForm has its own limits; for example, the documentation lists tables with deletion vectors as unsupported.[^uniform]

[^opensource]: [Open Sourcing Delta Lake](https://www.databricks.com/blog/2019/04/24/open-sourcing-delta-lake.html). *Databricks*, 2019-04-24. Retrieved 2026-11-22.
[^lf]: [The Delta Lake Project Turns to Linux Foundation to Become the Open Standard for Data Lakes](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/press-release/the-delta-lake-project-turns-to-linux-foundation-to-become-the-open-standard-for-data-lakes). *Linux Foundation*, 2019-10-16. Retrieved 2026-11-22.
[^release]: [Delta Lake 4.4.1](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/releases/tag/v4.4.1). *GitHub*, 2026-10-05. Retrieved 2026-11-22.
