# DuckDB

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">DuckDB Foundation and contributors; originally Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2019-06-27 (v0.1.0)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">2.0.1 (LTS)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-20</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">C++</Field>
  <Field name="type">In-process analytical SQL database</Field>
  <Field name="license">MIT License</Field>
  <Field name="website">[duckdb.org](https://duckdb.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/duckdb/duckdb](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the DuckDB release calendar, the v2.0.1 GitHub release and the DuckDB 2.0 documentation</Verified>

**DuckDB** is an open source, in-process SQL database management system designed for analytical query workloads. It runs embedded inside a host application instead of as a separate server process, and it uses a columnar, vectorized query engine.[^why] Through extensions, DuckDB reads [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) files and [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), which makes it a single-node engine for an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse).[^ext]

## History

DuckDB was created by Mark Raasveldt and Hannes Mühleisen at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.[^faq]

The first tagged release, v0.1.0, was published on GitHub on 27 June 2019.[^n1] Version 1.0.0 was released on 3 June 2024.[^n2] Version 2.0.0 was released on 21 October 2026 as a long-term support (LTS) release, followed by 2.0.1 on 20 November 2026.[^calendar]

The DuckDB Foundation is a non-profit organization that holds the intellectual property of the project, and its statutes keep DuckDB open source under the MIT License. DuckLabs, a company based in Amsterdam co-founded by Raasveldt and Mühleisen, provides commercial support and employs the core contributors.[^faq]

DuckLabs joined Amazon Web Services (AWS) in September 2026. According to the project FAQ, the intellectual property of DuckDB remained with the DuckDB Foundation and the project continues as open source.[^faq]

## Design

DuckDB runs embedded in the process of the application that uses it, by default without a separate database server. It has no external dependencies at build time or at run time; building it needs only a C++17 compiler.[^why]

DuckDB targets online analytical processing (OLAP): long-running queries that read large parts of a dataset, such as aggregations and joins across several tables. Its execution engine is columnar and vectorized, so it processes batches of values instead of one row at a time, which lowers the overhead per value.[^why]

DuckDB compiles for Linux, macOS and Windows on x86 and ARM processors, and it can run in a web browser through DuckDB-Wasm.[^why]

## Releases and support

Starting with version 1.4.0, every other DuckDB release is an LTS release, which receives community support for about one year. Version 2.0.0 is an LTS release with an end-of-life date of 22 October 2027. The release calendar lists version 2.1.0 as planned for the first half of 2027, with tentative dates.[^calendar]

## Extensions

DuckDB adds features through extensions. The core extensions maintained by the DuckDB team include:[^ext]
- `parquet`, to read and write Parquet files.
- `httpfs`, to read and write files over HTTP(S) and Amazon S3.
- `iceberg`, for the Apache Iceberg table format.
- `delta`, for the Delta Lake format.
- `ducklake`, for the DuckLake format.
- `unity_catalog`, for [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) connectivity.
- `glue`, for AWS Glue Data Catalog connectivity (marked experimental).

The DuckDB documentation classifies the `parquet` and `httpfs` extensions as primary, with community support, and the lakehouse format extensions as secondary, supported on a best-effort basis.[^ext]

## Use with Apache Iceberg

The DuckDB `iceberg` extension reads Iceberg tables in two ways. It can read a single table directly from storage by pointing at the table metadata, which needs no catalog and is read-only. It can also attach an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), which unlocks the full feature set, including writes.[^iceberg]

A REST catalog is attached with a secret that holds the OAuth client credentials and an `ATTACH` statement:[^iceberg]

```sql
CREATE SECRET iceberg_secret (
    TYPE iceberg,
    CLIENT_ID 'admin',
    CLIENT_SECRET 'password',
    OAUTH2_SERVER_URI 'https://catalog.example.com/v1/oauth/tokens'
);

ATTACH 'warehouse' AS my_catalog (
    TYPE iceberg,
    SECRET iceberg_secret,
    URI 'https://catalog.example.com'
);
```

The DuckDB documentation gives setup instructions for several catalogs, including Amazon S3 Tables, AWS Glue, Cloudflare R2 Data Catalog, [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), Lakekeeper, SeaweedFS and Google Cloud BigLake. The Polaris example sets `ACCESS_DELEGATION_MODE 'vended_credentials'`.[^n3]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), DuckDB is an engine that reads the same tables as distributed engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), through a shared catalog. The Unity Catalog documentation, for example, shows DuckDB attaching a Unity Catalog catalog with the `unity_catalog` and `delta` extensions, querying and appending to its Delta tables, and creating catalog-managed tables.[^n4]

## See also

- [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)
- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)
- [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)
- [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino)
- [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)

# Exactly-once semantics

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Exactly-once processing, exactly-once delivery, effectively-once</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), distributed systems</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Replayable source, checkpointed progress and state, idempotent or transactional sink</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), Kafka transactions and Kafka Streams ([Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka)), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming guides, the Apache Flink 2.3 documentation, the Apache Kafka 4.4 design and Streams documentation, the Delta Lake streaming documentation and the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Flink documentation</Verified>

In [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), **exactly-once semantics** is the guarantee that each input record affects the result exactly once, with nothing lost and nothing duplicated, even when parts of the system fail and work is retried. Engines usually achieve it by replaying input after a failure and making sure the replay does not change the result twice, not by literally processing each record once. For this reason the guarantee is sometimes called **effectively-once**.

## Delivery guarantees

The Apache Kafka documentation defines three levels of guarantee:[^kafka-design]

| Guarantee | Definition | Typical cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At-most-once | Messages may be lost but are never redelivered | No retry after a failure |
| At-least-once | Messages are never lost but may be redelivered | Retry or replay without deduplication |
| Exactly-once | Each message is processed once and only once | Replay combined with idempotent or transactional output |

Apache Flink describes the same three outcomes for recovery: no effort to recover (at most once), nothing lost but possible duplicates (at least once), and nothing lost or duplicated (exactly once).[^flink-ft]

## What it means and what it does not

Two guarantees are often confused, and the Spark Real-time Mode documentation separates them explicitly:[^ss-rtm]

- **Exactly-once processing** (or exactly-once state): each input record's effect on the state the engine manages, such as an aggregation count, is applied effectively once across failures and restarts. Flink states its guarantee in the same terms: every event affects the state managed by Flink exactly once.[^flink-ft]
- **End-to-end exactly-once** (or exactly-once delivery): each record affects the external system, such as a table or topic, exactly once. This is a property of the sink as well as the engine.[^ss-rtm]

Exactly-once does not mean that user code runs once per record. After a failure, an engine re-runs the work since the last checkpoint, so functions, API calls and log lines in that work can run again. Only effects that pass through a sink with the right guarantees are deduplicated.

## The end-to-end requirement

Engine documentation converges on three conditions:

1. **A replayable source.** After a failure the engine must be able to read the same data again from a recorded position, such as a Kafka offset. Spark assumes every source has offsets for this purpose; Flink requires that the source can rewind to the position stored in the checkpoint.[^ss-start][^flink-conn]
1. **Recorded progress and deterministic processing.** The engine records what it has read, and its state, in a checkpoint, so a replay starts from a consistent point. If processing is not deterministic, a replay can produce different output from the first attempt.
1. **An idempotent or transactional sink.** Writing the same output twice must have the same effect as writing it once (idempotent), or output must become visible atomically together with the recorded progress (transactional). Flink states that the sink must commit transactionally or write idempotently.[^flink-conn][^flink-ft]

## Implementations

### Spark Structured Streaming

<Hatnote>Main article: [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Hatnote>

Structured Streaming uses checkpointing and write-ahead logs to record the offset range processed in each trigger, and its built-in sinks are designed to be idempotent so that reprocessing is safe. The Spark documentation states that replayable sources and idempotent sinks together give end-to-end exactly-once semantics under any failure.[^ss-start]

The guarantee depends on the sink. In the Spark 4.3 documentation the file sink is exactly-once, while the Kafka sink and `foreach` sink are at-least-once, and for `foreachBatch` it "depends on the implementation".[^ss-apis] Real-time Mode keeps exactly-once processing, but because it commits offsets at the end of each batch, after records have reached the sink, a failure can re-write records; it does not yet ship an exactly-once sink.[^ss-rtm]

`foreachBatch` gives only at-least-once writes by default. The Spark guide recommends using the `batchId` passed to the function to deduplicate output and get exactly-once.[^ss-apis] [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) supports this directly: with the `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` writer options, Delta identifies a repeated write of the same batch and ignores it.[^delta-stream]

```python
APP_ID = "orders-to-silver"   # unique per streaming query

def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    (batch_df.write.format("delta")
        .option("txnAppId", APP_ID)
        .option("txnVersion", batch_id)   # a replayed batch is skipped
        .mode("append")
        .save("/data/silver/orders"))

(orders.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(write_batch)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/data/_checkpoints/orders-to-silver")
    .start())
```

If the checkpoint is deleted and the query restarts with a new one, batch IDs start again from 0, so the application ID must change; otherwise Delta ignores the new writes as duplicates.[^delta-stream]

### Kafka transactions and Kafka Streams

Since Kafka 0.11.0.0, the producer supports an idempotent mode that prevents duplicate log entries when a send is retried, and transactions that write to several topic partitions atomically. Consumers with the `read_committed` isolation level only see messages from committed transactions.[^kafka-design] Kafka Streams uses these features: with `processing.guarantee` set to `exactly_once_v2` (the default is `at_least_once`), it commits input offsets, state store updates and output records atomically. Exactly-once v2 requires brokers at version 2.5.0 or newer.[^kstreams]

The Kafka documentation notes that exactly-once delivery to other destination systems generally requires the cooperation of those systems; one approach is to store the consumer's offset in the same place as its output.[^kafka-design]

### Flink two-phase commit sinks

Flink takes consistent snapshots of operator state with checkpoint barriers, a variant of the Chandy-Lamport algorithm.[^flink-ft] For external sinks, Flink 1.4.0 introduced `TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction`: a sink pre-commits an external transaction when a checkpoint starts and commits it only after the checkpoint completes.[^flink-blog] Current sinks expose a `DeliveryGuarantee` of `NONE`, `AT_LEAST_ONCE` or `EXACTLY_ONCE`.[^flink-conn] With `EXACTLY_ONCE`, the Kafka sink writes records in a Kafka transaction committed on each checkpoint, so output becomes visible only after a checkpoint, and the Kafka transaction timeout must exceed the checkpoint and restart time to avoid data loss.[^flink-kafka]

## Why table formats make good sinks

[Open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) commit each write as a single atomic change to table metadata, which is the transactional sink the end-to-end requirement asks for. A streaming engine can tie each commit to its own checkpoint, so a replayed batch either is detected as already committed or replaces an uncommitted attempt. Delta Lake states that its transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch jobs write to the same table concurrently.[^delta-stream] The [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) Flink sink guarantees exactly-once semantics, committing to the Iceberg table after each successful Flink checkpoint.[^iceberg-flink] [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) lists exactly-once ingestion of new events from Kafka as a capability of its Hudi Streamer tool.[^hudi-streamer] This is one reason the [streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse) pattern writes streams directly into tables.

## Where it breaks

- **External side effects.** Calls to APIs, emails or writes to systems outside the sink run again on replay. Only the sink's effects are protected.
- **Non-idempotent `foreachBatch` code.** A function that appends to a table or calls a service without using `batchId` produces duplicates when a batch is retried.[^ss-apis]
- **At-least-once sinks.** The Spark Kafka sink and `foreach` sink are at-least-once, so downstream readers must tolerate or remove duplicates.[^ss-apis]
- **Non-replayable sources.** The Spark socket source, for example, does not provide end-to-end fault-tolerance guarantees and is meant only for testing.[^ss-apis]
- **Lost or reset checkpoints.** The checkpoint holds the recorded progress. Deleting it or reusing identifiers incorrectly breaks deduplication, as the Delta `txnAppId` rule shows.[^delta-stream]
- **Consumers outside the transaction.** Exactly-once through Kafka transactions holds for consumers that read only committed messages (the `read_committed` isolation level); the Flink Kafka sink documentation states the same condition.[^kafka-design][^flink-kafka]

# Executor

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark executor</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Task slots (cores), execution memory, storage memory, local disk for shuffle files</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/cluster-overview.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/tuning.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, docs/running-on-kubernetes.md), the Trino 484 concepts page and the Apache Flink 2.3 architecture page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), an **executor** is a process launched for one application on a worker node; it runs the application's tasks and keeps data in memory or on disk between them.[^cluster] The driver plans the work and the executors do it. The same word appears in other engines with a different meaning, so this page also compares the Spark executor with a [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) worker, an [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) TaskManager and a Kubernetes pod.

## What an executor runs

A Spark executor runs **tasks**. A task is the unit of work that the driver sends to one executor, and each task processes one [partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition) of a dataset.[^cluster][^rddguide] Spark divides each job into stages, and every task in a stage applies the same function to a different partition.[^dag]

An executor runs several tasks at the same time, each in its own thread inside the executor process.[^cluster] Besides running tasks, the executor stores cached data and writes the shuffle files that later stages read; it also serves those files to other executors unless an external shuffle service does that work.[^jobsched]

## Cores and task slots

The number of tasks an executor can run at once is set by its cores. `spark.executor.cores` sets the cores per executor; its default is 1 on YARN and all available cores of the worker in standalone mode. `spark.task.cpus` (default 1) sets the cores each task needs, and the number of concurrent tasks on an executor is `floor(executor cores / spark.task.cpus)`.[^config] These concurrent places for tasks are often called task slots.

A stage with more partitions than free slots runs in waves: when a task finishes, the slot takes the next pending task. If a task fails, Spark retries it; `spark.task.maxFailures` (default 4) is the number of consecutive failures of one task before the job fails.[^config]

## Memory

Each executor is a JVM process. `spark.executor.memory` (default `1g`) sets its heap. On YARN and Kubernetes, Spark also requests non-heap overhead memory, `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, which by default is the executor memory multiplied by `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor` (0.10), with a minimum of 384 MiB. The container size is the sum of executor memory, overhead, off-heap memory and PySpark memory.[^config]

Inside the heap, Spark uses a unified memory region for two purposes. **Execution memory** holds data for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations; **storage memory** holds cached data. `spark.memory.fraction` (default 0.6) sets the size of this region as a fraction of the heap minus 300 MiB, and the rest is left for user data structures and Spark metadata. Execution can evict cached blocks, but only down to the share set by `spark.memory.storageFraction` (default 0.5).[^tuning] When execution data does not fit, Spark spills it to local disk.[^rddguide]

## Lifetime and relation to the driver

Each Spark application gets its own executors. Without dynamic allocation they stay up for the whole application, and tasks from different applications never share a JVM. Two applications therefore cannot share in-memory data except through external storage.[^cluster] The driver must stay reachable from the executors for its whole lifetime, and executors send heartbeats to it, by default every 10 seconds, so that it knows they are alive.[^cluster][^config]

## Dynamic allocation

With dynamic resource allocation, Spark adds executors when tasks are waiting and removes executors that are idle. It is off by default (`spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled`) and works on standalone, YARN and Kubernetes.[^jobsched] Spark requests executors in rounds that grow exponentially (1, 2, 4, 8 and so on), and removes an executor after it has been idle for `spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout` (default 60 seconds). Executors that hold cached data are kept by default, because `spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout` defaults to infinity.[^jobsched][^config]

Removing an executor would lose the shuffle files it wrote. Dynamic allocation therefore needs one way to keep them: an external shuffle service, shuffle tracking (`spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled`, default true), shuffle block migration during decommissioning, or a shuffle storage plugin. Spark on Kubernetes does not support the external shuffle service.[^jobsched][^config]

## Spark executor compared with similar terms

|  | Spark executor | Trino worker | Flink TaskManager | Kubernetes pod running an executor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A process started for one Spark application[^cluster] | A server in a Trino cluster that runs tasks and processes data[^trino] | A JVM process that runs the subtasks of a dataflow and buffers and exchanges data streams[^flink] | A Kubernetes pod that contains one executor container[^k8s] |
| Coordinated by | The application's driver | The coordinator, which parses and plans queries[^trino] | The JobManager[^flink] | The Spark driver, through the Kubernetes API[^k8s] |
| Unit of concurrency | Task slots (executor cores divided by task CPUs) | Tasks, which run drivers over splits[^trino] | Task slots; each slot is a fixed share of managed memory, with no CPU isolation[^flink] | Same as the executor inside it; the pod CPU request does not change task concurrency[^k8s] |
| Shared between applications or queries? | No; only the jobs of one application use it | Yes; workers are servers of the cluster, and each query may use up to `query.max-memory-per-node` of user memory on a worker[^trino][^n1] | In a session cluster, jobs share the cluster; in an application cluster, only one application's jobs run[^flink] | No; the pod ends when the executor ends |
| Lifetime | The application, or shorter with dynamic allocation | The Trino cluster | The Flink cluster (session) or the application (application cluster)[^flink] | The executor; pods are cleaned up when the application completes[^k8s] |

A Flink task slot and a Spark task slot are close but not the same. A Flink slot reserves a fixed share of a TaskManager's managed memory, and by default subtasks of the same job can share a slot.[^flink] A Spark slot is a share of an executor's cores; all tasks on an executor draw on one unified memory pool.[^tuning]

On Kubernetes, the pod and the executor are two layers. The pod's memory request and limit are the sum of `spark.executor.memory` and `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, and `spark.kubernetes.executor.request.cores` can set the pod's CPU request apart from `spark.executor.cores`.[^k8s] Shuffle and spill files go to `emptyDir` volumes by default, which do not outlive the pod.[^k8s]

## Example

A configuration for executors with four task slots each, scaled by dynamic allocation:

```
spark.executor.cores                             4
spark.executor.memory                            8g
spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled                  true
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled  true
spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors             1
spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors             20
```

# GraphFrames

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">GraphFrames community (originally UC Berkeley, MIT and Databricks)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2016</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">0.12.3</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-05</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Graph processing library for Apache Spark (DataFrame-based)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[graphframes.io](https://graphframes.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/graphframes/graphframes](https://github.com/graphframes/graphframes)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the graphframes/graphframes repository at tag v0.12.3, the GitHub releases API (latest release v0.12.3) and graphframes.io</Verified>

<Status level="active">Latest release 0.12.3, published 5 October 2026.[^rel]</Status>

**GraphFrames** is an open source graph processing package for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) that represents a graph as a pair of Spark DataFrames, one of vertices and one of edges, and provides graph algorithms, the Pregel and AggregateMessages APIs, and a motif-finding query language on top of them.[^readme] It has APIs in Scala, Java and Python, and it is developed outside the Apache Spark project. When the Spark community voted in 2024 to deprecate Spark's RDD-based [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX) library, the vote result named GraphFrames as a migration target.[^vote]

## Data model

A GraphFrame is built from two DataFrames. The vertex DataFrame must have a column named `id` with a unique ID for each vertex. The edge DataFrame must have columns named `src` and `dst` with the source and destination vertex IDs. Both can have any other columns, which act as vertex and edge attributes. A GraphFrame can also be built from an edge DataFrame alone, in which case the vertices are inferred from the edges.[^create]

Because a GraphFrame is made of DataFrames, graph queries are planned by Spark's Catalyst optimizer and Adaptive Query Execution, and graph results can be joined, filtered and written like any other DataFrame.[^about]

## Relation to GraphX

<Hatnote>Main article: [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX)</Hatnote>

The GraphFrames documentation describes the project as aiming to provide the functionality of GraphX plus features that take advantage of DataFrames, such as motif finding and DataFrame-based serialization.[^about] The two libraries differ in representation and optimization:[^about]

|  | GraphX | GraphFrames |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Graph representation | `VertexRDD` and `EdgeRDD` | `vertices` and `edges` DataFrames |
| Optimization | Its own partitioning strategy and partition index | Catalyst optimizer and Adaptive Query Execution |
| Languages | Scala (Spark guide) | Scala, Java, Python |
| Part of Apache Spark | Yes | No (separate project) |

GraphFrames provides most algorithms either as a native DataFrame implementation or as a wrapper over GraphX. Its own benchmarks show GraphX can still be the better choice for small and medium graphs, so the library keeps conversion methods between the two.[^about] Since release 0.10.0, GraphFrames ships its own internal fork of GraphX (package `org.apache.spark.graphframes.graphx`, Maven artifact `graphframes-graphx`) instead of using the GraphX in Spark. The project treats the fork as internal API.[^about][^install][^quick]

The GraphFrames documentation states that GraphX is deprecated upstream and no longer maintained. Apache Spark itself had not marked GraphX deprecated as of Spark 4.3.0; see [GraphX#Status](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX#status).[^about]

## Motif finding

Motif finding searches a graph for structural patterns. GraphFrames expresses patterns in a small domain-specific language passed to `find`: `(a)-[e]->(b)` is an edge `e` from vertex `a` to vertex `b`, and patterns are joined with semicolons. The result is a DataFrame with one struct column per named vertex or edge.[^motif]

The language supports anonymous elements (`(a)-[]->(b)`), negated edges (`!(b)-[]->(a)`), undirected patterns (`(a)-[e]-(b)`), fixed-length paths (`(a)-[e*2]->(c)`) and bounded variable-length paths (`(a)-[e*1..3]->(c)`). Unbounded paths are not supported. Conditions on vertex or edge attributes are applied as DataFrame filters on the result. Motif finding is translated into a series of joins, and the documentation suggests enabling Spark's cost-based optimizer and join reordering to improve it.[^motif]

## Algorithms

The user guide covers centrality metrics, traversals and connectivity, community detection, subgraphs, message passing, Pregel, labeled property graphs and graph machine learning.[^readme] Algorithms listed in the documentation include:[^quick][^readme]
- Traversal and connectivity: breadth-first search, shortest paths, all simple paths, connected components and strongly connected components.
- Ranking and structure: PageRank, parallel personalized PageRank, triangle count, K-Core, cycle detection (Rocha-Thatte) and maximal independent set.
- Community detection: label propagation and power iteration clustering.
- Embeddings: random-walk embeddings with Word2Vec or Hash2Vec.

The quick start marks which algorithms have a native GraphFrames implementation. PageRank, parallel personalized PageRank, strongly connected components and SVD++ run through GraphX in that table.[^quick]

## Example

The following PySpark example builds a small graph, prints in-degrees and uses motif finding to find pairs where one vertex calls the other a friend and is called an enemy back. It follows the project README and runs on Spark 4.x after `pip install graphframes-py==0.12.3` and starting PySpark with `--packages io.graphframes:graphframes-spark4_2.13:0.12.3`.[^readme][^install]

```python
from graphframes import GraphFrame

v = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Alice"), (2, "Bob"), (3, "Charlie")], ["id", "name"])
e = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, 2, "friend"), (2, 1, "friend"), (2, 3, "friend"), (3, 2, "enemy")],
    ["src", "dst", "relationship"],
)
g = GraphFrame(v, e)

g.inDegrees.show()

(g.find("(a)-[e]->(b); (b)-[e2]->(a)")
  .filter("e.relationship = 'friend' AND e2.relationship = 'enemy'")
  .show())
```

## Spark Connect

GraphFrames supports [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) through a server plugin. The Spark Connect server is started with the `graphframes-connect` package and the setting `spark.connect.extensions.relation.classes=org.apache.spark.sql.graphframes.GraphFramesConnect`. The only client bundled with the package is the PySpark client, which detects a Spark Connect session and uses the plugin automatically. The documentation warns that the plugin is not compatible with Databricks' managed Spark Connect without a vendor-specific build.[^install] Spark Connect and Spark 4.x support were first released in GraphFrames 0.9.0.[^n1]

## Releases and governance

GraphFrames is published to Maven Central under the `io.graphframes` namespace, with separate artifacts per Spark major version and Scala version (for example `graphframes-spark4_2.13`), and to PyPI as `graphframes-py`. The installation page lists support for Spark 3.x and 4.x.[^install] The latest release, v0.12.3 of 5 October 2026, fixes connected-components correctness issues.[^rel]

The project was created as a collaboration among UC Berkeley, MIT, Databricks and the open source community, and is now maintained by a group of individual contributors. It is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 and is not an Apache Software Foundation project.[^readme] The project's blog post for release 0.9.2 describes a revival in 2025, after a long gap in development, prompted by the GraphX deprecation discussion in Spark; the same post announced the new Maven group ID, the new PyPI name and the graphframes.io site.[^n2] The design is described in the 2016 paper "GraphFrames: An Integrated API for Mixing Graph and Relational Queries" by Dave et al.[^n3]

# GraphX

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 0.9.0 (alpha); stable API since Spark 1.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala</Field>
  <Field name="type">Graph processing library (RDD-based)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[GraphX Programming Guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/graphx-programming-guide.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (graphx/)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/graphx)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (GraphX source and programming guide), the Spark 0.9.0, 1.2.0 and 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes, SPARK-50857 and the October 2024 dev-list vote</Verified>

<Status level="proposed">A dev-list vote to deprecate GraphX passed in October 2024, but the deprecation ticket (SPARK-50857) is still open and Spark 4.3.0 carries no deprecation annotation or notice for GraphX. The vote result described GraphX as not currently maintained and suggested [GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames) as a migration target.[^jira50857]</Status>

**GraphX** is the graph processing library of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark): it extends Spark's resilient distributed dataset (RDD) with a property graph, a directed multigraph with user-defined properties on each vertex and edge, and provides graph operators, a Pregel API and a library of graph algorithms.[^guide] GraphX still ships with Spark 4.3.0, but a 2024 proposal on the Spark dev mailing list noted no meaningful active development in the preceding three years.[^discuss] The Spark community then voted to deprecate it, and as of Spark 4.3.0 that decision has not been applied to the code or documentation.[^vote][^jira50857]

## Status

Whether GraphX is deprecated depends on which source is read, and the sources do not agree.

- **Spark code and documentation (4.3.0):** The `graphx` module at the v4.3.0 tag has no `@deprecated` annotations on its public API, and the GraphX programming guide has no deprecation notice.[^guide] The Spark 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes list no GraphX deprecation; the 4.0.0 notes deprecate SparkR and other APIs, but not GraphX.[^r400]
- **Spark dev mailing list:** In September 2024 a thread on the Spark dev mailing list proposed deprecating GraphX before the 4.0 branch was cut, noting no meaningful active development for over three years.[^discuss] The vote that followed closed on 7 October 2024 and was declared passed, with two -1 votes. The result email proposed a documentation note saying that GraphX "is not currently maintained and if maintainers are not found may be removed in future minor versions", and recommended GraphFrames or openCypher on Spark as migration targets.[^vote]
- **JIRA:** SPARK-50857, "Mark GraphX as deprecated", was opened in January 2025 with a link to the vote. It is unresolved and has no fix version.[^jira50857]
- **GraphFrames documentation:** The GraphFrames project states that GraphX "is deprecated in the upstream Apache Spark and is not maintained anymore", and its quick start says GraphX was deprecated in Spark 4.0.x.[^gfabout][^gfquick] The GraphFrames blog links its statement that GraphX was deprecated to the dev-list discussion thread.[^n1] No Spark 4.x release includes a GraphX deprecation.

In short: the Spark community voted to deprecate GraphX and the vote result described it as unmaintained, but no Spark release up to 4.3.0 marks it deprecated. The GraphX module and its API are still part of Spark 4.3.0. Both the vote result and the GraphFrames project point new graph work to [GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames).

## History

GraphX first shipped as an alpha component in Spark 0.9.0, where the release notes recommended it over the older Bagel API.[^n2] In Spark 1.2.0 GraphX graduated from alpha and gained a stable API, with a guarantee that applications written against it would keep working in future Spark versions without code changes. The same release introduced the `aggregateMessages` API and deprecated `mapReduceTriplets`.[^n3]

## Programming model

A GraphX graph is a pair of distributed collections: a `VertexRDD` of vertex IDs and properties and an `EdgeRDD` of edges with properties. Like RDDs, graphs are immutable, distributed and fault tolerant; operators return new graphs.[^guide]

The guide groups the API into:[^guide]
- **Property and structural operators**, such as `mapVertices`, `reverse`, `subgraph` and `mask`.
- **Join operators**, such as `joinVertices` and `outerJoinVertices`, that bring RDD data into a graph.
- **Neighborhood aggregation** through `aggregateMessages`, which sends messages along edges and merges them at each vertex.
- **Pregel**, a bulk-synchronous, vertex-centric API for iterative algorithms. The guide recommends it for iterative computation because it unpersists intermediate results correctly.
- **Graph builders**, such as `GraphLoader.edgeListFile`, `Graph.apply` and `Graph.fromEdges`.

The algorithm library at the v4.3.0 tag contains PageRank, connected components, strongly connected components, label propagation, shortest paths, triangle count and SVD++.[^n4]

The following Scala example runs in the Spark 4.3 shell in classic mode, where `sc` is the `SparkContext`. It builds a three-vertex graph and runs dynamic PageRank until the ranks change by less than the tolerance.

```scala
import org.apache.spark.graphx.{Edge, Graph}

val users = sc.parallelize(Seq((1L, "alice"), (2L, "bob"), (3L, "carol")))
val follows = sc.parallelize(Seq(
  Edge(1L, 2L, "follows"), Edge(2L, 3L, "follows"), Edge(3L, 1L, "follows")))

val graph = Graph(users, follows)
val ranks = graph.pageRank(0.0001).vertices

ranks.join(users).collect().foreach { case (_, (rank, name)) =>
  println(f"$name%s: $rank%.3f")
}
```

## Limitations

GraphX is built on RDDs and the `SparkContext`.[^guide] The Spark Connect documentation lists `SparkContext` and RDD as unsupported in Spark Connect for both Python and Scala, so GraphX programs need a classic Spark application rather than a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client.[^n5] Because GraphX works on RDDs, it does not use the Catalyst optimizer that plans DataFrame queries; the GraphFrames project cites this, and the memory cost of serializing JVM objects in RDDs, as reasons for its DataFrame-based design.[^gfabout]

## Alternatives

<Hatnote>Main article: [GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames)</Hatnote>

[GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames) is a separate open source package that represents a graph as two Spark DataFrames (vertices and edges). It adds motif finding and runs through the DataFrame engine. It provides conversion to and from GraphX, and from version 0.10.0 it ships its own internal fork of GraphX for the algorithms that it does not yet implement natively.[^gfquick] The October 2024 vote result also named openCypher on Spark as a possible target.[^vote]

# Hive Metastore

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">HMS, Hive metastore service</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data management, table catalogs</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Thrift API service, relational database for metadata, warehouse directory, optional Iceberg REST catalog endpoint</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive) (standalone metastore); clients in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Hive downloads page (releases to 4.2.1), MetastoreConf.java and HiveConf.java at rel/release-4.2.1, the standalone-metastore module at that tag, HIVE-28059 and HIVE-29062, HiveUtils.scala and docs/sql-data-sources-hive-tables.md at the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark, CatalogUtil.java at apache-iceberg-1.12.0 and the Trino 484 metastore documentation</Verified>

<Status level="active">No Hive release deprecates the metastore. Hive 4.1.0 ships it as a standalone component and adds an Iceberg REST catalog endpoint to it; the older Hive 1.x, 2.x and 3.x release lines are end of life.[^downloads]</Status>

The **Hive Metastore** (HMS) is the metadata service of [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive): it stores the names, schemas, partitions and storage locations of tables in a relational database and serves them to engines through a Thrift API.[^hivehome] Engines other than Hive, such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Impala and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), use the same service, which made it the shared table catalog of the Hadoop-era data lake. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse) the Hive Metastore is one of several [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) options, next to catalogs that implement the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) API.

## What the Hive Metastore stores

The Hive Metastore keeps metadata, not data. For each table it records the database (namespace), columns and types, partition values, the storage location of each partition and the file format and SerDe used to read it. The Hive project describes it as the central store of metadata for tables and partitions, reached through the metastore service API by clients that include Hive, Impala and Spark.[^hivehome]

The metadata lives in a relational database accessed through JDO. In Hive 4.2.1 the default connection URL is an embedded Apache Derby database (`jdbc:derby:;databaseName=metastore_db;create=true`), which suits tests; production deployments point it at a server database. The default warehouse directory for managed tables is `/user/hive/warehouse`, and the Thrift service listens on port 9083 by default.[^mconf]

## How engines use it

Each engine connects to the Hive Metastore with its own client and its own idea of what a table is.

- **[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)** uses the Hive Metastore as its persistent catalog when Hive support is enabled. Spark 4.3.0 bundles a Hive 2.3.10 client and can talk to metastores of versions 2.0.0 to 2.3.10, 3.0.0 to 3.1.3 and 4.0.0 to 4.1.0, set with `spark.sql.hive.metastore.version` and `spark.sql.hive.metastore.jars`.[^sparkhive][^n1]
- **[Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino)** uses a Thrift metastore (`hive.metastore=thrift`, the default) for its Hive, Delta Lake and Hudi connectors, configured with `hive.metastore.uri`, and offers `hive_metastore` as one Iceberg catalog type.[^trino]
- **[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)** ships a `HiveCatalog` (catalog type `hive`). It stores a pointer to the table's current metadata file in the metastore and uses the metastore to make commits atomic.[^icebergcat]

## Hive Metastore and the Iceberg REST catalog

The Hive Metastore and REST catalogs are often presented as old and new, but since Hive 4.1.0 the metastore can be both. HIVE-28059 added an Iceberg REST catalog to the metastore in 4.1.0, and HIVE-28658 added a REST catalog client in 4.2.0.[^hive28059][^n2] In Hive 4.2.1 the endpoint is a servlet that is off by default (`metastore.catalog.servlet.port` is -1), serves the path `iceberg`, and uses JWT authentication unless `metastore.catalog.servlet.auth` selects none, simple or OAuth 2.[^mconf]

|  | Hive Metastore (Thrift API) | Iceberg REST catalog |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protocol | Thrift RPC, port 9083 by default[^mconf] | HTTP and JSON, defined by an OpenAPI specification[^restspec] |
| Table formats | Hive tables in any supported file format; Iceberg tables through a metadata pointer | Iceberg tables and views |
| Commit model | Coordinated by each client; Iceberg's `HiveCatalog`, for example, takes a metastore lock around each commit[^n3] | The client sends updates with requirements; the server checks the requirements and applies the commit, or rejects it with a conflict[^restspec] |
| Client coupling | Clients must match a supported metastore version (for example Spark's version list)[^sparkhive] | Any client that speaks the REST specification |
| Example implementations | Hive standalone metastore | [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Project Nessie](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Nessie), the Hive Metastore REST endpoint[^hive28059] |

## Standalone metastore

The metastore code was moved into its own `standalone-metastore` module during Hive 3.0 work, so that it can run without the rest of Hive.[^n4] At the rel/release-4.2.1 tag that module contains separate client, common, server, tools and REST catalog submodules.[^n5] Hive 4.1.0 was the first release to provide the metastore as a standalone component in binary and Docker image form (HIVE-29062).[^downloads][^n6]

## Status

The Hive Metastore is not deprecated in any Hive release, and Hive 4.2.1, released on 24 August 2026, fixed security issues in it.[^downloads] What has ended is support for old release lines: the Hive community declared the 1.x line end of life in April 2024, the 2.x line in May 2024 and the 3.x line in October 2024.[^downloads]

This matters for Spark users. The Hive client bundled with Spark 4.3.0 is version 2.3.10, from a line that is end of life; a Spark application that connects to a Hive 4 metastore must load matching client jars through `spark.sql.hive.metastore.jars`.[^sparkhive]

## Limitations

- **Hive-shaped model.** The metastore models tables as directories of files with partitions. Table formats such as Iceberg keep their real metadata in their own files and use the metastore only for a pointer.[^icebergcat]
- **Version coupling.** Thrift clients must be compatible with the server version, which is why Spark lists the metastore versions it supports.[^sparkhive]
- **Governance.** The metastore records metadata; authorization is left to other projects. The Hive project names Apache Ranger for authorization and Apache Atlas for lineage.[^hivehome]

# Hive on Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_on_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark execution engine for Hive, `hive.execution.engine=spark`</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query execution</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Hive 1.1.0 (2015)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Hive compiler and metastore, Spark as the execution engine, the `spark-client` module</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive) 1.1 to 3.1</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive), [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Thrift Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Thrift_Server)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">HIVE-7292, HIVE-26134 and HIVE-23885, HiveConf.java, pom.xml and the ql and spark-client modules at the rel/release-3.1.3, 4.0.0-alpha-1, 4.0.0-alpha-2 and 4.0.0 tags of apache/hive, the Apache Hive downloads page, the Hive on Spark getting started page and the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (Hive tables and distributed SQL engine docs)</Verified>

<Status level="removed">Removed in Apache Hive 4.0.0 (first in 4.0.0-alpha-2). Use Apache Tez as the Hive engine, or Spark SQL with Hive support instead. Hive never marked the engine deprecated first; HIVE-26134 removed it from the main branch in April 2022. The last Hive line that had it, 3.x, was declared end of life in October 2024.[^hive26134]</Status>

**Hive on Spark** was an execution engine option in [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive) that ran HiveQL queries as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) jobs instead of MapReduce or Apache Tez jobs; users turned it on with `set hive.execution.engine=spark;`.[^gs] It was a Hive project feature: Hive kept its own parser, optimizer and [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), and used Spark only to run the work. It first shipped in Hive 1.1.0 and was removed in Hive 4.0, so it is unavailable in every maintained Hive release.[^hive7292][^hive26134]

## Status

Hive on Spark was removed without a deprecation release in between.

- **Removed from Hive's main branch in April 2022.** HIVE-26134, "Remove Hive on Spark from the main branch", was resolved on 26 April 2022. Its description links a dev-list discussion and says there was no activity on keeping the feature up to date, and that removing it would help ongoing development and make testing cheaper.[^hive26134] In that thread, a reply from February 2022 says the last development was around October 2018 and calls the code dead weight.[^thread]
- **First releases without it.** The `spark-client` module and the Spark execution package (`ql/.../exec/spark`) are present at the Hive 4.0.0-alpha-1 tag, which was cut before the removal, and absent from 4.0.0-alpha-2 (released 16 November 2022) and 4.0.0 (released 29 March 2024).[^downloads][^tree400] In Hive 4.0.0, `hive.execution.engine` accepts only `mr` and `tez`; in Hive 3.1.3 it also accepted `spark`.[^conf400][^conf313]
- **No maintained release has it.** The Hive community declared the 2.x line end of life in May 2024 and the 3.x line end of life in October 2024, which leaves only the 4.x line, where the engine does not exist.[^downloads]

An earlier ticket, HIVE-23885 "Remove Hive on Spark", was opened in July 2020 and closed as a duplicate.[^n1]

## History

HIVE-7292, the umbrella ticket for Hive on Spark, was opened in June 2014. It gave three reasons: many Hive users already ran Spark and could drop MapReduce or Tez from their clusters; the option would bring Spark users to Hive; and queries with several reduce stages would run faster.[^hive7292] The feature shipped in Hive 1.1.0, released on 8 March 2015.[^hive7292][^downloads]

Each Hive line was tested against one Spark version. The getting started page lists Spark 1.2.0 for Hive 1.1.x, Spark 2.0.0 for Hive 2.3.x and Spark 2.3.0 for Hive 3.0.x, and the Hive 3.1.3 build file still sets `spark.version` to 2.3.0.[^gs][^n2] No Hive release lists support for Spark 3 or later.

## How it worked

Hive compiled a HiveQL query into a plan of map and reduce work, as it did for its other engines, and with the Spark engine submitted that plan to a Spark application through its `spark-client` module. The getting started page required a Spark build that does not include the Hive jars, and it recommends building Spark with the `parquet-provided` profile (and `orc-provided` for Spark 2.3.0 and later) to avoid dependency conflicts.[^gs]

```sql
-- Hive 3.1.x and earlier only; Hive 4 rejects this value
set hive.execution.engine=spark;
SELECT country, count(*) FROM page_views GROUP BY country;
```

## What Hive on Spark is not

Several Spark and Hive combinations have similar names. Only the first row below is Hive on Spark.

| Name | Which project runs the SQL | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hive on Spark** (`hive.execution.engine=spark`) | Hive parses and plans; Spark executes | Removed in Hive 4.0[^hive26134] |
| **Shark** | A Spark-based project that replaced Hive's execution engine with Spark | Development ended in July 2014 in favor of Spark SQL[^shark] |
| **Spark SQL with Hive support** (`enableHiveSupport()`) | Spark parses, plans and executes; Hive supplies the metastore and SerDes | Active in Spark 4.3.0[^sparkhive] |
| **[Spark Thrift Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Thrift_Server)** | Spark SQL, behind a JDBC/ODBC server that corresponds to HiveServer2 | Active in Spark 4.3.0[^sts] |

The 2014 post that ended Shark described Hive on Spark as a separate Hive community effort, aimed at organizations with existing Hive investments that wanted to run them on Spark, while Spark SQL became the main path for SQL on Spark.[^shark] In Spark 4.3.0, Hive support means reading and writing Hive tables through a Hive metastore; Spark 4.3.0 bundles a Hive 2.3.10 client and can connect to metastores from 2.0.0 to 4.1.0.[^sparkhive]

## Replacements

A Hive deployment that used the Spark engine has two paths. It can stay on Hive and move to Hive 4 with Tez, the engine that Hive 4.1 and later use by default (see [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive)). Or it can move the SQL to Spark itself: Spark SQL reads the same tables through the [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), and the Spark Thrift Server gives JDBC and ODBC clients a HiveServer2-compatible endpoint.[^sparkhive][^sts] Queries need checking on either path, because HiveQL behavior and Spark SQL behavior differ.

# Iceberg File Format API

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_File_Format_API

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">FormatModel API; pluggable file formats in Iceberg</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats, data file input and output</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Iceberg 1.11.0 (May 2026)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`FormatModel`, `FormatModelRegistry`, read and write builders, compatibility test kit</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) Java library (Parquet, ORC, Avro; Spark, Flink, Arrow and generic object models)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache ORC](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_ORC), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">Apache Iceberg source at tags apache-iceberg-1.10.0, 1.11.0 and 1.12.0, the 1.11.0 and 1.12.0 release notes, the File Format API announcement post, GitHub issue apache/iceberg#12225 and its pull requests, and the dev@iceberg.apache.org discussion and vote threads</Verified>

The **Iceberg File Format API** is a set of Java interfaces in [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) that puts every data file format behind one common reader and writer contract, so that engines read and write Iceberg data files through a registry instead of format-specific code. A format supplies a `FormatModel`, which pairs a file format with an in-memory object model (for example Spark rows or Flink rows) and builds readers and writers for it; the `FormatModelRegistry` stores the available models.[^blog] The API shipped in Iceberg 1.11.0 with implementations for Parquet, ORC and Avro.[^pr15254][^releases] Support for additional formats, such as Vortex and Lance, is discussed and prototyped but is not part of any release.

## Status

The File Format API is a released part of the Iceberg Java library, not a change to the Iceberg table specification.

- **Shipped.** The 1.11.0 release notes, for the release of 19 May 2026, list the File Format API interfaces and the Parquet, ORC and Arrow format model implementations.[^releases] The `org.apache.iceberg.formats` package is absent at tag apache-iceberg-1.10.0 and present at 1.11.0 and 1.12.0.[^javadoc111] Iceberg 1.12.0, released on 29 September 2026, carries the same package.[^releases][^javadoc112]
- **Not shipped.** No new data file format has been added through the API. At 1.12.0 the Java `FileFormat` enumeration lists Puffin, ORC, Parquet, Avro and the metadata JSON file, and Appendix A of the table spec defines type mappings only for Avro, Parquet and ORC.[^fileformat][^icespec] A proof-of-concept pull request for Lance through the API was opened in March 2026 as a draft not intended for merge, and was closed.[^lance]
- **Documentation.** As of November 2026 the versioned Iceberg documentation has no page for the API; a pull request proposing one is open.[^docspr]

## Motivation

Before the API, Iceberg's Java code supported Parquet, Avro and ORC through format-specific readers and writers in each engine integration. The proposal issue states that new version 3 features, such as new column types and default values, need changes at the file format level, and that because these changes were made separately per format, not every feature was available for every format. It also names emerging formats, Vortex and Lance, as candidates for use cases such as fast random access.[^issue]

The announcement post describes the old code as fragmented: Spark, Flink and the generic Java implementation each kept their own format-specific readers, writers and feature handling, with large branching code paths, so that projection, filtering and delete file handling needed separate work for each format and engine pair.[^blog]

## How it works

A `FormatModel<D, S>` names the `FileFormat` it handles, the Java class of the rows it produces and consumes (`D`), and the class of the engine schema (`S`). It returns a `ReadBuilder` for an input file and a `ModelWriteBuilder` for an output file.[^javadoc112] Engines can define their own object models and register them, which lets custom in-memory representations use Iceberg's file format handling.[^javadoc112]

Engines then ask the registry for a builder by file format and row class, instead of branching on the format themselves.[^blog]

```java
// Builders obtained from the registry (method names as given in the announcement post)
FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, inputFile);
FormatModelRegistry.dataWriteBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, outputFile);
FormatModelRegistry.equalityDeleteWriteBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, outputFile);
FormatModelRegistry.positionDeleteWriteBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, outputFile);
```

At 1.12.0 the Iceberg source tree contains format models for Avro, Parquet and ORC, a generic model for Iceberg records, an Arrow model for vectorized reads, and Spark and Flink models.[^releases][^pr15254][^pr15329][^pr15328] The position delete writer builder is documented as applying to format version 2 tables only, since version 3 tables must not add position delete files and use [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) instead.[^pr15980][^icespec]

### Compatibility test kit

The announcement post called a Technology Compatibility Kit (TCK) the most important next step, to validate correctness, type support and compatibility of new format implementations.[^blog] A first TCK was merged in March 2026 and is part of 1.11.0, and further TCK tests (for example for the writer builder) were added for 1.12.0.[^tck][^tck2]

## History

Péter Váry opened the proposal issue and a discussion thread on the Iceberg dev mailing list on 11 February 2025, with a linked design document.[^issue][^discuss] The first implementation was a single large pull request that changed the interfaces, the format implementations and the engines together; the interfaces were later split into a separate pull request.[^pr12298]

In May 2025 a vote on the proposal was called on the dev list; it listed the expected results as the same performance, a formal API, simpler engine and format code, better testability, and the ability to introduce or deprecate file formats with little disruption.[^vote] Review continued on the design document and pull requests.

On 6 February 2026 Ryan Blue wrote on the dev list that the API was ready to be committed, starting with the interfaces pull request, with the aim of including it in the next release to help unblock the DataFusion Comet integration.[^discuss] The interfaces were merged that day, and the Spark and Flink integrations followed on 17 and 18 February 2026.[^pr15329][^pr12774][^pr15328] The project announced the finalized API on 20 February 2026, and it shipped in 1.11.0.[^blog][^releases]

## Planned work

The announcement post lists next steps that were not part of the release: moving the Spark Comet reader to a format model so it can live in the Comet repository, a full Vortex integration, completing the TCK, and column families (vertically split files that allow partial updates without rewriting whole files).[^blog] These are plans, not shipped features.

# Iceberg position delete

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_position_delete

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Position delete file; positional delete</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) format version 2</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Data file path, row position, optional deleted row values</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Deletion vector](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector), [Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg table spec at tags apache-iceberg-1.8.0, apache-iceberg-1.11.0 and apache-iceberg-1.12.0, the Iceberg 1.8.0, 1.9.0, 1.11.0 and 1.12.0 release notes, TableMetadata.java and the configuration, Spark queries and Spark procedures documentation at apache-iceberg-1.12.0</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="Iceberg format version 3">Use [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) instead. Writers must not add position delete files to v3 tables; existing ones in tables upgraded from v2 stay valid. Position delete files remain the normal merge-on-read output for v2 tables, and v2 is still the default format version in Iceberg 1.12.0.[^spec]</Status>

In [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), a **position delete** marks one row as deleted by naming the data file that holds it and the row's position in that file, counting from zero. In format version 2, position deletes are stored in **position delete files**, which are separate data files of (file path, position) pairs that readers apply when they scan the table.[^spec] Format version 3 deprecates position delete files and stores position deletes as [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) instead, one bitmap per data file.[^spec] Position delete files are one of the ways Iceberg implements [merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read).

## Status

The Iceberg table spec marks position delete files as deprecated in format version 3. Its section on position delete files says that existing position deletes must be written to deletion vectors when the deletes for a data file are next updated, and the row-level delete section says that position delete files must not be added to v3 tables, but existing position delete files are valid.[^spec] The same rules are in the spec at the apache-iceberg-1.8.0 tag, the first release that could write deletion vectors.[^spec180][^releases]

The deprecation applies to the format version, not to the Iceberg library. Iceberg 1.12.0 still creates new tables with format version 2 unless `format-version` is set, and in a v2 table a merge-on-read `DELETE`, `UPDATE` or `MERGE` still writes position delete files.[^tablemeta][^config] Position delete files are deprecated only for tables that have moved to format version 3 or later.

One part of the v2 design has been deprecated and removed in the Java library. The v2 spec allows a position delete file to also store the deleted row's values, but the spec notes that no implementation writes them; the Java implementation deprecated reading and writing that column in 1.11.0, and the 1.12.0 release notes list the removal of position delete files with row data.[^spec][^releases]

## How it works

A position delete file stores rows of a struct called `file_position_delete`. Each row has a `file_path`, the full URI of the target data file, and a `pos`, the ordinal position of the deleted row in that file. A third, optional column, `row`, can hold the deleted row's values.[^spec] The rows must be sorted by `file_path` and then `pos`, so that a columnar reader can skip entries for other files and can apply deletes while it streams through a data file instead of holding them in memory.[^spec]

At read time, a position delete file applies to a data file in the same partition whose data sequence number is less than or equal to the delete file's, unless a deletion vector already covers that data file. Because the comparison includes equal sequence numbers, a delete can remove rows added in the same commit.[^spec] One position delete file can hold deletes for many data files. When all its deletes are for one data file, the manifest entry can record that file in `referenced_data_file`, which lets planners skip the delete file for every other data file.[^spec]

Each delete operation adds new delete files, so a table that takes many small row-level changes collects many small position delete files. Iceberg provides the `rewrite_position_delete_files` Spark procedure to compact them and to drop entries that point to data files that are no longer live.[^procs] This is one form of the [small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem).

## Position delete file compared with related mechanisms

|  | Position delete file | Deletion vector | Equality delete file |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Format versions | v2; deprecated in v3, not allowed for new writes[^spec] | v3 and later[^spec] | v2 and later[^spec] |
| Identifies rows by | Data file path and row position | Row position, as a bitmap tied to one data file | Values of one or more columns, such as `id = 5` |
| Files per data file | Many; any number of delete files can cover a data file | At most one per data file in a snapshot | Many |
| Stored as | A Parquet, Avro or ORC file; the spec recommends the table's default file format | A blob in a Puffin file | A Parquet, Avro or ORC file |

[^spec]

Equality deletes are not affected by the v3 change. They delete rows by value rather than by position, and v3 tables can still add them.[^spec]

## Upgrading to format version 3

When a v2 table is upgraded to v3, its existing position delete files stay in table metadata and still apply. The first time a writer adds a deletion vector for a data file, it must merge that file's existing position deletes into the vector, and from then on readers can ignore position delete files that match a data file with a vector.[^spec] A position delete file that covers several data files has to stay in metadata until every data file it covers has a deletion vector.[^spec] Iceberg 1.9.0 added a Spark action to rewrite v2 position deletes as v3 deletion vectors.[^releases]

## Example

In Spark with an Iceberg catalog, a merge-on-read `DELETE` on a v2 table writes a position delete file, which the `position_deletes` metadata table shows:[^queries][^config]

```sql
CREATE TABLE demo.db.orders (id BIGINT, status STRING)
USING iceberg
TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '2', 'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read');

INSERT INTO demo.db.orders VALUES (1, 'open'), (2, 'open'), (3, 'closed');
DELETE FROM demo.db.orders WHERE id = 2;

SELECT file_path, pos, delete_file_path FROM demo.db.orders.position_deletes;
```

With `'format-version' = '3'`, the same `DELETE` writes a deletion vector instead; Iceberg 1.8.0 added support for showing deletion vectors in the `position_deletes` table.[^releases]

# Iceberg REST catalog

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Iceberg REST Catalog API, IRC</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">2022 (client in Apache Iceberg 0.14.0)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">OpenAPI specification, configuration endpoint, namespace, table and view endpoints, access delegation</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), Lakekeeper, Apache Gravitino, Project Nessie</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">rest-catalog-open-api.yaml at tag apache-iceberg-1.12.0 and the documentation of each listed implementation</Verified>

The **Iceberg REST catalog** is an OpenAPI specification, maintained in the [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) project, that defines an HTTP interface between Iceberg clients and a catalog service. It standardizes how an engine lists namespaces, loads and commits tables and views, and obtains access to the underlying storage, so that any engine with an Iceberg REST client can use any catalog that implements the specification.[^spec] In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), it is the common protocol that separates the choice of [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) from the choice of query engine.

## History

Apache Iceberg 0.14.0, released on 16 July 2022, added a common REST catalog client that uses change-based commits so that commit conflicts are resolved on the service side.[^releases]

The specification is a file named `rest-catalog-open-api.yaml` in the `open-api/` directory of the Iceberg repository. It is licensed under the Apache License 2.0, and its `info` block describes it as the specification for the first version of the REST Catalog API, with all routes under the `/v1/` path.[^spec]

## What the specification standardizes

The specification groups its routes into several areas:[^spec]
- **Configuration.** Clients call `GET /v1/config` first. The server returns default and override properties that configure the client, and an optional list of the endpoints it supports.
- **Namespaces.** Routes to list, create, load, check and drop namespaces and to update their properties.
- **Tables.** Routes to list, create, load, check, drop, rename, register and unregister tables, and to report metrics.
- **Commits.** A table commit has two parts: requirements, which the server checks before applying changes (for example `assert-ref-snapshot-id`), and updates to the table metadata. Servers must reject unknown requirements or updates with a 400 status code. A separate transactions route commits updates to several tables atomically.
- **Views.** Routes to list, create, load, replace, drop and rename views.
- **Server-side scan planning.** Routes through which a client can ask the catalog to plan a table scan.

Each route after `/v1/` takes an optional `{prefix}` path segment, which a server can use for its own hierarchy, such as one catalog per prefix.[^spec][^glue]

The `/v1/oauth/tokens` endpoint in the specification is deprecated. The specification says that it has been deprecated since Iceberg (Java) 1.6.0, that it will be removed in Iceberg (Java) 2.0, and that clients should set the `oauth2-server-uri` property to point at an OAuth server instead.[^spec]

## Credential vending and remote signing

The specification lets a catalog control access to the data files as well as the metadata. A client signals that it supports delegated access by sending the `X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation` header with one or both of the values `vended-credentials` and `remote-signing`. The server may supply access by any or none of the requested mechanisms.[^spec]

With **vended credentials**, the server returns storage credentials for Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, Google Cloud Storage or other stores in the `storage-credentials` field of the load-table response. Clients must check that field before looking for credentials in the table configuration. A separate route, `GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/credentials`, loads fresh vended credentials for a table.[^spec]

With **remote signing**, the client does not receive credentials. Instead, it sends each object storage request to the catalog's `sign` route, and the catalog returns a signed request.[^spec] Project Nessie's documentation describes the trade-off: vending needs a security token service but adds no round trip per request, while signing works without one but adds a REST call for every storage request.[^nessie]

## Implementations

The table lists catalogs whose own documentation states that they implement the Iceberg REST catalog API. It is not complete.

| Catalog | License or type | Endpoint path | Storage access documented |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) | Apache License 2.0[^n1] | See project docs | Vended credentials[^polaris] |
| [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) (open source) | Apache License 2.0[^n2] | `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg` | Vended credentials[^uc] |
| Lakekeeper | Apache License 2.0, written in Rust[^n3] | See project docs | Vended credentials for S3, ADLS and GCS; remote signing for S3[^n4][^n5] |
| Apache Gravitino | Apache License 2.0[^n6] | `/iceberg/` | Vended credentials for S3, GCS, OSS and ADLS; `remote-signing` is a configurable data access mode[^n7] |
| Project Nessie | Apache License 2.0[^n8] | `/iceberg` | Vended credentials and request signing; Iceberg REST support marked experimental[^nessie] |
| AWS Glue Data Catalog | Managed service | `/iceberg` on the regional Glue endpoint | S3 credentials vended for LoadTable; a subset of the REST operations[^glue] |

## Clients

Engines connect to a REST catalog through their Iceberg integration. [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) selects it with `iceberg.catalog.type=rest` and uses vended credentials when `iceberg.rest-catalog.vended-credentials-enabled` is set to true (the default is false).[^n9] [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) attaches a REST catalog with `ATTACH ... (TYPE iceberg)`, and attaching a catalog is required for writes.[^n10] [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) uses the Iceberg `SparkCatalog` with the catalog type set to `rest`.[^glue]
