# INT96 timestamp

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/INT96_timestamp

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">INT96; Impala timestamp</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data storage formats</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Physical type in [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet); written for timestamps by Impala, Hive and Spark</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">12 bytes: nanoseconds within the day (8 bytes) and a Julian day number (4 bytes)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (read only)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">parquet.thrift at parquet-format tags 2.4.0, 2.5.0, 2.12.0 and 2.14.0, the parquet-format 2.5.0 changelog, PARQUET-323 and PARQUET-1065, Apache Spark SQLConf.scala at v3.1.1, v3.5.0, v4.0.0 and v4.3.0, ParquetSchemaConverter.scala and DateTimeUtils.scala at v4.3.0, the Spark 3.5 to 4.0 SQL migration guide, SPARK-46440 and SPARK-46447, and the Apache Iceberg spec at apache-iceberg-1.12.0</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="parquet-format 2.5.0">Use an `INT64` column with the Parquet `TIMESTAMP` [logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type) instead. Apache Spark 4.3.0 still writes timestamps as INT96 by default.[^pq323]</Status>

An **INT96 timestamp** is a timestamp stored in the 12-byte `INT96` physical type of [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet): 8 bytes of nanoseconds within the day followed by 4 bytes of day number.[^thrift] The encoding was introduced for nanosecond timestamps in Impala, and [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) originally used the same timestamp type as Impala and Hive.[^sparkconv] INT96 carries no [logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type) annotation, so a reader has to know the convention to treat it as a timestamp. The Parquet format has marked INT96 as deprecated since parquet-format 2.5.0, but the type is still common because Spark writes it by default.[^pq323][^conf]

## Status

**Parquet format.** PARQUET-323, "INT96 should be marked as deprecated", was fixed in parquet-format 2.5.0, together with PARQUET-1065, which deprecated type-defined sort ordering for INT96 statistics.[^pq323][^changes] In `parquet.thrift`, the `INT96` entry has no comment at 2.4.0, is commented "deprecated, only used by legacy implementations" from 2.5.0, and since 2.12.0 reads "deprecated, new Parquet writers should not write data in INT96".[^thrift240][^thrift250][^thrift2120] The type has not been removed: parquet-format 2.14.0 added an `INT96_TIMESTAMP_ORDER` column order, which tells readers that INT96 statistics are ordered chronologically, and the thrift file notes that INT96 is still used in many legacy systems.[^thrift]

**Apache Spark.** Spark has not deprecated writing INT96. In Spark 4.3.0, `spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType` still defaults to `INT96`, as it has since the setting was added in Spark 2.3.0.[^conf] A comment in Spark's Parquet schema converter says that `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` is recommended but INT96 stays the default to keep earlier behaviour.[^sparkconv]

## How it works

An INT96 value is 12 bytes. The thrift definition describes the legacy ordering rule: the last 4 bytes are the day as a little-endian 32-bit signed integer, and the first 8 bytes are nanoseconds as a little-endian 64-bit signed integer.[^thrift] Spark interprets the day as a Julian day number and converts the value to microseconds since the Unix epoch, dividing the nanoseconds by 1,000, so sub-microsecond precision is lost on read.[^dtu]

Because the type has no logical type, nothing in the file says whether a value is UTC-normalized or local time. Spark's `spark.sql.parquet.int96TimestampConversion` (default `false`) applies a time zone adjustment for INT96 data written by Impala, which the setting's documentation says uses a different offset than Hive and Spark.[^conf] Spark reads INT96 as a timestamp only while `spark.sql.parquet.int96AsTimestamp` is `true`, the default; otherwise it rejects the column.[^conf][^sparkconv]

## Calendar rebasing in Spark

Spark 3.0 moved from the hybrid Julian and Gregorian calendar to the Proleptic Gregorian calendar, which changes the meaning of very old dates and timestamps.[^mig30] Spark 3.1 added `spark.sql.legacy.parquet.int96RebaseModeInRead` and `InWrite`, defaulting to `EXCEPTION`, so that reading or writing INT96 timestamps before 1900-01-01 failed instead of silently shifting.[^conf311][^mig40]

Spark 4.0.0 changed the defaults of these rebase settings to `CORRECTED`, which reads and writes values as they are (SPARK-46440), and removed the `spark.sql.legacy` names in favour of `spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInRead` and `spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInWrite` (SPARK-46447).[^s46440][^s46447][^mig40] Both settings are internal in Spark 4.3.0 and default to `CORRECTED`.[^conf]

## INT96 compared with standard Parquet timestamps

|  | INT96 timestamp | INT64 with TIMESTAMP logical type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status in Parquet | Deprecated since parquet-format 2.5.0[^pq323] | Current |
| Size | 12 bytes | 8 bytes |
| Precision | Nanoseconds in storage; Spark keeps microseconds[^dtu] | Unit stated in the annotation: `MILLIS`, `MICROS` or `NANOS`[^lt] |
| UTC or local time | Not recorded in the file | Recorded by `isAdjustedToUTC`[^lt] |
| Spark write setting | `spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType=INT96` (default)[^conf] | `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` or `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS`[^conf] |
| Apache Iceberg | Not used in the spec's Parquet type mapping; readable in imported data files[^icespec][^ice6962] | The spec's mapping for `timestamp` and `timestamptz`[^icespec] |

## Example

In Spark, setting the output type before writing produces standard `INT64` timestamps instead of INT96:[^conf]

```python
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS")

df = spark.sql("SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-11-22 10:00:00' AS ts")
df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/tmp/ts_micros")
```

The setting changes only new files. Files already written with INT96 keep that encoding until they are rewritten.

# Logical type

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Type annotation; LogicalType (Parquet); primitive type (Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data storage formats</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Physical type, logical type annotation, ConvertedType (deprecated)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Variant type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Variant_type), [Apache ORC](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_ORC)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">parquet-format 2.14.0 (LogicalTypes.md, README.md, parquet.thrift), the Apache Iceberg table spec at tag apache-iceberg-1.12.0, Apache Arrow 26.0.1 (Schema.fbs and the C++ Parquet documentation), and Apache Spark 4.3.0 (SQLConf.scala, ParquetSchemaConverter.scala and the 4.3.0 documentation)</Verified>

A **logical type** is an annotation that tells a reader how to interpret a stored value, layered on top of a small set of physical (storage) types. In [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), for example, a string is stored with the physical type `BYTE_ARRAY` and the logical type `STRING`, and a date is an `INT32` with the logical type `DATE`.[^pqlt] Logical types keep the set of storage types small while letting files carry richer types such as decimals, timestamps and UUIDs. Because each engine and table format has its own type system, the mapping between logical types is where data written by one tool can be read differently by another.

## Physical types and logical types

The Apache Parquet format defines a deliberately minimal set of physical types: `BOOLEAN`, `INT32`, `INT64`, `INT96`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`, `BYTE_ARRAY` and `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY`. The README explains that 16-bit integers, for example, are not stored separately because 32-bit integers with an efficient encoding cover them.[^pqreadme]

A Parquet logical type is stored in the file metadata as a `LogicalType` field on the column. Some logical types take parameters. `DECIMAL` has a precision and a scale and can annotate `INT32` (precision up to 9), `INT64` (precision up to 18), `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY` or `BYTE_ARRAY`. `UUID` annotates a 16-byte fixed-length array in big-endian order. `DATE` annotates an `INT32` that counts days from 1 January 1970.[^pqlt]

If a reader finds a logical type it does not recognize, the specification tells it to ignore the annotation and the column order and read the column using only its physical type.[^pqlt] A newer annotation therefore degrades to raw integers or bytes in an older reader instead of failing.

### Timestamps

The Parquet `TIMESTAMP` logical type annotates an `INT64` and has two parameters. `unit` is `MILLIS`, `MICROS` or `NANOS`. `isAdjustedToUTC` selects the semantics: when true, the value is an instant normalized to UTC; when false, the value is a local date and time that does not refer to one point on the time-line.[^pqlt] With the `NANOS` unit, the range of an `INT64` limits values to the years 1677 to 2262.[^pqlt]

### ConvertedType

`ConvertedType` is the older representation of the same annotations. It is a Thrift enum, so it cannot carry parameters such as the timestamp unit and UTC flag; `LogicalType`, a union of structs, replaced it. The specification marks `ConvertedType` as deprecated, but writers must still write the matching `ConvertedType` next to the `LogicalType` so that old readers work, and readers should fall back to it when no `LogicalType` is present.[^pqlt] For example, `STRING` corresponds to the `UTF8` converted type, and a microsecond UTC timestamp corresponds to `TIMESTAMP_MICROS`. Writers must also annotate local (non-UTC) timestamps with the legacy `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS` or `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` annotations, because some older libraries used those for local timestamps.[^pqlt]

### INT96 timestamps

`INT96` is a physical type with no logical type. The Parquet Thrift definition marks it as deprecated and says new writers should not write data in it.[^pqthrift] The same file notes that, at the time of writing, it was still used for legacy timestamps, and parquet-format 2.14.0 added a chronological sort order for INT96 statistics.[^pqthrift][^n1] [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) reads INT96 as a timestamp by default (`spark.sql.parquet.int96AsTimestamp=true`), for compatibility with systems such as Impala that store timestamps this way.[^sparkconf]

## How other systems map onto Parquet

Engines and table formats define their own types and choose a Parquet representation for each.

- **[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)** calls its types primitive types and defines them in the table spec, for example `timestamp` (microseconds, without time zone), `timestamptz` (microseconds, stored as UTC), and from format version 3 `timestamp_ns` and `timestamptz_ns`. Appendix A of the spec fixes the Parquet physical type and logical type for each one.[^icespec]
- **[Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow)** has a `Timestamp` type with a unit (seconds to nanoseconds) and an optional time zone string. A timestamp with a non-empty time zone is a point in time relative to the UTC epoch; one with no time zone is a wall-clock value in an unknown zone, and the Arrow format states that an empty time zone must not be read as UTC.[^arrowfbs] The Arrow C++ Parquet library documents which Arrow type each Parquet logical type maps to, and recognizes and writes deprecated converted types for compatibility.[^arrowpq]
- **Spark SQL** has `TimestampType` (timestamp with local time zone, `TIMESTAMP_LTZ`) and `TimestampNTZType` (without time zone). The SQL keyword `TIMESTAMP` is an alias for one of them, set by `spark.sql.timestampType`, whose default is `TIMESTAMP_LTZ`.[^sparkdt]

## Mapping of common types

The table shows how each system represents common types in Parquet, or (for Arrow) which Arrow type a Parquet logical type is read as.

| Meaning | Parquet physical type and logical type | [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow) type | [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) type | Spark SQL type written to Parquet |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| UTF-8 string | `BYTE_ARRAY` + `STRING` (converted type `UTF8`)[^pqlt] | String, LargeString or StringView[^arrowpq] | `string`, stored as `binary` + `UTF8`[^icespec] | `StringType`, stored as `BINARY` + string annotation[^sparkconv] |
| Decimal | `DECIMAL(P,S)` on `INT32`, `INT64`, `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY` or `BYTE_ARRAY`[^pqlt] | Decimal32, Decimal64, Decimal128 or Decimal256[^arrowpq] | `decimal(P,S)`, P at most 38; `int32` if P is at most 9, `int64` if at most 18, else `fixed`[^icespec] | `DecimalType`: `INT32`, `INT64` or fixed-length array by precision, unless `spark.sql.parquet.writeLegacyFormat` (default false) is set[^sparkconv][^sparkconf] |
| Date | `INT32` + `DATE`[^pqlt] | Date32[^arrowpq] | `date`[^icespec] | `DateType`, `INT32` + `DATE`[^sparkconv] |
| Instant (UTC-normalized timestamp) | `INT64` + `TIMESTAMP(isAdjustedToUTC=true, unit)`[^pqlt] | Timestamp with a non-empty time zone[^arrowfbs] | `timestamptz`, microseconds, `adjustToUtc=true`[^icespec] | `TimestampType`: `INT96` by default; `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` or `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS` if `spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType` is set[^sparkpq][^sparkconv] |
| Local date-time (no time zone) | `INT64` + `TIMESTAMP(isAdjustedToUTC=false, unit)`[^pqlt] | Timestamp with no time zone[^arrowfbs] | `timestamp`, microseconds, `adjustToUtc=false`[^icespec] | `TimestampNTZType`, `INT64` + `TIMESTAMP(false, MICROS)`[^sparkconv] |
| Nanosecond timestamp | `TIMESTAMP` with unit `NANOS`[^pqlt] | Timestamp with nanosecond unit[^arrowpq] | `timestamp_ns` and `timestamptz_ns`, format version 3 only[^icespec] | Preview types `TIMESTAMP_NTZ(p)` and `TIMESTAMP_LTZ(p)`, enabled by `spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled` (default false)[^sparkdt][^sparkconf] |
| UUID | `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY(16)` + `UUID`[^pqlt] | Extension type `arrow.uuid`, when Arrow extensions are enabled in the reader[^arrowpq] | `uuid`, `fixed_len_byte_array[16]` + `UUID`[^icespec] | Not among the Spark SQL data types[^sparkdt] |

## Interoperability pitfalls

The same word, "timestamp", means different things in different systems. Iceberg `timestamp` and Spark `TimestampNTZType` are local date-times, while Spark `TimestampType` and Iceberg `timestamptz` are instants.[^icespec][^sparkdt] A tool that maps one to the other without checking `isAdjustedToUTC` can shift values by the session time zone.

Spark 4.3.0 still writes `TimestampType` as INT96 by default. Its source code calls `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` the recommended setting and keeps INT96 as the default to preserve earlier behaviour.[^sparkconv] INT96 is deprecated in Parquet and carries no logical type annotation, so a reader has to know the legacy convention to treat it as a timestamp; the Iceberg spec's Parquet mapping does not use INT96 for any type.[^pqthrift][^icespec] Setting the output type to a standard logical type avoids this:

```sql
-- Spark SQL: write TimestampType columns as INT64 + TIMESTAMP(isAdjustedToUTC=true, MICROS)
SET spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType = TIMESTAMP_MICROS;
```

Parquet itself does not store a time zone. The Arrow C++ writer can store the serialized Arrow schema in the file metadata (`store_schema`) so that an Arrow reader can restore the original time zone string.[^arrowpq] Spark, in the same way, writes its own schema into the Parquet footer and uses it on read, so `spark.sql.parquet.inferTimestampNTZ.enabled` only affects files not written by Spark.[^sparkconf]

# mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState

<Infobox type="concept" name="mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Arbitrary stateful operations (version 1); `[flat]MapGroupsWithState`; `applyInPandasWithState` in Python</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Grouping key, user function, `GroupState` object, `GroupStateTimeout`, output mode, optional initial state</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 2.2 and later (Scala, Java); `applyInPandasWithState` in Python from 3.4</Field>
  <Field name="related">[transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v2.2.0, v3.2.0, v3.5.0 and v4.0.0 to v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (KeyValueGroupedDataset.scala, GroupState.scala, python/pyspark/sql/pandas/group_ops.py, python/pyspark/sql/connect/group.py, docs/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.md), the Spark 2.2.0, 3.4.0 and 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes, a JIRA search for deprecation tickets, and SPARK-19067, SPARK-35897, SPARK-40434, SPARK-43084, SPARK-43511 and SPARK-50770</Verified>

<Status level="active">Not deprecated in any Spark release up to 4.3.0: the methods carry no deprecation annotation and no release note or migration guide deprecates them. Since Spark 4.0 the documentation calls them legacy and encourages [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState) for new stateful applications.[^ssguide]</Status>

In [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), **mapGroupsWithState** and **flatMapGroupsWithState** are the original operators for arbitrary stateful processing: they call a user function for each grouping key with that key's new values and a `GroupState` object that holds the key's state between micro-batches.[^gs] They were added to [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) in version 2.2.0 for the Scala and Java Dataset API, and Spark 3.4.0 added the Python counterpart `applyInPandasWithState`.[^r220][^r340] Spark 4.0 introduced [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState) as their successor, but as of Spark 4.3.0 none of these operators is deprecated.[^ssguide]

## Status

Whether these operators are "deprecated" is a common question, and the primary sources answer it the same way: they are not.
- **Code (4.0.0 to 4.3.0):** The `mapGroupsWithState` and `flatMapGroupsWithState` methods of `KeyValueGroupedDataset`, in the shared API, the classic implementation and the [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client, have no `@deprecated` annotation, and the PySpark `applyInPandasWithState` docstring has no deprecation notice.[^kvgd][^groupops]
- **Release notes:** The Spark 4.0.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes do not deprecate them.[^r400][^r410][^r420][^r430] The Structured Streaming migration guide lists no deprecation of them either.[^n1]
- **Documentation:** The Spark 4.3.0 programming guide describes them as the "legacy" operators and says that since Spark 4.0 users are encouraged to use `transformWithState`.[^ssguide] The transformWithState guide calls that operator their "next generation replacement".[^twsguide]
- **Stability:** From Spark 2.2.0 to 3.5, the `GroupState` interface was annotated `@Experimental` and `@Evolving`. Spark 4.0.0 removed `@Experimental` (SPARK-50770), so in Spark 4.x it carries only `@Evolving`.[^gs220][^jira50770][^gs]

In short: the operators are supported and maintained in Spark 4.3.0 and existing queries keep working. New stateful applications are pointed to [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState).

## How it works

A query groups a Dataset with `groupByKey` and passes a function to one of the two operators. For each key that has new data in a trigger, Spark calls the function with the key, an iterator over the new values and the key's `GroupState`. The function reads the state with `get`, `getOption` or `exists`, changes it with `update`, and deletes it with `remove`. For a batch Dataset, the function is called once per group with empty state, which makes the operators the same as `mapGroups` and `flatMapGroups`.[^gs]

The two operators differ in their output:[^gs]
- **mapGroupsWithState** returns exactly one record per call, and the query must use the Update output mode. Aggregations are not allowed in the same query.[^ssguide]
- **flatMapGroupsWithState** returns any number of records, including none, and takes an output mode parameter, Append or Update. In Append mode, aggregations are allowed after the operator.[^ssguide]

The guide also says that neither operator can be used before or after a stream-stream join.[^ssguide]

### Timeouts

A query sets one timeout type for all groups with `GroupStateTimeout`: `NoTimeout`, `ProcessingTimeTimeout` or `EventTimeTimeout`. Each group then sets its own timeout with `setTimeoutDuration` (processing time) or `setTimeoutTimestamp` (event time, which needs a [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark)). When the timeout passes, Spark calls the function for that group with no values and `hasTimedOut` set to true. A timeout never fires early, but there is no upper bound on how late it fires, because it is checked only when a trigger runs. The timeout is cleared on every call, so the function must set it again each time.[^gs]

### Initial state

Spark 3.2.0 added overloads that take an initial state as a `KeyValueGroupedDataset`, to start a query with state loaded from elsewhere (SPARK-35897).[^kvgd][^n2]

## Language and Spark Connect support

| API | Language | Added in | Spark Connect support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `KeyValueGroupedDataset.mapGroupsWithState`, `flatMapGroupsWithState` | Scala, Java | 2.2.0[^r220] | 3.5.0 (SPARK-43511)[^n3] |
| `GroupedData.applyInPandasWithState` | Python (pandas) | 3.4.0 (SPARK-40434)[^r340][^groupops] | 3.5.0 (SPARK-43084)[^n4] |

## Comparison with transformWithState

<Hatnote>Main article: [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState)</Hatnote>

|  | mapGroupsWithState / flatMapGroupsWithState | transformWithState |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Added in | Spark 2.2.0[^r220] | Spark 4.0.0[^r400] |
| User code | One function of key, values and `GroupState`[^gs] | A stateful processor class with separate methods for input, timers, initial state and cleanup[^twsguide] |
| State per key | One object[^gs] | Any number of named value, list and map variables[^twsguide] |
| Timers | One timeout per key, reset on every call[^gs] | Many timers per key that persist until they fire or are deleted[^twsguide] |
| Automatic expiry (TTL) | No | Yes, per state variable, processing time only[^twsguide] |
| State store providers | HDFS-backed (default) or RocksDB | RocksDB only[^n5] |
| Real-time Mode (4.3.0) | `flatMapGroupsWithState` not yet supported[^rtm] | Scala and Java API supported[^rtm] |
| Deprecated? | No | No |

## Example

A running count per word in Scala. `words` is a streaming `Dataset[String]` and `spark.implicits._` is imported; the query must be written in Update output mode.

```scala
import org.apache.spark.sql.streaming.{GroupState, GroupStateTimeout}

val counts = words
  .groupByKey(identity)
  .mapGroupsWithState[Long, (String, Long)](GroupStateTimeout.NoTimeout) {
    (word: String, values: Iterator[String], state: GroupState[Long]) =>
      val updated = state.getOption.getOrElse(0L) + values.size
      state.update(updated)
      (word, updated)
  }
```

# Medallion architecture

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Multi-hop architecture; bronze, silver and gold layers</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering, data modeling</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Bronze (raw), silver (cleaned and conformed), gold (aggregated for consumers)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Databricks medallion architecture glossary, the Azure Databricks medallion architecture documentation, the openlakehouse.io batch and streaming medallion reference architectures and the Spark Declarative Pipelines programming guide</Verified>

A **medallion architecture** is a data design pattern that organizes the tables of a lakehouse into layers of increasing quality, usually called bronze, silver and gold. Bronze tables hold raw data as it arrived from source systems, silver tables hold cleaned, validated and conformed data, and gold tables hold aggregated or modeled data shaped for a specific use such as reporting or machine learning.[^dbx-glossary] The pattern is also called a multi-hop architecture, because data passes through several hops on its way from source to consumer.[^dbx-glossary] It is a convention for organizing tables, not a technology, and it can be built on any [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format).

## Layers

### Bronze

The bronze layer is where data from external source systems first lands. Databricks documentation describes bronze tables as matching the structure of the source tables "as-is", often with added metadata columns such as load time or process identifier. The layer serves as a historical archive of the source, supports lineage and auditing, and allows reprocessing without reading the source system again.[^dbx-glossary]

The Azure Databricks documentation recommends minimal validation in bronze and suggests storing most fields as strings, VARIANT or binary values to protect against unexpected schema changes in the source. It describes bronze data as intended for workloads that build silver tables, not for direct use by analysts.[^ms-medallion]

### Silver

The silver layer holds data from bronze that has been matched, merged, conformed and cleansed. Databricks documentation describes silver as an enterprise view of key business entities and transactions, such as deduplicated transactions or master customer records.[^dbx-glossary]

The Azure Databricks documentation states that silver should always include at least one validated, non-aggregated representation of each record, and recommends building silver tables from bronze or other silver tables rather than writing to them directly from ingestion.[^ms-medallion]

### Gold

The gold layer holds data organized for consumption by a particular project, team or business domain. Gold tables are often aggregated, denormalized and optimized for reads, and are commonly modeled as dimensional (star schema) models or data marts.[^dbx-glossary] Because gold models a business domain, some organizations keep several gold layers for different needs, such as finance or human resources.[^ms-medallion]

| Layer | Contents | Typical consumers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bronze | Raw records as received, plus load metadata | Pipelines that build silver tables |
| Silver | Validated, deduplicated, conformed records | Data engineers, analysts, data scientists |
| Gold | Aggregates and dimensional models for one domain | Business intelligence, reporting, machine learning |

The table summarizes the descriptions in the Databricks glossary and the Azure Databricks documentation.[^dbx-glossary][^ms-medallion]

## Status as a recommendation

The medallion architecture is a convention, not a rule. The Azure Databricks documentation describes it as a recommended best practice but not a requirement.[^ms-medallion] The layer names describe data quality, not storage location; in one example in that documentation, each layer is a separate schema in the same catalog (`ops.bronze`, `ops.silver`, `ops.gold`).[^ms-medallion]

## Implementation in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), each layer is a set of tables in an open table format such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) or [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), registered in a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog). Because the tables are open, the engine that writes bronze and silver does not have to be the engine that reads gold.

The openlakehouse.io batch medallion reference architecture defines each layer with [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) as a table or materialized view, lets Spark resolve the dependency graph, stores the tables as Iceberg in Unity Catalog OSS, schedules runs and backfills with [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow), and reads the gold tables from [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) through the catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint.[^olio-batch]

A streaming variant applies the same layout to event streams. In the openlakehouse.io streaming medallion reference architecture, a [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) query appends events from Apache Kafka to a bronze Iceberg table, and a Spark Declarative Pipeline derives silver and gold.[^olio-stream]

Declarative pipeline frameworks fit the pattern because each layer is defined from the layer before it, and the framework works out the order of execution. Spark Declarative Pipelines is described in the Apache Spark documentation as a declarative framework in which users define the transformations and the framework handles pipeline execution.[^sdp]

## Benefits

The Databricks glossary lists the following benefits of the pattern: a simple data model, incremental ETL, and the ability to recreate downstream tables from raw data at any time.[^dbx-glossary] Keeping raw data in bronze means that a bug in a silver or gold transformation can be fixed and the affected tables rebuilt without fetching data from the source system again.[^dbx-glossary]

## Criticism and limitations

The layer names are informal, and the boundaries between them vary between organizations. The Azure Databricks documentation notes, for example, that aggregate tables that drive many downstream workloads may live in silver, though they usually belong in gold.[^ms-medallion]

## See also

- [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)
- [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)
- [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)
- [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)
- [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow)

[^ms-medallion]: [What is the medallion lakehouse architecture?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/lakehouse/medallion). *Microsoft Learn*. Retrieved 2026-11-22.
[^olio-batch]: [Batch medallion with Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/batch-medallion). *openlakehouse.io*. Retrieved 2026-11-22.

# MinIO

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MinIO

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">MinIO, Inc.</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2014 (first commit in the GitHub repository)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">RELEASE.2025-10-15T17-29-55Z (last community release on GitHub)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2025-10-16</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Go</Field>
  <Field name="type">Object storage server with an Amazon S3 compatible API</Field>
  <Field name="license">GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (Apache License 2.0 before 2021)</Field>
  <Field name="website">[github.com/minio/minio](https://github.com/minio/minio)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/minio/minio](https://github.com/minio/minio) (archived)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the minio/minio GitHub repository (archive state, LICENSE history, README commits and releases), the MinIO blog post on the AGPLv3 change and apache/iceberg PR 18247</Verified>

<Status level="archived" since="25 April 2026">The minio/minio repository is archived and its README says it is no longer maintained. It entered maintenance mode in December 2025, and from October 2025 the community edition was distributed as source code only. MinIO, Inc. points users to its AIStor product.[^repo]</Status>

**MinIO** is an object storage server, written in Go, that implements the Amazon S3 API, so that tools written for S3 can store and read objects on hardware or clusters that the operator runs.[^readme0525] In open lakehouse setups MinIO was often the S3 endpoint for local development and self-hosted deployments of table formats such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg). The project changed its license from Apache 2.0 to the GNU AGPLv3 in 2021, moved the community edition to source-only distribution in October 2025, and archived its GitHub repository in April 2026.[^repo]

## Status

The state of the community edition changed in steps, each recorded in the repository's README:

- **October 2025, source-only distribution.** A README change stated that the MinIO community edition "is now distributed as source code only" and that MinIO would no longer provide pre-compiled binary releases for it. Users were told to install with `go install` or to build their own Docker image from the Dockerfile.[^srconly] The last release published on GitHub is `RELEASE.2025-10-15T17-29-55Z`.[^releases]
- **December 2025, maintenance mode.** The README gained a "Maintenance Mode" section: no new features, enhancements or pull requests would be accepted, critical security fixes "may be evaluated on a case-by-case basis", and existing issues and pull requests would not be actively reviewed.[^maint]
- **January and February 2026, AIStor editions.** README updates pointed users to two editions of MinIO's commercial product, AIStor: a free-license standalone edition and a distributed enterprise edition.[^n1][^n2]
- **April 2026, archived.** GitHub shows the repository as archived by its owner on 25 April 2026, and the README opens with "THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED".[^repo]

The AGPLv3 source code stays available in the archived repository, and existing binaries keep working, but the README says these legacy binaries will not receive updates.[^repo] AIStor is a separate product under MinIO's own licenses; it is not the community edition under a new name.[^repo]

## License history

MinIO was released under the Apache License 2.0 until 2021. The commit that replaced the `LICENSE` file with the GNU Affero General Public License v3 and updated the file headers was committed on 23 April 2021.[^agplcommit] The `LICENSE` file at the tag `RELEASE.2021-04-22T15-44-28Z` is still Apache 2.0, and at `RELEASE.2021-05-11T23-27-41Z` it is AGPLv3, so the May 2021 release was the first under the new license.[^n3] MinIO announced the change in a blog post that described the server, gateway and client as fully licensed under AGPLv3.[^n4]

The AGPLv3 is an open source license approved by the Open Source Initiative.[^n5] Its network clause requires that users who interact with a modified version over a network can get its source code. The MinIO README stated that all use of MinIO in an application stack "requires validation against AGPLv3 obligations" and offered commercial licensing for proprietary use.[^srconly] MinIO did not move to the [Business Source License](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Business_Source_License) or another source-available license; the community edition stayed AGPLv3 until the repository was archived.[^repo]

## Use in an open lakehouse

Because MinIO speaks the S3 API, engines and table formats that write to S3 can use it by changing the endpoint and turning on path-style access. A typical Spark configuration for Iceberg's `S3FileIO` against a MinIO-style endpoint looks like this:

```
spark.sql.catalog.lake.io-impl               org.apache.iceberg.aws.s3.S3FileIO
spark.sql.catalog.lake.s3.endpoint           http://object-store:9000
spark.sql.catalog.lake.s3.path-style-access  true
```

Any S3-compatible server can sit behind that endpoint. In September 2026 the Apache Iceberg project replaced MinIO with RustFS, another S3-compatible server, in its AWS and Kafka Connect integration tests, and the Spark quickstart in its documentation now runs a RustFS container under the network alias `minio`.[^n6]

## What MinIO is not

- **Not a table format or a catalog.** MinIO stores objects (files). Table semantics come from a format such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) or [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), and table names come from a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog).
- **Not Amazon S3.** MinIO implements the S3 API; S3 itself is an AWS service. Compatibility covers the API, and behaviour outside the API (consistency guarantees, limits, pricing) depends on the server.
- **Not the same as AIStor.** The community edition is the AGPLv3 code in the archived repository; AIStor is MinIO, Inc.'s commercial product.[^repo]

# MLlib

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 0.8.0 (RDD-based API); `spark.ml` previewed in Spark 1.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, with Python, Java and R APIs</Field>
  <Field name="type">Machine learning library</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[MLlib Main Guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/ml-guide.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (mllib/)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/mllib)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[spark.mllib (RDD-based API)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark.mllib_(RDD-based_API)), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/ml-guide.md, docs/ml-migration-guide.md, python/pyspark/ml/util.py, python/pyspark/ml/connect/, sql/connect/server/.../connect/ml/), the Spark 0.8.0, 1.2.0, 2.0.0, 3.5.0 and 4.0.0 release notes, SPARK-50812 and SPARK-50828</Verified>

<Status level="active">MLlib is not deprecated. Its RDD-based `spark.mllib` package has been in maintenance mode since Spark 2.0; the DataFrame-based `spark.ml` package is the primary API.[^guide]</Status>

**MLlib** is the machine learning library of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark). It provides distributed learning algorithms (classification, regression, clustering, collaborative filtering), feature transformations, ML Pipelines, model persistence and utilities such as linear algebra and statistics.[^guide] MLlib has two APIs: the DataFrame-based API in the `spark.ml` package, which is the primary API, and the older [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD)-based API in the `spark.mllib` package, which has been in maintenance mode since Spark 2.0.[^guide] Neither API, and not MLlib as a whole, is deprecated.[^guide]

## Two APIs

|  | `spark.ml` (DataFrame-based) | `spark.mllib` (RDD-based) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status in Spark 4.3.0 | Primary API; new features go here | Maintenance mode since Spark 2.0: bug fixes only, no new features |
| Data type | [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) with feature vector columns | [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) of objects such as `LabeledPoint` |
| Building blocks | Estimators, transformers, evaluators and pipelines | Algorithm objects with `train` methods |
| Linear algebra types | `org.apache.spark.ml.linalg` | `org.apache.spark.mllib.linalg` |
| Spark Connect | Supported from Spark 4.0.0 (Python) | Not supported, because Connect has no RDD API |

Sources: the MLlib guide and migration guide,[^guide][^migration] the Spark Connect overview[^connect] and SPARK-50812.[^jira50812]

The MLlib guide gives the reasons for the move to DataFrames: a friendlier API, Spark data sources, SQL queries, the Catalyst and Tungsten optimizations, one API across languages, and practical ML Pipelines, especially for feature transformations.[^guide]

## What "Spark ML" means

"Spark ML" is not an official name. The MLlib guide says it is sometimes used for the DataFrame-based API, because of the `org.apache.spark.ml` package name and the early term "Spark ML Pipelines". The official name of the library, covering both APIs, is MLlib.[^guide] In code, `pyspark.ml` is the DataFrame-based API and `pyspark.mllib` is the RDD-based one.

## History

MLlib was introduced in Spark 0.8.0 as a library of machine learning and optimization algorithms, developed with the UC Berkeley MLbase project.[^n1] Spark 1.2.0 previewed a new set of machine learning APIs in a package called `spark.ml`, built around learning pipelines and using Spark SQL's SchemaRDD (the predecessor of the DataFrame) to represent datasets.[^n2] In Spark 2.0.0 the DataFrame-based API became the primary API and the RDD-based API entered maintenance mode.[^r200] The Spark 2.x versions of the MLlib guide said the RDD-based API was expected to be removed in Spark 3.0; that sentence was dropped from the guide for the 3.0 release, and the RDD-based API is still part of Spark 4.3.0.[^n3][^jira30934] See [spark.mllib (RDD-based API)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark.mllib_(RDD-based_API)) for what was removed from that package.

## MLlib and Spark Connect

Spark has had two attempts at machine learning over [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).

- **`pyspark.ml.connect` (Spark 3.5.0).** Spark 3.5.0 added a separate package, `pyspark.ml.connect`, with its own estimators, transformers, pipelines and cross-validation for Connect clients.[^n4] This package was deprecated in Spark 4.0.0 (SPARK-50828); its classes carry a `deprecated:: 4.0.0` note at the v4.3.0 tag.[^jira50828][^n5]
- **`pyspark.ml` on Connect (Spark 4.0.0).** Spark 4.0.0 made the regular `pyspark.ml` API work on Spark Connect (SPARK-50812), listed as "ML on Spark Connect" in the release highlights.[^r400][^jira50812] When the session is remote, `pyspark.ml` sends fit and transform calls to the Connect server, which runs the Scala implementation in its ML handler.[^n6][^n7]

The RDD-based `spark.mllib` API cannot run over Connect, because Connect does not support RDDs or the `SparkContext`.[^connect]

## Example

A DataFrame-based pipeline in PySpark. The same code runs in a classic session and, from Spark 4.0.0, in a Spark Connect session.

```python
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.feature import VectorAssembler

train = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(0.0, 1.1, 0.1), (1.0, 2.0, 1.0), (0.0, 1.3, -0.5), (1.0, 2.2, 1.5)],
    ["label", "x1", "x2"])

pipeline = Pipeline(stages=[
    VectorAssembler(inputCols=["x1", "x2"], outputCol="features"),
    LogisticRegression(maxIter=10),
])
model = pipeline.fit(train)
model.transform(train).select("label", "prediction").show()
```

# Model Context Protocol

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Model_Context_Protocol

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Agentic AI Foundation ([Linux Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Linux_Foundation)); created by [Anthropic](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Anthropic)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2024</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Specification 2026-07-28</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-07-28</Field>
  <Field name="type">Protocol for connecting AI applications to data and tools</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0 for new contributions (transitioning from MIT)</Field>
  <Field name="website">[modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Model Context Protocol specification revision 2026-07-28 on modelcontextprotocol.io and its GitHub release</Verified>

The **Model Context Protocol** (**MCP**) is an open protocol that connects applications built on large language models (LLMs) to external data sources and tools. MCP defines a standard way for an application to share context with a model, expose tools that the model can call, and build workflows from several integrations.[^spec] In an [agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse), MCP is one way for an AI agent to look up tables in a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), run queries and check pipelines through tools that a server exposes.

## Architecture

MCP uses a client-host-server architecture. The **host** is the LLM application; it creates and manages clients, enforces security policy and consent, and coordinates the model. Each **client** lives inside the host and talks to exactly one server. A **server** provides context and capabilities, and can run as a local process or as a remote service.[^arch]

The MCP design keeps servers isolated. A server receives only the context it needs, the full conversation stays with the host, and a server cannot see into other servers; the host controls any interaction between them.[^arch]

### Base protocol

MCP messages use JSON-RPC 2.0.[^spec] In revision 2026-07-28, MCP is stateless: every request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities in its `_meta` field, and servers advertise their capabilities in response to a `server/discover` request.[^arch] Revisions up to 2025-11-25 instead opened a session with an `initialize` handshake. A server or client may support both styles, and the specification gives rules for detecting which style the other side uses.[^versioning]

### Server features

Servers offer three primitives, each controlled by a different party.[^server]

| Primitive | Controlled by | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tools | The model | Functions the model can call to take actions or retrieve information |
| Resources | The application | Structured data or content attached as context |
| Prompts | The user | Templates or instructions the user invokes, such as slash commands |

A client lists a server's tools with `tools/list` and calls one with `tools/call`. Each tool has a name, a description and an input schema written in JSON Schema, and may declare an output schema for structured results.[^tools]

### Client features

Clients may offer elicitation, through which a server asks the user for more information.[^spec] In revision 2026-07-28, such requests arrive inside a server's reply as an `InputRequiredResult`. Sampling and roots are deprecated as of that revision.[^arch]

### Transports

The specification defines two standard transports. With **stdio**, the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over standard input and output. With **Streamable HTTP**, each message is an HTTP POST to one MCP endpoint, and replies come back as a JSON object or a server-sent events stream for that request. Custom transports are allowed if they keep the JSON-RPC format and message patterns.[^transports]

### Extensions

Optional extensions add functionality beyond the core protocol and must be supported by both sides. Examples named in the specification include Tasks, for long-running asynchronous operations, and MCP Apps, for interactive interface elements.[^spec]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), an MCP server can stand between an agent and lakehouse systems, so that the agent acts through a defined set of tools whose inputs the server validates and whose access the server controls.[^tools] Examples of such tools include the following.

- **Catalog lookups.** A server can expose tools or resources that list catalogs, schemas and tables in a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) such as [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) or [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), or return a table's schema, before the agent writes a query.
- **Running a query.** A tool can take SQL as an argument, run it on an engine such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) or [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), and return rows as structured content that matches the tool's output schema.[^tools]
- **Dry-running a pipeline.** A tool can wrap `spark-pipelines dry-run` from [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), which checks a pipeline for syntax, analysis and graph errors without reading or writing data.[^n1] The agent can then fix errors before a real run spends compute.

The following request calls a hypothetical `run_query` tool. As in the specification's own examples, the required `_meta` fields are left out for brevity.[^tools]

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "run_query",
    "arguments": {
      "sql": "SELECT region, count(*) FROM sales.orders GROUP BY region"
    }
  }
}
```

The openlakehouse.io [agentic lakehouse guide](https://openlakehouse.io/agentic-lakehouse) covers how agents, catalogs and pipelines fit together in more depth.

## History

[Anthropic](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Anthropic) announced and open sourced the Model Context Protocol on 25 November 2024. The announcement included the specification and software development kits (SDKs), local MCP server support in the Claude Desktop apps, and a repository of open source servers.[^announce]

On 9 December 2025, Anthropic donated MCP to the newly formed Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, where MCP became a founding project.[^aaif]

Specification revisions are named by date. Published revisions include 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28.[^releases] The project is moving its license from MIT to the Apache License 2.0; new code and specification contributions are licensed under Apache 2.0.[^license]

## Limitations

MCP does not enforce security at the protocol level. The specification states that tools represent arbitrary code execution, that hosts must obtain user consent before invoking a tool, and that implementors should build their own consent, authorization and access controls.[^spec] It recommends a human in the loop who can deny tool calls, and clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.[^tools]

Revision 2026-07-28 changed how sessions work. Clients that only use the older `initialize` handshake cannot talk to servers that only implement the newer revision.[^versioning] Tool names are unique only within one server, so a host that combines several servers should handle name collisions, for example by adding a server prefix.[^tools]

Because MCP has no protocol-level session in revision 2026-07-28, a server that keeps state across calls, such as an open database transaction, must return an explicit handle and receive it on later calls.[^tools]

# Open lakehouse

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Open data lakehouse</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering, data management</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">2020 (term "lakehouse"); formalized in a 2021 paper</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Object storage, [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), query engines</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse), [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the CIDR 2021 lakehouse paper, the Databricks January 2020 lakehouse post, the Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake specifications, the Unity Catalog OSS and Apache Polaris documentation</Verified>

An **open lakehouse** is a data platform architecture in which tables are stored as open file formats on low-cost object storage, managed by an open [table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), registered in an open [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), and processed by any compatible engine. It combines the cheap, directly accessible storage of a data lake with the transactions, versioning and performance features of a data warehouse. The word "open" means that no layer depends on a single vendor: data written by one engine can be read by another without copying or conversion.

## Definition

The lakehouse paper presented at the Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR) in January 2021 defines a lakehouse as a data management system built on low-cost, directly accessible storage that also provides analytical database features such as ACID transactions, data versioning, auditing, indexing, caching and query optimization.[^cidr] The same paper characterizes lakehouses by open direct-access data formats such as Apache Parquet and ORC, first-class support for machine learning and data science, and state-of-the-art performance.[^cidr]

An open lakehouse applies that definition with an added constraint: the formats, the table specification, the catalog interface and the engines are open source or openly specified. The openlakehouse.io guides describe this as an architecture assembled from open table formats, open catalogs, open compute engines and open machine learning tools, on storage the organization controls.[^olio-osde]

## History

Databricks described the lakehouse as a new, open architecture that combines elements of data lakes and data warehouses in a blog post published on 30 January 2020.[^dbx2020] The CIDR 2021 paper by Michael Armbrust, Ali Ghodsi, Reynold Xin and Matei Zaharia set out the argument in academic form.[^cidr]

The CIDR paper frames the lakehouse as a third generation of analytics platforms. The first generation loaded operational data into on-premises data warehouses that coupled compute and storage. The second generation put raw data into data lakes, which are low-cost storage systems with a file API holding open formats such as Parquet and ORC, and copied a subset of that data into a warehouse for business intelligence.[^cidr] The lakehouse removes the second copy by adding warehouse features directly on top of the lake.

The enabling technology, according to the paper, is a metadata layer over the files in the lake. The paper names [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) (begun at Databricks in 2016), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (started at Netflix) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) (started at Uber) as systems of this kind.[^cidr] These metadata layers are now usually called open table formats.

## Architecture

An open lakehouse is usually described as a stack of independent layers. Each layer talks to the next through a published specification, so any one layer can be replaced.

| Layer | Role | Open source examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Object storage | Holds data files and metadata files | Any S3-compatible store, HDFS |
| File format | Stores rows in columnar files | [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)[^parquet] |
| Table format | Groups files into tables with snapshots and atomic commits | [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) |
| Catalog | Names tables, stores the pointer to current metadata, enforces access | [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), any [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) |
| Engines | Read and write tables for SQL, batch, streaming and machine learning | [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) |
| Pipelines and orchestration | Define and schedule transformations | [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow) |

The table format is the layer that turns a directory of files into a table. In Apache Iceberg, every change writes a new metadata file and replaces the old one with an atomic swap, which gives readers serializable isolation without locks.[^icespec] In Delta Lake, writers add a new entry to a transaction log stored next to the data, and readers use the log to select the files that make up one consistent snapshot.[^deltaproto]

The catalog is the layer that makes tables discoverable and governable. The CIDR paper notes that a metadata layer can check whether a client may access a table before giving it credentials to read the underlying files.[^cidr] Unity Catalog OSS implements this as credential vending: the catalog issues short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table or volume.[^ucwhat]

## What makes a lakehouse open

A lakehouse is open when each interface between layers is public and implemented by more than one project. In practice this covers four interfaces: the data file format (for example Parquet), the table format specification (for example the Iceberg table spec or the Delta transaction log protocol), the catalog API (for example the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification), and the engine connectors that read them.

The Iceberg REST catalog specification is a common example of an open interface. The Iceberg project created it so that a new language or engine can work with any catalog through one client implementation.[^icerest] Apache Polaris implements this API and lists Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Trino and other engines as clients.[^polaris]

Openness across table formats is partial. Delta Lake's Universal Format (UniForm) generates Iceberg metadata for a Delta table so that Iceberg clients can read it from the same data files.[^uniform] Apache XTable, an incubating Apache project, translates metadata between Hudi, Delta Lake and Iceberg.[^xtable]

## Comparison with data warehouses and data lakes

| Property | Data warehouse | Data lake | Open lakehouse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Storage | Managed by the warehouse | Files on low-cost storage | Files on low-cost storage |
| Data format | Internal to the system | Open file formats | Open file formats plus an open table format |
| ACID transactions | Yes | No | Yes, through the table format |
| Access by other engines | Through the warehouse only | Direct file access | Direct access through the table format and catalog |

The comparison follows the generations described in the CIDR 2021 paper.[^cidr]

## Limitations

The CIDR 2021 paper noted that Delta Lake, Iceberg and Hudi supported transactions on only one table at a time, and that storing a transaction log in an object store limits the commit rate because of object store latency.[^cidr] The Iceberg REST catalog specification lists multi-table commits among the features the REST protocol enables.[^icerest]

Catalog-based access control applies only to requests that go through the catalog. The Unity Catalog OSS documentation warns that anyone with direct storage credentials can bypass catalog checks, so the storage itself must also be locked down.[^ucwhat]

## Use with AI agents

<Hatnote>Main article: [Agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse)</Hatnote>

An [agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse) is an open lakehouse designed so that AI agents can find, query and change data under platform-enforced controls. It adds agent tools, often served over the [Model Context Protocol](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Model_Context_Protocol), declarative pipelines that the platform validates before they run, and policies on every tool call.[^olio-agentic]

- [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)
- [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture)
- [Agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse)
- [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)

# Open table format

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Lakehouse table format, metadata layer</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data management</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Data files, table metadata, snapshots, atomic commits</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg table spec, the Delta transaction log protocol (PROTOCOL.md on the master branch), the Apache Hudi table types and timeline documentation, the Delta UniForm and Apache XTable documentation</Verified>

An **open table format** is a publicly specified way of organizing data files and metadata on file or object storage so that a collection of files behaves as a single database table, with atomic commits, consistent snapshots and schema management. The format is a specification, not an engine: any engine that implements it can read and write the same table. Open table formats are the layer that turns a data lake into an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse). The best-known open table formats are [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi).

## Purpose

Plain files in a data lake have no notion of a transaction. Readers cannot tell a half-written batch from a complete one, and there is no record of which files belong to which version of a table. The CIDR 2021 lakehouse paper calls the solution a metadata layer: a record of which objects are part of a table version, updated transactionally, on top of open file formats such as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and ORC.[^cidr]

According to the same paper, metadata layers add transactions, zero-copy cloning and time travel to past table versions, and are a natural place to enforce data quality rules and access control.[^cidr]

## History

The CIDR 2021 paper traces the current open table formats to three origins. Databricks began developing Delta Lake in 2016, storing the list of a table's objects as a transaction log in the data lake itself. Apache Iceberg started at Netflix with a similar design. Apache Hudi started at Uber with a focus on streaming ingestion into data lakes.[^cidr]

Today Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi are projects of the Apache Software Foundation, and Delta Lake is a Linux Foundation project.[^iceberg-home][^hudi-overview][^deltaio]

## How it works

All three formats share a pattern. Data lives in immutable files, usually Parquet. A separate set of metadata files records which data files make up each version of the table. A writer prepares new files first, then commits by atomically publishing new metadata. Readers always see a complete version.

- **Apache Iceberg** keeps table state in metadata files. Each change creates a new metadata file and replaces the old one with an atomic swap, usually by updating a pointer held in a [catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog). A snapshot lists its data files through manifest files, which are reused across snapshots.[^icespec]
- **Delta Lake** keeps a transaction log in a `_delta_log` directory next to the data. Each commit is a newline-delimited JSON file named by version number, and periodic checkpoints summarize the log in Parquet. Writers first write data files optimistically, then commit by adding a new log entry.[^deltaproto]
- **Apache Hudi** records every change to the table (writes, table services, schema changes) as an action on a timeline. Each action has a requested instant, which acts as its transaction identifier, and a completed instant.[^hudi-timeline]

## Comparison

The table compares features as described in each project's own specification or documentation.

| Feature | [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) | [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) | [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Origin (per CIDR 2021 paper)[^cidr] | Netflix | Databricks (2016) | Uber |
| Governance | Apache Software Foundation | Linux Foundation | Apache Software Foundation |
| Metadata structure | Table metadata files, manifest lists and manifests[^icespec] | Transaction log of JSON commits with Parquet checkpoints[^deltaproto] | Timeline of actions at instants[^hudi-timeline] |
| Commit mechanism | Atomic swap of the table metadata pointer[^icespec] | New entry appended to the log; optimistic writes[^deltaproto] | Action moves from requested to completed on the timeline[^hudi-timeline] |
| Row-level deletes | Delete files; deletion vectors from format version 3[^icespec] | Optional deletion vectors[^deltaproto] | Copy-on-write rewrites base files; merge-on-read writes log files merged at query time[^hudi-types] |
| Reading past versions | Snapshots of the table at points in time[^icespec] | Snapshots by table version[^deltaproto] | Time travel queries at timeline instants[^hudi-types] |
| Incremental reads | Engines can read only the data appended between two snapshots, for example with the Spark `start-snapshot-id` and `end-snapshot-id` read options[^n1] | Readers can tail the log to find added data[^deltaproto] | Incremental and change data capture queries[^hudi-types] |
| Schema and partition evolution | Full schema evolution and partition spec evolution[^icespec] | Column mapping supports renaming and dropping columns without rewriting data[^deltaproto] | Supports schema evolution on write and through SQL DDL[^n2] |

## Format versions

Open table formats evolve through versioned specifications so that older readers do not misread newer tables.

Apache Iceberg numbers its format versions. Version 1 defines analytic tables over immutable Parquet, Avro and ORC files. Version 2 adds row-level deletes. Version 3 adds new data types (including variant, geometry and geography), column default values, row lineage, binary deletion vectors and table encryption keys. As of November 2026, the specification describes version 4 as under active development and not formally adopted.[^icespec]

Delta Lake versions its protocol with a reader version and a writer version. Reader version 3 and writer version 7 add named table features, which let a table declare the individual capabilities a client must support.[^deltaproto]

## Interoperability between formats

Because Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi all store Parquet data files under their own metadata, tools can expose one copy of the data in more than one format.

Delta Lake's Universal Format (UniForm) generates Iceberg metadata, and in preview Hudi metadata, for a Delta table, so that Iceberg and Hudi clients can read it.[^uniform]

Apache XTable, an incubating Apache project formerly named OneTable, reads a table's existing metadata and writes metadata for one or more of the other formats, in any direction among Hudi, Delta Lake and Iceberg.[^xtable]

## Relationship to catalogs

<Hatnote>Main article: [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Hatnote>

A table format defines how one table is stored. A catalog maps table names to the current metadata of each table and coordinates commits. In Iceberg, the catalog stores the pointer to each table's current metadata file and performs the atomic update of that pointer.[^polaris-docs] Delta Lake's protocol also defines catalog-managed tables, in which the catalog is the source of truth for whether a commit succeeded.[^deltaproto]

# Partition

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="field">Data engineering</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Spark partitions, table partitions (Hive-style, Iceberg, Delta Lake), Kafka topic partitions</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs and PySpark source), a run on a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 spec and partitioning docs, the Delta Lake protocol at v4.4.1 and the clustering docs, and the Apache Kafka 4.4 introduction</Verified>

A **partition** is a subset of a dataset that a system stores or processes as one unit. In a lakehouse the word has several distinct meanings, depending on whether it refers to how an engine splits work, how a table lays out files, or how a message log splits a topic. An [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) partition is a slice of data processed by one task. A table partition in Hive, [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) or [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) is a group of files that share partition values. An [Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka) partition is an ordered log inside a topic. These meanings interact (a Spark job reads table partitions into Spark partitions, and a Kafka source maps topic partitions to Spark partitions), but they are not the same thing.

## Spark in-memory partition

<Hatnote>Main article: [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Hatnote>

In Spark, a partition is a piece of an RDD or DataFrame, and Spark runs one task for each partition.[^rddguide] The number of partitions therefore sets how much parallel work a stage can do on the cluster's [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor). When Spark reads files, it packs at most `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (default 128 MB) into one partition; after a join or aggregation, it uses `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (default 200) partitions, which adaptive query execution can coalesce at runtime.[^perf]

Two DataFrame methods change the number of partitions. `repartition` hash-partitions the data and always causes a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle).[^repartition][^rddguide] `coalesce` only reduces the number of partitions and creates a narrow dependency without a shuffle: going from 1,000 partitions to 100, each new partition claims 10 old ones.[^coalesce]

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.range(0, 1_000_000)
wide = df.repartition(8, "id")   # shuffle into 8 hash partitions
narrow = wide.coalesce(2)        # merge into 2 partitions, no new shuffle

narrow.select(F.spark_partition_id()).distinct().count()   # 2
```

A Spark partition exists only while a job runs. It is not stored, and it is unrelated to the directory layout of the table being read, except that file and partition layout influence how Spark splits its input.

## Hive-style table partitioning

Hive-style partitioning stores a table's files in directories named after partition column values, such as `gender=male/country=US/`. The partition values are encoded in the path of each directory. Spark's built-in file sources discover this layout automatically and add the partition columns to the schema.[^parquet]

Queries skip directories only when they filter on the partition column itself. In Hive, a table partitioned by `event_date` has an explicit `event_date` column, and a query without an `event_date` filter scans every file, even when it filters on the timestamp that the date was derived from.[^icebergpart] Very fine partitioning also produces many small files; see [small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem).

## Apache Iceberg hidden partitioning and partition evolution

<Hatnote>Main article: [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Hatnote>

Iceberg uses **hidden partitioning**. A partition spec derives partition values from table columns through transforms such as `identity`, `bucket[N]`, `truncate[W]`, `year`, `month`, `day` and `hour`. Because the table records the transform, Iceberg turns a filter on the source column into a partition filter, and users do not have to add partition predicates to their queries.[^ispec][^icebergpart] Partition values are stored in manifests for each data file, not taken from directory names.[^ispec]

Iceberg also supports **partition evolution**: a table's partitioning can change by adding, removing, renaming or reordering partition fields. Each change creates a new partition spec, and files written under an older spec keep it; at scan time, Iceberg converts filters using the spec each manifest was written with.[^ispec]

## Delta Lake partitioning and liquid clustering

<Hatnote>Main article: [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Hatnote>

A [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) table can have partition columns, recorded in the table metadata. The transaction log stores each file's partition values, and readers must take the values from the log. The reference implementation writes files into Hive-style `column=value` directories, but the protocol says this layout only follows convention and is not required.[^dproto]

**Liquid clustering** is Delta Lake's alternative to partitioning and `ZORDER`. A table declares clustering columns with `CLUSTER BY`, `OPTIMIZE` clusters the data incrementally, and the clustering columns can be changed later with `ALTER TABLE` without rewriting existing data. Clustering cannot be combined with partitioning or `ZORDER` on the same table. It is available from Delta Lake 3.1.0, and the preview flag was removed in 3.2.[^dcluster] The protocol requires writers of clustered tables to record per-file statistics for the clustering columns, which readers use for data skipping.[^dproto]

## Apache Kafka topic partitions

A Kafka topic is split into partitions spread over brokers. Events with the same key go to the same partition, consumers read each partition in the order its events were written, and replication works per partition.[^kafka] Ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not across a topic.

When [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) reads from Kafka, Spark by default maps each Kafka topic partition to one Spark partition. The `minPartitions` option asks Spark to split large Kafka partitions into more Spark partitions.[^sskafka]

## Which partition am I looking at?

| Meaning | Where it lives | Lifetime | Who decides it | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spark partition | Memory and local disk of executors | One job or stage | Spark (file split size, shuffle partitions, AQE) or the user | `repartition`, `coalesce`, SQL hints[^perf] |
| Hive-style table partition | Directory names in storage (`col=value/`) | Permanent, part of the table | Table author (partition columns) | Writing the data into a new directory layout |
| Iceberg partition | Partition tuples in manifests, derived by transforms | Permanent, per partition spec | Table author (partition spec) | Partition evolution; old files keep their spec[^ispec] |
| Delta Lake partition or cluster | Partition values or statistics in the transaction log | Permanent | Table author (`PARTITIONED BY` or `CLUSTER BY`) | Clustering columns via `ALTER TABLE`[^dcluster] |
| Kafka topic partition | Brokers | Lifetime of the topic | Topic configuration; the event key decides which partition an event goes to[^kafka] | Kafka topic administration |
