# Predicate pushdown

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Filter pushdown, data skipping (at the file level)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Data source API, file format statistics (Parquet row groups, page indexes, bloom filters), table format metadata, catalog</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (connector read interfaces, PushDownUtils.scala, FileSourceStrategy.scala, SQLConf.scala, docs), EXPLAIN runs on a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, the parquet-format 2.12.0 Thrift definition and parquet.apache.org docs, the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 spec and REST catalog OpenAPI definition, and the Delta Lake protocol at v4.4.1</Verified>

**Predicate pushdown** is a query optimization in which an engine sends the filter conditions of a query (the predicates in a `WHERE` clause) down to the layer that reads the data, so that rows, files or whole partitions that cannot match are never read. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse) the predicate can travel through several layers: from the engine to the data source connector, from the connector to the file format, from the table format's metadata, and sometimes to the [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog). Each layer skips data in a different way, and a predicate may be used at one layer and not at another.

## Engine to data source

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a connector built on the Data Source V2 API opts in to pushdown by implementing mix-in interfaces on its `ScanBuilder`. `SupportsPushDownFilters` (since Spark 3.0.0) receives filters as `org.apache.spark.sql.sources.Filter` objects.[^spdf] `SupportsPushDownV2Filters` (since 3.3.0) receives V2 `Predicate` objects and is the preferred interface.[^spdv2] Sibling interfaces push down column pruning, limits, aggregates, top-N and joins.[^readpkg]

The source returns the predicates it cannot fully apply, and Spark evaluates those after the scan. A predicate can also be **partially** pushed: the Spark interface uses the Parquet row-group filter as its example of a filter that the source uses to skip data but that Spark must still evaluate on the rows that come back.[^spdf] Pushdown therefore reduces the data read; it does not always remove the `Filter` operator from the plan.

Spark can also push filters that it learns only at runtime. With `SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering` (since 3.4.0), a scan can drop planned input partitions using predicates that Spark infers during execution, for example from the other side of a join.[^runtime] Dynamic partition pruning, on by default (`spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled`), uses a join key to generate a predicate on a partition column.[^sqlconf]

For its built-in file sources, Spark sorts filters into four groups: filters on partition columns, which prune directories; filters on bucket columns, which can prune files; filters on data columns, which are pushed into the file reader; and filters that must be evaluated again after the scan.[^fss]

## Engine to file format

<Hatnote>Main article: [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Hatnote>

[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) files carry statistics that a reader can compare with a predicate before decoding data:

- **Column chunk statistics.** The file metadata holds optional statistics for each column chunk in each row group, including minimum and maximum values and a null count.[^thrift] A reader skips a row group when, for example, its maximum is below the lower bound of a range filter.
- **Page index.** The optional column index stores lower and upper bounds for each data page, and the offset index locates pages by row number, so a reader can skip pages inside a row group.[^pageindex]
- **Bloom filters.** Minimum and maximum values cannot rule out a value that falls inside the range. A split block bloom filter answers whether a value might be present; it can return false positives but never false negatives, which makes it useful for equality filters on high-cardinality columns.[^bloom]

In Spark, Parquet filter pushdown is controlled by `spark.sql.parquet.filterPushdown` (default true); ORC has the equivalent `spark.sql.orc.filterPushdown`.[^sparkparquet][^sqlconf]

## Table format metadata

Table formats keep statistics for each data file in their metadata, so an engine can skip whole files before opening any of them.

In [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), scan planning first skips manifests whose partition summaries show no match. For the remaining manifests, Iceberg converts the query's predicates into partition predicates using the partition spec each manifest was written with, and then filters data files by the column lower and upper bounds and counts stored in the manifests.[^ispec] Because partition values come from transforms, a filter on a timestamp column can prune files of a table partitioned by `day(ts)`.[^ispec]

In [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), `add` actions in the transaction log can carry per-file statistics (record count, per-column minimum and maximum values and null counts), which the protocol describes as usable for eliminating files based on query predicates.[^dproto] Delta Lake collects these statistics automatically on write for columns up to the position set by `delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols`.[^dskip]

## Catalog

Some catalogs accept predicates too. Spark pushes some partition predicates to the Hive metastore so that it lists only matching partitions (`spark.sql.hive.metastorePartitionPruning`, default true).[^sqlconf] The [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification defines a server-side scan planning endpoint (`planTableScan`) whose request includes a filter predicate, so the catalog service can plan which files a client reads.[^rest]

## When pushdown does not happen

A predicate is pushed only if the engine can translate it into a form the source understands. Common reasons it stays in the engine:

- **Casts on the column.** Comparing a string column with a number makes Spark cast the column (`cast(code as bigint) = 7`), which has no translation to a source filter. Only `IsNotNull(code)` is pushed in the example below.
- **Functions and UDFs.** A predicate such as `upper(code) = 'A'` or a user-defined function cannot be compared with stored minimum and maximum values, so it is evaluated after the scan.
- **Non-deterministic expressions.** Spark does not push down non-deterministic filters, such as one that uses `rand()`, because a source might evaluate them a different number of times than Spark does.[^pdu][^fss]
- **Missing statistics.** File skipping needs statistics on the filtered column; Delta Lake, for example, collects none for columns past `delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols`.[^dskip]

## How to check

In Spark, `EXPLAIN` shows what was pushed. For a file scan, `PartitionFilters` lists predicates used to prune directories, `PushedFilters` lists filters handed to the file reader, and `DataFilters` lists data-column predicates before translation. The following output, from a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, shows a partition column filter, a pushed range filter, and a cast that blocks pushdown (paths shortened):

```
EXPLAIN SELECT order_id FROM orders
WHERE order_date = DATE'2026-11-01' AND amount > 100;

FileScan parquet spark_catalog.default.orders[order_id#20L,amount#21,order_date#23]
  DataFilters: [isnotnull(amount#21), (amount#21 > 100.0)],
  PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(order_date#23), (order_date#23 = 2026-11-01)],
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount), GreaterThan(amount,100.0)]

EXPLAIN SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE code = 7;   -- code is a STRING

Filter (isnotnull(code#22) AND (cast(code#22 as bigint) = 7))
+- FileScan parquet ... PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(code)]
```

A filter listed in `PushedFilters` can still appear in a `Filter` operator above the scan, because Parquet skips data by row group and page, not by row. The plan shows what was pushed, not how much data was skipped; the SQL tab of the Spark web UI shows run-time metrics for the scan, such as `number of output rows` and `scan time`.[^spdf][^webui]

  <Field name="type">Transactional data catalog with Git-like versioning</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[projectnessie.org](https://projectnessie.org/)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/projectnessie/nessie](https://github.com/projectnessie/nessie)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the projectnessie/nessie GitHub releases (latest nessie-0.110.1) and CHANGELOG.md, the Nessie README, transactions guide, Iceberg REST guide and configuration reference, the August 2024 Nessie blog post on Apache Polaris, the October 2020 Dremio announcement, CatalogUtil.java at apache-iceberg-1.12.0 and the Trino 484 metastore documentation</Verified>

<Status level="active">Nessie is still released (0.110.1 on 21 November 2026) and no Nessie release or announcement deprecates it. In 2024 the Nessie team announced an intent to contribute Nessie's versioning features to [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris); that plan has not retired Nessie.[^releases]</Status>

**Project Nessie** is an open source transactional [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) for data lakes that versions table metadata with Git-like commits, branches and tags.[^readme] A change to several tables can be made on a branch and published with one merge, so readers see all of the changes or none of them.[^tx] Nessie works with [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables and is reached through its own API or through the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) API.[^readme][^rest]

## How it works

Nessie keeps a commit log of catalog changes, not of data files. Each commit records the operations it made, a timestamp and the user, and a single commit can change many tables at once.[^tx] For an Iceberg table, the catalog entry points to the table's current metadata; the data and metadata files stay in object storage.

- **Branches** are named, movable pointers to commits. Work done on a branch is invisible on `main` until it is merged.[^tx]
- **Tags** are named references to a fixed commit, used to pin a consistent state of many tables.[^guides]
- **Merges** publish a series of commits from one branch to another as one consistent view, which is how Nessie gives cross-table visibility to engines that have no multi-table transactions of their own.[^tx]

The transactions guide describes three optimistic isolation levels (read committed, repeated read and serializable), with conflicts detected per table; pessimistic locking is not available.[^tx] Nessie stores its commit log in a pluggable version store; the configuration reference covers JDBC, RocksDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, Bigtable and in-memory stores.[^config]

## How engines connect

Engines reach Nessie in two ways.

|  | Nessie catalog client | Iceberg REST API |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Endpoint | Nessie's own REST API | `/iceberg` on the Nessie server (port 19120 in the default Docker image)[^rest][^readme] |
| Client side | Iceberg's `NessieCatalog` (catalog type `nessie`); Trino's `nessie` Iceberg catalog type[^icebergcat][^n1] | Any Iceberg REST client |
| Choosing a branch | A client property naming the reference | The branch or tag name in the URI, with a mandatory `\|` before the warehouse name, for example `/iceberg/experiments\|sales`[^rest] |
| Maturity | The original integration | Added in Nessie 0.90.2 (June 2024) as beta;[^changelog] the current guide calls it experimental[^rest] |

With the Iceberg REST API, Nessie also manages table locations and vends storage credentials; the guide requires at least one object store and one warehouse to be configured, and notes that some storage integrations are still experimental.[^rest]

## Status

Nessie is an active project. Its latest release is 0.110.1, published on 21 November 2026, and the 0.x version numbers continue; no release marks the project or its server as deprecated.[^releases] Individual parts have been deprecated inside the project, for example the older JDBC, Cassandra and MongoDB version store types in favor of their `JDBC2`, `CASSANDRA2` and `MONGODB2` replacements.[^changelog]

On 2 August 2024, after Snowflake open-sourced the Polaris catalog, the Nessie project wrote that the intent is to contribute Nessie's capabilities, such as catalog-level versioning, Git-like semantics and multi-table transactions, to [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris).[^polaris] The post did not announce an end date for Nessie, and Nessie releases have continued since.[^polaris][^releases]

## History

Dremio announced Project Nessie on 1 October 2020; the announcement by Jacques Nadeau said a small team at Dremio had spent more than a year building it.[^n2] In October 2024 Dremio announced a commercial catalog built on Nessie.[^n3]

# Project Tungsten

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Tungsten, Tungsten execution engine</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query execution performance</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Spark 1.4.0 (first pieces); phase 1 completed in Spark 1.5.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Explicit (on-heap or off-heap) memory management, `UnsafeRow` binary row format, cache-aware sorting and hashing, code generation including whole-stage code generation</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer), [Whole-stage code generation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">SPARK-7075, SPARK-7081, SPARK-9697, SPARK-10708 and SPARK-12795, the Spark 1.4.0, 1.5.0 and 2.0.0 release notes, the v1.5.0, v1.6.0, v2.0.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (SQLConf, SetCommand, SparkEnv, ShuffleManager, MemoryManager, TaskMemoryManager, UnsafeRow, WholeStageCodegenExec, docs/configuration.md) and EXPLAIN output from a Spark 4.3 build</Verified>

<Status level="active">Project Tungsten is not deprecated in any Spark release. It was a performance initiative, not a feature with an on/off switch; its code is the default execution path in Spark 4.3.0. Only its old configuration flag, `spark.sql.tungsten.enabled`, was deprecated (Spark 1.6.0) and later dropped.[^mm430]</Status>

**Project Tungsten** is the name of an [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) engineering initiative, started in 2015, to make Spark's execution more efficient in CPU and memory by managing memory explicitly, storing rows in a compact binary format, using CPU caches better and generating code at run time.[^jira7075] Tungsten is not a separate engine or a module that can be installed or turned off: its results (for example the `UnsafeRow` format, Tungsten-managed memory pages and whole-stage code generation) are part of how Spark SQL and DataFrame queries run in every current release. The name survives mostly in source code, configuration aliases and older documentation.

## What the name referred to

The umbrella ticket SPARK-7075, "Project Tungsten (Spark 1.5 Phase 1)", states the premise: most Spark workloads observed by its authors were bottlenecked by CPU and memory rather than by I/O or network. It names three areas of work:[^jira7075][^blog2015]

- **Memory management and binary processing.** Keep data in a binary format instead of as Java objects, to reduce garbage collection overhead and memory use; account for memory in bytes; and let operators that know the data types work directly on the binary data without serialization.
- **Cache-aware computation.** Algorithms and data structures, such as sorting and hashing, laid out to make better use of CPU caches.
- **Code generation.** Generate code at run time for expression evaluation and serialization, to use modern compilers and CPUs better.

The work arrived over several releases. The Spark 1.4.0 release notes list SPARK-7081, a faster sort-based shuffle path, as "Initial performance improvements in project Tungsten".[^r140][^n1] Phase 1 (SPARK-7075) has fix version 1.5.0, and the 1.5.0 release notes say that optimized execution with manually managed memory (Tungsten) was now on by default, together with code generation for expression evaluation.[^jira7075][^r150] A phase 2 umbrella followed (SPARK-9697).[^n2] Whole-stage code generation (SPARK-12795) shipped in Spark 2.0.0, and a 2016 Databricks post by Spark developers presented it as the core of a "second generation Tungsten engine".[^jira12795][^blog2016] The Spark 2.0.0 release notes describe whole-stage code generation without using the Tungsten name.[^n3]

## What remains in Spark 4

Project Tungsten has no deprecation or removal in any Spark release. Its pieces are ordinary parts of the engine:

- **Tungsten memory.** Spark's memory manager still allocates "Tungsten" memory pages for sorting, hashing and shuffle, on the JVM heap by default or off-heap through `sun.misc.Unsafe` when `spark.memory.offHeap.enabled` is true (default false, available since 1.6.0).[^mm430][^tmm430][^conf430] See [Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management).
- **The `UnsafeRow` format.** Spark SQL's internal row format is backed by raw memory instead of Java objects: a null-tracking bit set, one 8-byte word per field, and a variable-length region for strings and other variable-length values.[^unsaferow]
- **Whole-stage code generation.** Enabled by default through the internal setting `spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage` (default true, since 2.0.0). In `EXPLAIN` output, an operator compiled into a generated stage is prefixed with `*(n)`, where n is the code generation stage ID.[^sqlconf430][^wscg430] See [Whole-stage code generation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation).
- **The `tungsten-sort` shuffle alias.** Spark 1.5.0 mapped `spark.shuffle.manager=tungsten-sort` to a separate `UnsafeShuffleManager`. SPARK-10708 merged it into the sort shuffle manager in 1.6.0, and since then `tungsten-sort` is an alias for `SortShuffleManager`, as it still is in 4.3.0.[^env150][^n4][^sm430]

### The `spark.sql.tungsten.enabled` flag

The one Tungsten item that was deprecated is a configuration flag. In Spark 1.5.0, `spark.sql.tungsten.enabled` (default true) switched the Tungsten execution backend and code generation on or off.[^r150][^n5] Spark 1.6.0 removed the option to turn off the unsafe (Tungsten) and code generation paths (SPARK-11644)[^n6] and moved the flag to a list of deprecated keys: setting it logged a warning that the property "is deprecated and will be ignored. Tungsten will continue to be used."[^n7] By Spark 2.0.0 the `SET` command no longer has any special handling for it.[^n8] There has been no way to turn Tungsten off as a whole since 1.6.0.

## Example

This PySpark query runs a filter and an aggregation. After the query has run, `explain()` shows the final adaptive plan, where the `*(1)` prefix marks the three operators that were compiled together into one generated function.

```python
df = spark.range(1000).filter("id % 2 = 0").selectExpr("sum(id)")
df.collect()
df.explain()
```

Part of the output from a Spark 4.3 build:

```
   ResultQueryStage 0
   +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[sum(id#0L)])
      +- *(1) Filter ((id#0L % 2) = 0)
         +- *(1) Range (0, 1000, step=1, splits=1)
```

## What Tungsten is not

- **Not the optimizer.** The [Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer) decides what plan to run; Tungsten work concerns how the chosen physical operators use memory and CPU. The MLlib guide, for example, lists "Tungsten and Catalyst optimizations" as benefits of DataFrames.[^n9]
- **Not a native engine.** Tungsten code runs in the JVM and generates Java code. Native execution engines for Spark, such as Apache Gluten (with Velox) and Apache DataFusion Comet, replace JVM operators with native code; Photon is a proprietary Databricks engine. See [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)).
- **Not available to RDD code.** The binary row format and generated code apply to DataFrame, Dataset and SQL operators, which know the data types. Programs that use the [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) API with arbitrary JVM objects do not get these benefits.[^jira7075]

# RDD

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Resilient distributed dataset</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Partitions, lineage of transformations, lazy transformations and actions, storage levels for persistence</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame), [Dataset (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX), [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/quick-start.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md, core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/rdd/RDD.scala, python/pyspark/core/rdd.py, python/pyspark/sql/connect/dataframe.py), the Spark 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes and the NSDI 2012 RDD paper</Verified>

<Status level="active">The RDD API is not deprecated in any Spark release up to 4.3.0; only some individual methods are. It is not supported by [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).[^connect]</Status>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **resilient distributed dataset** (**RDD**) is an immutable collection of elements split into partitions across the nodes of a cluster, which can be processed in parallel and is rebuilt from its lineage when a partition is lost.[^guide] The RDD was Spark's main programming interface before Spark 2.0; since then the Spark documentation recommends the [Dataset](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)) and [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) APIs, which run through the Catalyst optimizer, while stating that the RDD interface is still supported.[^quick] RDDs still underlie older libraries such as [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX) and [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)), but they are not available to [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) clients.[^connect]

## Status

The RDD API is not deprecated. The `RDD` class at the v4.3.0 tag of Spark carries no deprecation annotation, and the Spark 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes list no deprecation of the RDD API.[^rddscala][^r400] Only single methods are deprecated; for example, PySpark's `mapPartitionsWithSplit` is deprecated in favor of `mapPartitionsWithIndex`.[^pyrdd]

The practical limit is Spark Connect. The Spark Connect documentation lists `SparkContext` and RDD as unsupported for both Python and Scala clients.[^connect] In the PySpark Connect client, `DataFrame.rdd` raises a not-implemented error.[^n1] Code that uses RDDs therefore needs a classic Spark application, which is the default: `spark.api.mode` defaults to `classic` in Spark 4.3.0.[^n2]

## How it works

An RDD is created from a file in a Hadoop-supported file system, from a collection in the driver program, or by transforming another RDD.[^guide] The design was described in the 2012 paper *Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing* by Matei Zaharia and others at the University of California, Berkeley.[^paper]

RDDs support two kinds of operations. **Transformations**, such as `map` and `filter`, return a new RDD. **Actions**, such as `reduce` and `collect`, return a value to the driver. Transformations are lazy: Spark records them and computes nothing until an action needs a result.[^guide] Each RDD is divided into [partitions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), and the executors process one partition per task.

Fault tolerance comes from **lineage**, the record of the transformations that built an RDD. If a partition is lost, Spark recomputes it from that record instead of restoring a replica.[^guide][^paper] An RDD can be kept for reuse with `persist()` or `cache()`; `cache()` uses the default storage level `MEMORY_ONLY`, and other storage levels keep the data serialized, on disk or replicated.[^guide]

## RDD compared with DataFrame and Dataset

|  | RDD | DataFrame | Dataset |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Element type | Any JVM or Python object, opaque to Spark | Rows with a schema of named, typed columns | Typed JVM objects with an encoder (Scala and Java only) |
| Optimization | None by Spark SQL; the user's functions run as written | Spark SQL uses the schema to optimize the query | Spark SQL uses the schema to optimize the query |
| Languages | Scala, Java, Python | Scala, Java, Python, R | Scala, Java |
| Spark Connect | Not supported | Supported | Supported in the Scala client |

The Spark quick start recommends the Dataset over the RDD because it is strongly typed like an RDD but has better performance.[^quick] The Spark SQL guide describes the Dataset, added in Spark 1.6, as combining the benefits of RDDs (strong typing and lambda functions) with Spark SQL's optimized execution engine, and a DataFrame as a Dataset organized into named columns. Python and R have no Dataset API but use DataFrames.[^n3][^connect]

## Where RDDs still appear

- **Older libraries.** [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX) represents graphs as RDDs, and a DStream in [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)) is a sequence of RDDs.[^n4] The RDD-based machine learning package, [spark.mllib (RDD-based API)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark.mllib_(RDD-based_API)), is in maintenance mode.
- **Low-level control.** The RDD API gives direct control over partitioning and over functions applied to each element, which some programs use for work that does not fit a tabular schema.
- **Execution internals.** DataFrame and SQL queries also end up as RDDs: in Spark 4.3.0, executing a physical plan node (`SparkPlan.execute()`) returns an RDD of internal rows.[^n5]

## Example

A word count with the RDD API in PySpark, in classic mode:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[*]").getOrCreate()
sc = spark.sparkContext

lines = sc.parallelize(["a b", "b c", "c"])
counts = (lines.flatMap(lambda line: line.split())
               .map(lambda word: (word, 1))
               .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b))

print(sorted(counts.collect()))  # [('a', 1), ('b', 2), ('c', 2)]
```

The same result with the DataFrame API also runs through Spark Connect:

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.createDataFrame([("a b",), ("b c",), ("c",)], ["line"])
df.select(F.explode(F.split("line", " ")).alias("word")).groupBy("word").count().show()
```

# Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Scala_2.12_and_2.13_in_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Scala binary version; Scala cross-build</Field>
  <Field name="field">Build and dependency management</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Scala 2.12 builds in Spark 2.4.0; Scala 2.13 builds in Spark 3.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Scala binary version, artifact suffix (`_2.12`, `_2.13`), Maven profiles</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">pom.xml at the v2.4.0, v3.0.0, v3.2.0, v3.5.0, v4.0.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark, docs/index.md and docs/building-spark.md at v3.5.0 and v4.3.0, the Spark 3.2.0, 3.5.0 and 4.0.0 release notes, SPARK-14220, SPARK-26132, SPARK-25075, SPARK-34218, SPARK-43836 and SPARK-45314, gradle.properties at apache-iceberg-1.12.0, and the Scala binary compatibility documentation</Verified>

<Status level="removed">Removed in Apache Spark 4.0.0. Use Scala 2.13 instead. This status is for Scala 2.12 support. Spark 3.5.0 announced the removal, and from Spark 4.0.0 Scala 2.13 is the only Scala version Spark is built for.[^s45314]</Status>

**Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark** refers to the two Scala versions that [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) was built for during the Spark 3 series, and to the requirement that Scala and Java applications, libraries and connectors use the same Scala version as the Spark build they run on.[^index43] Spark 3.2.0 to 3.5.x published artifacts for both Scala 2.12 and 2.13, with 2.12 as the default build. Spark 4.0.0 removed Scala 2.12, so every Spark 4 release is built only for Scala 2.13.[^s45314] The version shows up in artifact names such as `spark-sql_2.13`, and it has to match for every jar that contains Scala code, including connectors and table format runtimes.

## Status

Scala 2.12 support was removed in Spark 4.0.0 by SPARK-45314, "Drop Scala 2.12 and make Scala 2.13 by default".[^s45314][^r400] The Spark 3.5.0 release notes had announced it in an "Upcoming Removal" section, which said that support for Scala 2.12 would be removed in the next major release and that the minimum Scala version would be 2.13.[^r350] An earlier proposal to make 2.13 the default already in Spark 3.5 (SPARK-43836) was closed as Won't Do.[^s43836]

At the v4.3.0 tag, the root `pom.xml` sets Scala 2.13.18 with binary version 2.13 and defines only a `scala-2.13` profile; there is no Scala 2.12 or Scala 3 build.[^pom430] The Spark 4.3.0 documentation says that Spark runs on Scala 2.13 and that applications using the Scala API must use the Scala version Spark was compiled for, which since Spark 4.0.0 is 2.13.[^index43]

## History

| Spark release | Default Scala build | Other Scala build | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2.4.0 | 2.11 | 2.12 | Scala 2.12 build added (SPARK-14220)[^s14220][^pom240] |
| 3.0.0 | 2.12 | None published (2.13 artifacts came in 3.2.0) | Scala 2.11 removed (SPARK-26132)[^s26132] |
| 3.2.0 | 2.12 | 2.13 | Scala 2.13 build and published artifacts (SPARK-25075, SPARK-34218)[^s25075][^r320] |
| 3.5.0 | 2.12 | 2.13 | Removal of 2.12 announced for the next major release[^r350] |
| 4.0.0 | 2.13 | None | Scala 2.12 removed (SPARK-45314)[^s45314] |
| 4.3.0 | 2.13 | None | No change; Scala 2.13.18[^pom430] |

In the Spark 3 series the 2.13 build was an alternative, not the default. The Spark 3.5.0 build documentation lists Scala 2.12 and 2.13 as supported and explains that switching requires `./dev/change-scala-version.sh 2.13` and the `scala-2.13` Maven or sbt profile.[^build350][^pom350]

## Why the Scala version matters

Scala's binary compatibility guarantee covers releases within one series, such as 2.13.x, and not across series, so code compiled for Scala 2.12 is not guaranteed to run with the Scala 2.13 library.[^scalabc] For that reason Scala libraries are published once per Scala binary version, with the version appended to the artifact name, and Spark follows the same convention: `spark-core_2.12` and `spark-core_2.13` are separate artifacts.[^pom350] The Spark 3.5.0 documentation gives the rule directly: when using Scala 2.13, use Spark compiled for 2.13 and compile applications for 2.13 as well.[^index350]

The rule reaches beyond user code. Connector and table format jars that contain Scala code are built per Scala version too. For example, the [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) documentation lists Spark runtime jars such as `iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.12` and `iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.13`, where the first number is the Spark version and the suffix is the Scala version; at apache-iceberg-1.12.0 the build knows Scala 2.12 and 2.13 and Spark 3.5, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2.[^icegradle] Adding a `_2.12` connector to a Spark 4 cluster is a mismatch, because no Spark 4 build uses Scala 2.12.

Python users of PySpark and clients of [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) do not compile against Spark's Scala classes, so the Scala version is mostly invisible to them. It still matters when they add JVM packages to the server or session, for example with `--packages`, because those jars load into the Scala 2.13 JVM.

## Example

A Maven dependency for Spark SQL 4.3.0 names the Scala binary version in the artifact ID:[^pom430]

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.spark</groupId>
  <artifactId>spark-sql_2.13</artifactId>
  <version>4.3.0</version>
  <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>
```

The equivalent sbt line is `"org.apache.spark" %% "spark-sql" % "4.3.0" % "provided"` with `scalaVersion` set to a 2.13 release; the `%%` operator appends the project's Scala binary version to the artifact name.[^sbt]

# Shuffle

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Exchange (Trino; the `Exchange` operator in Spark plans)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Map side (shuffle write), shuffle files, reduce side (shuffle fetch), stage boundary</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, core DAGScheduler.scala), an EXPLAIN run on a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, the Trino 484 docs and the Apache Flink 2.3 docs</Verified>

A **shuffle** is the step in a distributed query engine that redistributes data across the cluster so that it is grouped differently across [partitions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), for example so that all rows with the same key end up in the same task.[^rddguide] The term is most used in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), where a shuffle copies data between [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) and machines and is one of the most costly operations in a job. Other engines do the same work under other names: [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) calls it an exchange, and [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) distinguishes pipelined shuffles for streaming jobs from blocking shuffles for batch jobs.

## Why a shuffle happens

A Spark task works on one partition at a time. Operations such as `groupBy`, `reduceByKey` or a join need all the values for a key in one place, but those values are usually spread over many partitions and machines. Spark must read from all partitions and bring the values for each key together; this all-to-all step is the shuffle.[^rddguide]

Operations whose output partition depends on many input partitions are often called **wide** transformations, and they cause a shuffle. Operations such as `map` and `filter` have **narrow** dependencies: each output partition depends on one input partition, so Spark can run them together in the same task.[^dag] The Spark documentation lists repartition operations, most `ByKey` operations and joins as operations that can cause a shuffle.[^rddguide] A broadcast join avoids a shuffle by sending the small side to every executor; Spark plans one automatically when a table is smaller than `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (default 10 MB).[^perf]

## Stages and shuffle files

Spark builds stages by cutting the job's graph at shuffle boundaries. One stage writes a set of map output files; the next stage reads those files after all of them are written.[^dag] The writing side is called the map side and the reading side the reduce side, names taken from MapReduce rather than from Spark's own `map` and `reduce` functions.[^rddguide]

On the map side, each task keeps its output in memory until it no longer fits, then sorts it by target partition and writes it to a single file. Reduce tasks then read the sorted blocks that belong to them.[^rddguide] The files go to the directories in `spark.local.dir` (default `/tmp`) and are compressed by default (`spark.shuffle.compress`).[^config] Spark keeps shuffle files until the data that uses them is garbage collected, so that lost work can be recomputed without writing them again; long-running applications can therefore use a lot of disk.[^rddguide]

In a DataFrame or SQL plan, a shuffle shows up as an `Exchange` operator. The plan below, from `EXPLAIN` on a `GROUP BY` with adaptive query execution turned off, aggregates each partition first (`partial_sum`), shuffles by the grouping key into 200 partitions, and then finishes the aggregation:

```
*(2) HashAggregate(keys=[code#14], functions=[sum(amount#13)])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(code#14, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=35]
   +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[code#14], functions=[partial_sum(amount#13)])
      +- *(1) Project [amount#13, code#14]
         +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
            +- FileScan parquet [amount#13,code#14,order_date#15] ...
```

The 200 comes from `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, whose default is 200.[^perf]

## Spill

Shuffle operations build in-memory structures to organize records before or after the transfer. When these do not fit in the [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)'s execution memory, Spark spills them to disk, which adds disk I/O and garbage collection.[^rddguide] Spilled data is compressed by default (`spark.shuffle.spill.compress`).[^config] Spill is a different thing from shuffle files: shuffle files are the normal output of the map side, while spill files are temporary overflow inside one task.

## Adaptive query execution

Adaptive query execution (AQE) re-plans a query while it runs, using statistics from completed shuffle stages. It is on by default since Spark 3.2.0.[^perf]

- **Coalescing partitions.** After a shuffle, AQE merges small contiguous shuffle partitions so that a query does not run many tiny tasks. The target size is `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes` (default 64 MB), but by default (`spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.parallelismFirst` is true) Spark favors parallelism and only enforces a minimum partition size of 1 MB.[^perf]
- **Skew join handling.** A shuffle partition is treated as skewed when it is larger than 5 times the median partition size and larger than 256 MB (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor` and `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes`). AQE splits such partitions in sort-merge joins into smaller tasks, replicating the other side where needed.[^perf]
- **Join conversion.** When runtime statistics show that one side of a sort-merge join is small, AQE can switch to a broadcast hash join and read the shuffle files locally.[^perf]

A storage partition join avoids the shuffle altogether when both sides of a join come from a V2 data source, such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), that reports a compatible partitioning; the plan then has no `Exchange` before the join.[^perf]

## External shuffle service and push-based shuffle

By default, an executor serves its own shuffle files to other executors. The **external shuffle service** is a long-running process on each node that serves shuffle files instead, so they stay available after the executor that wrote them is removed. It is enabled with `spark.shuffle.service.enabled` (default false) and matters most for dynamic allocation.[^jobsched][^config] Spark on Kubernetes does not support it; there, shuffle tracking or decommissioning keeps shuffle data available instead.[^jobsched]

**Push-based shuffle**, added in Spark 3.2.0, has map tasks push their blocks to external shuffle services, which merge them per shuffle partition. Reduce tasks then read a mix of merged partitions and original blocks, which turns many small random disk reads into large sequential reads. It is off by default (`spark.shuffle.push.enabled`) and is supported only on YARN with the external shuffle service.[^config]

## Comparison: how engines exchange data between stages

|  | Apache Spark | Trino | Apache Flink |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Name | Shuffle (`Exchange` in plans) | Exchange[^trino] | Shuffle (pipelined or blocking network exchange)[^flinkshuffle] |
| How data moves | Map tasks write sorted files to local disk; the next stage fetches them after the map stage is done[^dag] | Tasks write into output buffers; tasks of the next stage read them through an exchange client[^trino] | Streaming: pipelined exchange between running tasks. Batch: blocking shuffle (data is persisted and read after it is fully produced) or experimental hybrid shuffle[^flinkshuffle] |
| Failure handling | Lost shuffle output makes Spark rerun the stages that produced it[^dag] | By default a node failure fails the query; with `retry-policy=TASK`, intermediate data is spooled through an exchange manager to storage such as S3 or HDFS[^trinofte] | Batch blocking shuffle keeps persisted results that consumers read later; hybrid shuffle can store data on remote storage[^flinkshuffle] |

# Small files problem

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Small file problem; file fragmentation</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data storage, table maintenance</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Target file size, compaction, write-time file sizing, clustering</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read), [Deletion vector](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 documentation (configuration, maintenance, Spark procedures, Spark writes, Spark Structured Streaming), the Delta Lake optimizations documentation, the Apache Hudi file sizing, clustering and configuration documentation (version 1.2.1), and Apache Spark 4.3.0 (SQLConf.scala and the 4.3.0 documentation)</Verified>

The **small files problem** is the slowdown and extra cost that occur when a table's data is spread across many files that are much smaller than the size the storage and query engines work best with. Every file adds metadata to track, a request to open it, and planning and scheduling work, so a table with many small files is slower to query and maintain than the same data in fewer, larger files.[^hudi-size][^ice-proc] In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), small files come mostly from frequent small writes, and every major [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) provides compaction and write-time sizing to control them.

## Causes

**Streaming and micro-batch writes.** Each batch commits its own files. The Iceberg documentation notes that the amount of data written by a streaming process is typically small, which makes the table metadata track many small files.[^ice-stream] Hudi's clustering documentation describes the same tension: ingestion prefers small files for parallelism and freshness, while queries degrade with many small files.[^hudi-cluster]

**Many partitions per write task.** A file cannot span a table partition, and in Spark a file cannot be larger than the task that writes it. When one Spark task writes to several Iceberg partitions, each partition gets its own, smaller file.[^ice-writes] High-cardinality [partitioning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition) multiplies the number of files per commit.

**Compression and columnar encoding.** The size on disk is much smaller than the in-memory size of the task's rows, because the data is compressed and columnar. The Iceberg documentation gives the example that a 100 MB Spark task produces a file much smaller than 100 MB.[^ice-writes]

**Row-level changes.** Merge-on-read writes add small delete files. Iceberg's maintenance guide recommends compacting small position delete files because of the metadata and file-open overhead they add.[^ice-maint]

## Costs

- **Metadata.** Iceberg tracks every data file in manifests, so more files means more metadata, and small files cause an unnecessary amount of it.[^ice-proc]
- **File open and request cost.** Hudi's documentation points out that object stores such as S3 rate-limit requests per prefix, and that each file needs at least one request regardless of size, plus fixed costs to open and close it.[^hudi-size] Spark models this fixed cost with `spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes` (default 4 MB) when packing files into read partitions.[^sparkconf]
- **Planning and scheduling.** More files mean more tasks, which adds scheduling overhead and memory pressure to Spark, Flink or Hive jobs.[^hudi-size]
- **Storage efficiency.** Many small files can compress less well and need more index and statistics metadata.[^hudi-size]

## Remedies by project

### Apache Iceberg

Iceberg writers roll over to a new file when it reaches `write.target-file-size-bytes`, default 536870912 bytes (512 MB); delete files have a separate target, `write.delete.target-file-size-bytes`, default 64 MB.[^ice-conf] Because a Spark task may be too small to reach the target, the Iceberg documentation advises controlling what data each task receives with `write.distribution-mode` or an explicit repartition.[^ice-writes]

For existing files, the `rewrite_data_files` procedure compacts small files into larger ones, using bin-packing by default or a sort. Its options include `target-file-size-bytes` (defaulting to the table's target), `min-file-size-bytes` (75% of the target), `max-file-size-bytes` (180% of the target) and `min-input-files` (5).[^ice-proc] The `rewrite_manifests` procedure addresses the matching problem in metadata, since fast appends in streaming workloads can leave many small manifest files.[^ice-stream]

```sql
-- Apache Iceberg (Spark SQL): compact one day's files toward 512 MB
CALL catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table   => 'db.events',
  where   => 'event_date = "2026-11-21"',
  options => map('target-file-size-bytes', '536870912')
);
```

### Delta Lake

Delta Lake's `OPTIMIZE` command (from 1.2.0) coalesces small files into larger ones by bin-packing and can be limited to a partition predicate with `WHERE`.[^delta-opt]

Auto compaction (from 3.1.0) runs synchronously after a successful write and compacts small files in the affected partitions. It is enabled with the table property `delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact` or the session setting `spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.enabled`, uses a 128 MB target by default, and is tuned with `spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.maxFileSize` and `spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.minNumFiles`.[^delta-opt]

Optimized writes (from 3.1.0) shuffle data before writing so that each partition receives fewer, larger files, at the cost of extra write latency. The feature is off by default and is enabled with the table property `delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite`, the setting `spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled`, or the writer option `optimizeWrite`; `spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.binSize` (default 512 MiB) sets the target in-memory size of each output file.[^delta-opt]

### Apache Hudi

Hudi sizes files during writes. On insert and upsert, it adds records to existing files smaller than `hoodie.parquet.small.file.limit` (default 104857600 bytes, 100 MB) until they approach `hoodie.parquet.max.file.size` (default 125829120 bytes, 120 MB). The `bulk_insert` operation does not size files this way.[^hudi-size] For merge-on-read tables, `hoodie.merge.small.file.group.candidates.limit` (default 1) limits how many small file groups an upsert may expand, to limit rewriting.[^hudi-size]

After writes, Hudi's clustering table service stitches small files into larger ones and can sort data for locality. It runs inline after each write when `hoodie.clustering.inline` is true, or asynchronously with `hoodie.clustering.async.enabled`; both default to false.[^hudi-cluster][^hudi-conf] Files under `hoodie.clustering.plan.strategy.small.file.limit` (default 314572800 bytes) are candidates.[^hudi-conf]

### Apache Spark

Spark settings shape how many files a write produces, independent of the table format.

- `spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile` caps the rows in one output file; the default 0 means no limit.[^sparkconf]
- The `COALESCE`, `REPARTITION`, `REBALANCE` and `REBALANCE_BY_SIZE` SQL hints, and the matching `coalesce` and `repartition` Dataset methods, control the number of output files. `REBALANCE` asks adaptive query execution (AQE) for output partitions of reasonable size, to avoid files that are too small or too big, and is ignored when AQE is disabled.[^spark-hints]
- With AQE (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`, default true), `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled` (default true) merges small shuffle partitions toward `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`.[^spark-tuning][^sparkconf] The Iceberg documentation notes that this advisory size measures shuffle data, not the compressed columnar file, so it must be set larger than the desired file size.[^ice-writes]
- On the read side, `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (default 128 MB) and `spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes` control how many small files are packed into one read partition.[^sparkconf]

# Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Upgrading from Spark 3.5 to 4.0</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">ANSI SQL mode by default, Java 17 and Scala 2.13 only, Python 3.9 minimum, removed Mesos support, deprecated SparkR</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 4.0.0 (released 2025-05-23)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [SparkR](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkR), [Apache Mesos support in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark), [Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Scala_2.12_and_2.13_in_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v3.5.0, v4.0.0, v4.1.0, v4.2.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (docs/index.md, docs/sql-migration-guide.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md, python/docs/source/migration_guide/pyspark_upgrade.rst, SQLConf.scala), the Spark 4.0.0 release notes, the Spark news page and the Spark versioning policy</Verified>

**Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration** is the work of moving [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) applications from the 3.x line (in practice 3.5) to Spark 4.0 or later, the first major release since 3.0. Spark 4.0.0 was released on 23 May 2025.[^news] The changes most likely to break an upgrade are platform minimums (Java 17, Scala 2.13 only, Python 3.9) and the switch of Spark SQL to ANSI mode by default, which turns many silent nulls and overflows into runtime errors.[^r400] Spark 4.0 also removed Apache Mesos support and deprecated SparkR. This page summarizes those changes from the official migration guides; it does not replace them.

## Platform requirements

|  | Spark 3.5 | Spark 4.0 | Spark 4.3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Java | 8, 11, 17 | 17, 21 | 17, 21, 25 |
| Scala | 2.12, 2.13 | 2.13 | 2.13 |
| Python | 3.8+ | 3.9+ | 3.11+ |
| R (SparkR) | 3.5+ | 3.5+ (deprecated) | 4.0+ (deprecated) |

Sources: the "Spark runs on" line of `docs/index.md` at each tag.[^idx350][^idx400][^idx430] Spark 4.1 raised the Python minimum to 3.10, and Spark 4.2 added Java 25.[^n1][^n2]

- **Java.** SPARK-45315 dropped JDK 8 and 11 and made JDK 17 the default.[^r400] Hive metastore clients older than Hive 2.0.0 are no longer supported, because they need JDK 8.[^sqlmig]
- **Scala.** SPARK-45314 dropped Scala 2.12 and made 2.13 the default. Applications and libraries compiled for Scala 2.12 must be rebuilt for 2.13.[^r400][^idx400] See [Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Scala_2.12_and_2.13_in_Spark).
- **Python.** SPARK-47993 dropped Python 3.8. PySpark 4.0 also raised the minimum versions of pandas to 2.0.0, NumPy to 1.21 and PyArrow to 11.0.0.[^pymig]

## ANSI SQL mode by default

SPARK-44444 made Spark SQL use ANSI mode by default.[^r400] In Spark 4.0, `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` defaults to true unless the environment variable `SPARK_ANSI_SQL_MODE` is set to `false`.[^conf] In ANSI mode Spark throws an error at runtime, instead of returning null, when the inputs to a SQL operator or function are invalid; examples are integer overflow and invalid casts from string to a number.[^conf][^n3]

```sql
-- Spark 3.5 default: returns NULL.  Spark 4.0 default: fails with a CAST_INVALID_INPUT error.
SELECT CAST('abc' AS INT);

-- Works in both: try_cast returns NULL for invalid input.
SELECT try_cast('abc' AS INT);

-- Restore the Spark 3 behaviour for a session.
SET spark.sql.ansi.enabled = false;
```

Pipelines that relied on silent nulls should move to the `try_*` functions or fix the data, rather than turning ANSI mode off everywhere. The pandas API on Spark is a special case: in Spark 4.0.0 it fails with a `PANDAS_API_ON_SPARK_FAIL_ON_ANSI_MODE` error when ANSI mode is on, unless the pandas-on-Spark option `compute.fail_on_ansi_mode` is set to `False` (SPARK-52026).[^n4]

## Other SQL behaviour changes

The Spark 3.5 to 4.0 section of the SQL migration guide lists many changes. Among those most likely to matter in a lakehouse:[^sqlmig]

| Change in Spark 4.0 | Setting to restore the old behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `CREATE TABLE` without `USING` or `STORED AS` uses `spark.sql.sources.default` (Parquet by default) instead of Hive. | `spark.sql.legacy.createHiveTableByDefault=true` |
| The default ORC compression codec changed from `snappy` to `zstd`. | `spark.sql.orc.compression.codec=snappy` |
| `spark.sql.maxSinglePartitionBytes` defaults to `128m` instead of `Long.MaxValue`. | Set it to `9223372036854775807` |
| The `spark.sql.legacy.*` datetime rebase configs for Parquet and Avro were removed. | Use the same names without `legacy.`, for example `spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInWrite` |
| `spark.sql.legacy.timeParserPolicy` defaults to `CORRECTED` instead of `EXCEPTION`. | Set it back to `EXCEPTION` |
| Views tolerate column type changes in the underlying query and compensate with casts. | `spark.sql.legacy.viewSchemaCompensation=false` |
| JDBC type mappings changed for PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and DB2 (for example timestamps and small integer types). | Per-database `spark.sql.legacy.*` flags listed in the guide |

## Core and cluster changes

From the core migration guide for 3.5 to 4.0:[^coremig]
- Support for Apache Mesos as a resource manager was removed (SPARK-44442).[^r400] See [Apache Mesos support in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark).
- Internal servlet API references moved from `javax` to `jakarta`, which affects custom UI and servlet code.
- Event logs are rolled and compressed by default (`spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled`, `spark.eventLog.compress`).
- Speculative execution is less aggressive: `spark.speculation.multiplier=3` and `spark.speculation.quantile=0.9`.
- On Kubernetes, executor pods are allocated in batches of 10, and persistent volume claims use `ReadWriteOncePod`.
- The default Ivy user directory is `~/.ivy2.5.2`.

## Removed and deprecated APIs

| Item | Status in Spark 4.0 | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apache Mesos resource manager | Removed | SPARK-44442[^r400] |
| Scala 2.12 builds | Removed | SPARK-45314[^r400] |
| Java 8 and 11 | No longer supported | SPARK-45315[^r400] |
| [SparkR](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkR) | Deprecated, still shipped (the `R` directory is present at the v4.3.0 tag) | SPARK-49347[^r400][^idx430] |
| Hive metastore versions before 2.0.0 | Removed | SPARK-45328[^r400] |
| Deprecated pandas API on Spark methods (for example `DataFrame.append`, `iteritems`, `to_koalas`) | Removed | PySpark migration guide[^pymig] |
| `pyspark.ml.connect` | Deprecated in favour of `pyspark.ml` on Spark Connect | SPARK-50828[^r400] |

## Spark Connect in Spark 4

Spark 4.0 is the first major release in which [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) is close to the classic API. The release notes list Scala client parity with the Dataset and DataFrame API, `pyspark.ml` support on Connect, a lightweight `pyspark-client` Python package, an extra release tarball with Connect enabled by default, and the `spark.api.mode` setting to switch an application between classic and Connect.[^r400] A migration is therefore a natural point to check whether code uses APIs that Connect does not have, such as RDDs and `SparkContext`.

## Timing

Spark 3.5 has an extended long-term support period that ends in November 2027, during which only security fixes are released.[^policy] Non-LTS release branches are generally maintained with bug fix releases for six months, and the policy names Spark 4.5.0 as the planned LTS release of the 4.x line.[^policy] Later 4.x releases have their own migration sections (4.0 to 4.1, 4.1 to 4.2, 4.2 to 4.3) in the same guide.[^n5]

# Spark Connect

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 3.4.0 (2023)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Client-server protocol for Apache Spark</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Spark Connect overview](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-connect-overview.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (sql/connect)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/sql/connect)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Spark Connect documentation and source at tag v4.3.0, Spark release notes 3.4.0, 3.5.0 and 4.0.0, and PyPI</Verified>

**Spark Connect** is a client-server interface for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) in which a thin client library sends DataFrame operations to a remote Spark server as unresolved logical plans and receives the results over the network.[^overview] Spark Connect separates the application process from the Spark driver, so an application can run in an IDE, a notebook or a service without sharing a process or dependencies with the cluster. It was introduced in Spark 3.4.[^overview]

## How it works

The Spark Connect client translates DataFrame operations into unresolved logical query plans, encodes them with Protocol Buffers and sends them to the server with gRPC.[^overview]

The Spark Connect endpoint on the server translates the received plans into Spark's logical plan operators, much as Spark parses a SQL query, and then runs them through the normal Spark optimizer and execution engine. Results return to the client over gRPC as Apache Arrow-encoded row batches.[^overview]

By default, a Spark Connect server listens on port 15002. The port is set by the static configuration `spark.connect.grpc.binding.port`, which has existed since Spark 3.4.0.[^overview][^n1] Clients address the server with a connection string that starts with `sc://`, for example `sc://localhost:15002`, given either in code or in the `SPARK_REMOTE` environment variable.[^overview]

## Differences from classic Spark

Spark Connect changes what an application can reach, because the client runs outside the driver process:[^overview]

- The client cannot access the driver JVM. In PySpark, the client does not use Py4J, so private fields such as `df._jdf` are not available.
- The protocol describes work as logical plans, so it does not support every Spark execution API. Most importantly, RDDs are not supported.
- Each client gets its own session. The client cannot change cluster-wide settings, and it has no access to the static Spark configuration or to the `SparkContext`.

The Spark documentation names stability, upgradability and debuggability as operational reasons for this split: an application that uses too much memory affects only its own process, the server can be upgraded independently of client applications, and applications can be debugged in a local IDE.[^overview]

## Using Spark Connect

A server is started from a Spark distribution with the `sbin/start-connect-server.sh` script. A PySpark application then connects by passing a remote address when it builds the session:[^overview]

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
spark.range(10).filter("id % 2 = 0").show()
```

The shells accept the same address with `--remote`, for example `./bin/pyspark --remote "sc://localhost"`.[^overview] Scala applications use the `spark-connect-client-jvm` artifact and the same `remote` builder method. Scala code that contains user-defined functions must upload its class files and JAR dependencies to the server, for example with `SparkSession#addArtifact`.[^overview]

For Python, the `pyspark-client` package on PyPI contains only the Spark Connect client, without the JVM parts of PySpark.[^overview] Its latest version on 22 November 2026 is 4.3.0.[^n2]

Since Spark 4.0, the `spark.api.mode` configuration (values `classic` or `connect`, default `classic`) lets an existing classic application run through Spark Connect without code changes, by starting a local Spark Connect server for it.[^n3][^n4]

## Clients

| Client | Where it lives | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python (PySpark) | apache/spark | First released in Spark 3.4.0[^r340] |
| Scala | apache/spark | First released in Spark 3.5.0[^r350] |
| Go | [apache/spark-connect-go](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-go) | Announced with Spark 3.5.0[^r350] |
| Swift | [apache/spark-connect-swift](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-swift) | Announced with Spark 4.0.0[^r400] |
| Rust | [apache/spark-connect-rust](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust) | [^n5] |

## History

Spark Connect was proposed in the Spark Project Improvement Proposal (SPIP) tracked as SPARK-39375, filed in June 2022.[^n6] Spark 3.4.0 shipped the Python client.[^r340] Spark 3.5.0 added the Scala client, Structured Streaming support in Python and Scala, and pandas API on Spark support for the Python client.[^r350] Spark 4.0.0 added the `pyspark-client` package, an extra release tarball with Spark Connect enabled by default, the `spark.api.mode` setting and machine learning on Spark Connect.[^r400] Spark 4.3.0 added REST endpoints for inspecting sessions and operations, operation IDs for request attribution, and a more complete JDBC driver.[^n7]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Spark Connect lets light clients such as notebooks, services and AI agents run queries on a shared Spark cluster that holds the catalog and table format configuration. [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) depends on it: in Spark 4.3 the `spark-pipelines` launcher requires `spark.api.mode` to be `connect` and rejects any other value.[^n8]

# Spark Declarative Pipelines

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 4.1.0 (2025-12-16)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Declarative data pipeline framework</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/declarative-pipelines-programming-guide.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (python/pyspark/pipelines)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/python/pyspark/pipelines)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Declarative Pipelines programming guide, the pyspark.pipelines and SparkPipelines sources at tag v4.3.0, SPARK-51727, and the Spark 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes</Verified>

**Spark Declarative Pipelines** (**SDP**) is a framework in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) for building batch and streaming data pipelines by declaring the datasets a pipeline should produce and the queries that fill them, while Spark handles execution order, parallelism, checkpoints and retries.[^r410] SDP was added in Spark 4.1.0.[^r410] Pipelines are written in Python or SQL and run with the `spark-pipelines` command line tool.[^guide]

## Key concepts

A **flow** reads data from a source, applies processing logic and writes the result into a target dataset. Flows support both streaming and batch semantics. A statement such as `CREATE STREAMING TABLE target_table AS SELECT * FROM STREAM source_table` creates both the table and a flow that writes new source data into it.[^guide]

A **dataset** is a queryable object produced by one or more flows. SDP has three kinds of dataset:[^guide]

| Dataset | Written by | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Streaming table | One or more streaming flows | A table that processes only new data as it arrives (incremental processing). |
| Materialized view | Exactly one batch flow | A view whose result is precomputed and stored as a table. |
| Temporary view | Its defining query | A view scoped to one run of the pipeline, used to share intermediate logic between flows; it cannot be read outside the pipeline. |

A **pipeline** is the unit of development and execution. When a pipeline runs, SDP analyzes the dependencies between its datasets and flows and decides the order of execution and which parts run in parallel.[^guide]

A **sink** lets a pipeline write to a destination outside its own tables, such as Apache Kafka, using any target that a [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) query can write to.[^guide]

## Pipeline spec file

A **pipeline project** is a set of `.py` and `.sql` source files plus a YAML spec file, conventionally named `spark-pipeline.yml` or `spark-pipeline.yaml`. The spec requires `name`, `libraries` (paths to the source files) and `storage` (a directory for streaming checkpoints). It may also set a default `catalog`, a default `database` (alias `schema`) and a `configuration` map of Spark properties.[^guide] An example for Spark 4.3:

```yaml
name: my_pipeline
libraries:
  - glob:
      include: transformations/**
storage: file:///absolute/path/to/storage/dir
catalog: my_catalog
database: my_db
configuration:
  spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "1000"
```

## Defining datasets

The Python API lives in the `pyspark.pipelines` module, conventionally imported as `dp`. In Spark 4.3 it exports `materialized_view`, `table`, `temporary_view`, `append_flow`, `create_streaming_table`, `create_auto_cdc_flow` and `create_sink`.[^n1] A function decorated with `@dp.materialized_view` that returns a batch DataFrame defines a materialized view; one decorated with `@dp.table` that returns a streaming DataFrame defines a streaming table. The dataset takes the function's name unless a `name` argument is given.[^guide]

Since Spark 4.2, SDP injects the `spark` session into each pipeline file, so the file does not need to create one. In Spark 4.1 each file had to assign `spark = SparkSession.active()` itself.[^guide]

```python
from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame

@dp.table
def raw_orders() -> DataFrame:
    return spark.readStream.table("orders_source")

@dp.materialized_view
def orders_by_state() -> DataFrame:
    return spark.table("raw_orders").groupBy("state").count()
```

The same datasets can be declared in SQL with `CREATE STREAMING TABLE ... AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM ...`, `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` and `CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW`. Several flows can append to one streaming table with `@dp.append_flow` in Python or `CREATE FLOW` in SQL.[^guide]

## The spark-pipelines CLI

The `spark-pipelines` CLI is built on `spark-submit` and accepts all of its arguments except `--class`, so it works with every cluster manager that `spark-submit` supports.[^guide] It has three commands:[^guide]

- `spark-pipelines init --name my_pipeline` creates a new project directory with a spec file and example definitions.
- `spark-pipelines run` runs the pipeline and monitors it until it completes. Options include `--spec` (path to the spec file), `--refresh` (update listed datasets), `--full-refresh` (clear and recompute listed datasets, including their checkpoints) and `--full-refresh-all`. Without these options, the run is an incremental update.
- `spark-pipelines dry-run` builds and checks the pipeline without reading or writing any data.

In Spark 4.3, the launcher always runs the pipeline in Spark Connect mode: it sets `spark.api.mode=connect` and fails if a user passes any other value.[^n2] A run can target a remote [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) server with `--remote sc://host:15002`.[^guide]

### Dry runs

A dry run catches many errors that would otherwise appear only during a real run: syntax errors in Python or SQL code, analysis errors such as a reference to a table or column that does not exist, and graph validation errors such as cyclic dependencies between datasets.[^guide] Because it reads and writes no data, a dry run can check a pipeline before it uses compute on real data.

## Change data capture

Spark 4.2.0 added **Auto CDC** to SDP, which applies a stream of insert, update and delete events to a target streaming table as Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD) Type 1 upserts.[^n3] Spark 4.3.0 added SCD Type 2, which keeps the history of how each record changed.[^r430] An Auto CDC flow needs key columns and a sequencing expression, and its target must be a streaming table backed by a format that supports row-level operations (MERGE); Spark's built-in file formats, including Parquet, do not qualify.[^guide]

## History

SDP was proposed in the Spark Project Improvement Proposal tracked as SPARK-51727, opened in April 2025 and resolved with fix version 4.1.0.[^n4] On 11 June 2025, Databricks announced that it would contribute its declarative ETL framework to Apache Spark as Spark Declarative Pipelines.[^n5] A Databricks blog post from the next day traces that framework to Databricks' DLT product.[^n6] Databricks documentation states that its Lakeflow pipelines product is built on SDP.[^n7]

## Use in an open lakehouse

SDP writes its datasets through Spark's catalogs, so the spec's `catalog` and `database` fields can point at a catalog such as an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) or [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog). A pipeline of streaming tables feeding materialized views maps onto the bronze, silver and gold layers of a [medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture). An orchestrator such as [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow) can run `spark-pipelines` as one task in a larger workflow.
