# Spark Streaming (DStreams)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark Streaming, DStream API, discretized streams</Field>
  <Field name="field">Stream processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 0.7.0 (alpha)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`StreamingContext`, DStream, receivers, batch interval, checkpointing</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (`streaming` module)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (streaming module source, PySpark StreamingContext, streaming programming guide), the Spark 0.7.0 and 3.4.0 release notes and SPARK-42075</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="Apache Spark 3.4.0">Use [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) instead. Still included in Spark 4.3.0; the documentation calls it a legacy project that receives no further updates.[^jira][^r340]</Status>

**Spark Streaming**, also called the **DStream API**, is the original stream processing library of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), in which a live data stream is divided into small batches and represented as a **discretized stream** (DStream): a continuous series of RDDs, each holding the data received in one time interval.[^guide] The API has been deprecated since Spark 3.4.0. Spark's documentation calls it the previous generation of Spark's streaming engine and directs all new streaming applications to [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming).[^guide][^jira]

## Status

The DStream API was deprecated in Apache Spark 3.4.0 under SPARK-42075, "Deprecate DStream API", and the 3.4.0 release notes list the deprecation.[^jira][^r340] At the v4.3.0 tag the deprecation is still in place:

- The Scala `StreamingContext` and the Java `JavaStreamingContext` carry `@deprecated("DStream is deprecated. Migrate to Structured Streaming.", "Spark 3.4.0")`.[^scala]
- The PySpark `StreamingContext` constructor issues a `FutureWarning`: "DStream is deprecated as of Spark 3.4.0. Migrate to Structured Streaming." Its docstring adds that there are no longer updates to DStream and that it is a legacy project.[^py]
- The Spark 4.3.0 programming guide opens with a note that Spark Streaming "is the previous generation of Spark's streaming engine", that "there are no longer updates to Spark Streaming and it's a legacy project", and that users should use Structured Streaming.[^guide]

The API has not been removed. The `streaming` module and its programming guide are still part of Spark 4.3.0, and the guide still documents the Kafka and Kinesis integrations.[^guide] No Spark release up to 4.3.0 announces a removal date.

## Programming model

A Spark Streaming application creates a `StreamingContext` with a **batch interval**, such as one second. **Input DStreams** receive data from a source; every input DStream except file streams is associated with a **receiver**, which receives the data and stores it in Spark's memory for processing. Basic sources include sockets and file systems, and advanced sources such as Kafka and Kinesis come from separate artifacts (`spark-streaming-kafka-0-10` and `spark-streaming-kinesis-asl`).[^guide]

Each operation on a DStream becomes an operation on the RDDs underneath it. The API offers RDD-style transformations (`map`, `flatMap`, `reduceByKey`), window operations such as `reduceByKeyAndWindow`, stateful `updateStateByKey`, `transform` for arbitrary RDD-to-RDD functions, and output operations such as `foreachRDD`. Stateful transformations, such as `updateStateByKey` or `reduceByKeyAndWindow` with an inverse function, require a checkpoint directory.[^guide] The window length and sliding interval of a window operation must be multiples of the batch interval.[^guide]

The following PySpark example, adapted from the programming guide, counts words in one-second batches from a socket. On Spark 4.3 it runs but prints the deprecation warning.[^guide][^py]

```python
from pyspark import SparkContext
from pyspark.streaming import StreamingContext

sc = SparkContext("local[2]", "NetworkWordCount")
ssc = StreamingContext(sc, 1)  # 1-second batches; emits a FutureWarning

lines = ssc.socketTextStream("localhost", 9999)
counts = (lines.flatMap(lambda line: line.split(" "))
               .map(lambda word: (word, 1))
               .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b))
counts.pprint()

ssc.start()
ssc.awaitTermination()
```

DStreams are built on RDDs and the `SparkContext`, which the Spark Connect documentation lists as unsupported, so DStream applications cannot run through a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client.[^connect]

## History

Spark Streaming first appeared as an alpha in Spark 0.7.0, which described it as an extension adding near-real-time processing, with transformations such as `map`, `filter`, `reduce` and sliding windows.[^n1] Structured Streaming, built on the Spark SQL engine, arrived as an experimental API in Spark 2.0.0.[^n2] The Spark 4.3 documentation recommends it for all new streaming applications and pipelines.[^guide]

## Migration to Structured Streaming

<Hatnote>Main article: [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Hatnote>

There is no automatic converter. Migration means rewriting the job against the DataFrame API. The table maps DStream concepts to their usual Structured Streaming counterparts in Spark 4.3.[^guide][^ssapis]

| DStream API | Structured Streaming |
| --- | --- |
| `StreamingContext` with a batch interval | `SparkSession`; `spark.readStream` to read, `writeStream` with a processing-time trigger to set the micro-batch interval |
| DStream (series of RDDs) | Streaming DataFrame or Dataset (an unbounded table) |
| RDD transformations (`map`, `reduceByKey`) | DataFrame operations (`select`, `groupBy`, `agg`) or SQL |
| `window`, `reduceByKeyAndWindow` (multiples of the batch interval) | `groupBy(window(...))` on an event-time column, with a [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) for late data |
| `updateStateByKey`, `mapWithState` (Scala and Java)[^n3] | Built-in stateful aggregations, or `transformWithState` (Spark 4.0 and later) for arbitrary state[^tws] |
| `foreachRDD` | `foreachBatch` or a built-in sink |
| `ssc.checkpoint(dir)` | `checkpointLocation` option on each query |
| `spark-streaming-kafka-0-10` | Kafka source and sink in `spark-sql-kafka-0-10`[^n4] |

The word count above becomes the following query, taken from the Structured Streaming quick example.[^ssstart] One semantic difference matters: the DStream version prints counts for each batch, while this query keeps a running count over all data received, because the result table is cumulative and is written in complete mode.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import explode, split

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("StructuredNetworkWordCount").getOrCreate()

lines = (spark.readStream.format("socket")
         .option("host", "localhost").option("port", 9999).load())
words = lines.select(explode(split(lines.value, " ")).alias("word"))
counts = words.groupBy("word").count()

query = counts.writeStream.outputMode("complete").format("console").start()
query.awaitTermination()
```

Unlike DStreams, Structured Streaming queries run on the optimized Spark SQL engine and provide end-to-end [exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics) through checkpointing and write-ahead logs.[^ssindex] Most of the Structured Streaming API, including `DataStreamReader`, `DataStreamWriter` and `StreamingQuery`, is supported in [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).[^connect]

# spark.mllib (RDD-based API)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark.mllib_(RDD-based_API)

<Infobox type="software" name="spark.mllib (RDD-based API)">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 0.8.0 (as MLlib)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, with Python and Java APIs</Field>
  <Field name="type">Machine learning API (RDD-based)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[MLlib: RDD-based API guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/mllib-guide.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (mllib/.../mllib)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/mllib/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/mllib)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/ml-guide.md, docs/mllib-guide.md, docs/ml-migration-guide.md, docs/mllib-pmml-model-export.md, python/pyspark/mllib/), the v2.0.0 to v2.4.0 tags of docs/ml-guide.md, the Spark 2.0.0 and 4.0.0 release notes and SPARK-30934</Verified>

<Status level="maintenance" since="Apache Spark 2.0.0">Use the DataFrame-based `spark.ml` API of [MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib) instead. Only bug fixes are accepted. The package as a whole is not deprecated in any release up to 4.3.0 and is still included.[^guide][^r200]</Status>

**spark.mllib** is the original, [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD)-based API of [MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib), the machine learning library of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), found in the `org.apache.spark.mllib` package in Scala and Java and `pyspark.mllib` in Python.[^rddguide] Since Spark 2.0 it has been in maintenance mode: it receives bug fixes but no new features, and the DataFrame-based `spark.ml` package is the primary machine learning API.[^guide][^r200] The MLlib guide states that neither API is deprecated; spark.mllib is still part of Spark 4.3.0, but it cannot be used from a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client.[^guide][^connect]

## Status

**Is spark.mllib deprecated?** No, as a package it is in maintenance mode, not deprecated.

- **Maintenance mode since 2.0.** The Spark 2.0.0 release notes say the DataFrame-based API became the primary API and the RDD-based API entered maintenance mode.[^r200] The MLlib guide at v4.3.0 says that MLlib still supports the RDD-based API with bug fixes and will not add new features to it.[^guide] The Python package docstring says the same for `pyspark.mllib`.[^pyinit]
- **Planned removal that did not happen.** The MLlib guide in Spark 2.0.0 through 2.4.0 said the RDD-based API was "expected to be removed in Spark 3.0".[^guide240] The guide update for the 3.0 release removed that sentence, and the package was not removed. The package's Scala documentation at v4.3.0 still says the package "will be deprecated" once the DataFrame-based API reaches feature parity, while the MLlib guide says that parity was reached in the Spark 2.x releases; no release has deprecated it.[^n1][^guide][^jira30934]
- **Individual APIs deprecated and removed.** Some classes and methods in the package were deprecated and later removed. Spark 3.0 removed, among others, the Scala classes `LogisticRegressionWithSGD`, `LinearRegressionWithSGD`, `LassoWithSGD` and `RidgeRegressionWithSGD` (deprecated in 2.0), and the `runs` parameter of `KMeans.train` (deprecated in 2.1).[^migration] For the SGD classes, removal meant the public API: at v4.3.0 the Scala classes remain with constructors private to the `mllib` package, used by the PySpark wrappers.[^n2] Those PySpark wrappers are still public in 4.3.0, marked deprecated since 2.0.0, and emit a `FutureWarning`.[^n3]
- **No Spark Connect.** The Spark Connect documentation lists RDD and `SparkContext` as unsupported, so spark.mllib code needs a classic Spark application.[^connect] The DataFrame-based `pyspark.ml` API works on Spark Connect from Spark 4.0.0.[^n4]

## What the package contains

The RDD-based guide at v4.3.0 covers data types (local vectors and matrices, `LabeledPoint`, distributed matrices), basic statistics, linear models, naive Bayes, decision trees and tree ensembles, isotonic regression, alternating least squares, clustering (including streaming k-means), dimensionality reduction (SVD and PCA), feature extraction, frequent pattern mining (FP-growth, association rules, PrefixSpan), evaluation metrics, PMML model export and low-level optimization (SGD and L-BFGS).[^rddguide] Export to the Predictive Model Markup Language (PMML) is documented for spark.mllib models.[^n5]

## spark.mllib compared with spark.ml

|  | spark.mllib | spark.ml |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) of `LabeledPoint` or vectors | [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) with a vector column |
| Training call | Static `train` methods on algorithm objects | `Estimator.fit`, usually inside a `Pipeline` |
| Vector type | `org.apache.spark.mllib.linalg.Vector` | `org.apache.spark.ml.linalg.Vector` |
| New features | None (maintenance mode) | Yes |
| Spark Connect | Not supported | Supported from Spark 4.0.0 (Python) |

The two vector types are separate since Spark 2.0; the RDD-based API still depends on `spark.mllib.linalg`. To move data between them, the migration guide points to `asML` on an mllib vector or matrix, `Vectors.fromML` and `Matrices.fromML`, and the column converters in `MLUtils`.[^migration]

## Migrating to spark.ml

The Spark 3.0 entries in the migration guide name replacements for the removed classes: for example, `org.apache.spark.ml.classification.LogisticRegression` (or `LogisticRegressionWithLBFGS`) instead of `LogisticRegressionWithSGD`, and `org.apache.spark.ml.regression.LinearRegression` with `elasticNetParam` set to 1.0 instead of `LassoWithSGD`. The guide notes that default regularization differs: `regParam` was 0.01 for `LassoWithSGD` and `RidgeRegressionWithSGD`, but is 0.0 for `LinearRegression`.[^migration]

## Example

The same logistic regression in both APIs, in a classic PySpark session where `spark` is the `SparkSession`:

```python
# spark.mllib (RDD-based): classic mode only
from pyspark.mllib.classification import LogisticRegressionWithLBFGS
from pyspark.mllib.regression import LabeledPoint

rdd = spark.sparkContext.parallelize([
    LabeledPoint(0.0, [1.1, 0.1]), LabeledPoint(1.0, [2.0, 1.0]),
    LabeledPoint(0.0, [1.3, -0.5]), LabeledPoint(1.0, [2.2, 1.5])])
old_model = LogisticRegressionWithLBFGS.train(rdd, iterations=10)

# spark.ml (DataFrame-based): also runs on Spark Connect from 4.0.0
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.linalg import Vectors

df = spark.createDataFrame([
    (0.0, Vectors.dense(1.1, 0.1)), (1.0, Vectors.dense(2.0, 1.0)),
    (0.0, Vectors.dense(1.3, -0.5)), (1.0, Vectors.dense(2.2, 1.5))],
    ["label", "features"])
new_model = LogisticRegression(maxIter=10).fit(df)
```

# SparkR

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkR

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 1.4.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">R, Scala</Field>
  <Field name="type">R language frontend for Apache Spark</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[SparkR (R on Spark)](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/sparkr.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (R/)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/R)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.0.0 to v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (docs/sparkr.md, docs/sparkr-migration-guide.md, R/pkg/DESCRIPTION, R/pkg/R/zzz.R), the Spark 1.4.0, 4.0.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, SPARK-49347 and the August 2024 dev-list discussion and vote</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="Apache Spark 4.0.0">Use the separately maintained sparklyr package instead. SparkR is still included in Spark 4.3.0 and has not been removed.[^jira49347]</Status>

**SparkR** is the R package that ships with [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) and lets R programs use Spark: it provides a distributed data frame, the `SparkDataFrame`, with selection, filtering and aggregation, and access to Spark's machine learning library.[^guide] SparkR is deprecated as of Spark 4.0.0 and will be removed in a future version, but it is still part of every release up to Spark 4.3.0.[^guide][^jira49347] The Spark project points R users to sparklyr, a separate R package for Spark.[^zzz]

## Status

SparkR was deprecated in Spark 4.0.0 under SPARK-49347, after a vote on the Spark dev mailing list.[^jira49347][^r400] The deprecation shows up in three places in Spark 4.x:

- **Programming guide.** The SparkR guide opens with the sentence that SparkR is deprecated from Spark 4.0.0 and will be removed in a future version.[^guide]
- **Migration guide.** The SparkR migration guide says, under "Upgrading from SparkR 3.5 to 4.0", that SparkR is deprecated and will be removed in a future version.[^n1]
- **Startup message.** When the package is attached, SparkR prints a warning that it is deprecated and recommends sparklyr. Setting the environment variable `SPARKR_SUPPRESS_DEPRECATION_WARNING` to any non-empty value hides the message.[^zzz]

SparkR has not been removed. The `R/pkg` directory is present at the v4.1.0, v4.2.0 and v4.3.0 tags, with the package version matching each Spark release.[^desc] The Spark 4.1.0 release notes do not mention SparkR. The 4.2.0 release notes list maintenance work on it, such as Java 25 support and dropping support for R 3.x, and none of the 4.x release notes announce a removal.[^n2][^r420][^n3]

## Why it was deprecated

The proposal came from Shivaram Venkataraman, who created the original SparkR package as research at UC Berkeley. In an August 2024 thread on the Spark dev mailing list he argued that sparklyr is more idiomatic R than SparkR's Scala-like API, that contributions to SparkR had slowed, that sparklyr's newer Spark Connect based architecture removed the need to align its version with Spark's, and that sparklyr is maintained on CRAN while SparkR could not stay there under Spark's release process.[^discuss] The vote to deprecate SparkR followed on 21 August 2024, and the deprecation was merged for Spark 4.0.0.[^n4][^jira49347]

## History

Spark 1.4.0 was the first release to package SparkR, described in the release notes as an R binding built on Spark's then-new DataFrame API.[^n5] The SparkR package in Spark 4.3.0 requires R 4.0 or later and Java 17 or later.[^desc]

## How it works

SparkR starts or connects to a Spark application through `sparkR.session()`, which creates a `SparkSession`. From RStudio or another R environment, SparkR uses `SPARK_HOME` to find a Spark installation and can download one if none is found.[^guide] R code talks to the Spark driver JVM through a backend in Spark core (`org.apache.spark.api.r.RBackend`).[^n6] The guide also documents running R functions on the data with `dapply` and `gapply`, Apache Arrow for faster transfer between the JVM and R, and MLlib model training.[^guide]

The following R example runs with the Spark 4.3 distribution. It starts a session, converts the built-in `faithful` data frame to a `SparkDataFrame` and filters it.

```r
library(SparkR)
sparkR.session(appName = "faithful-example")

df <- createDataFrame(faithful)
head(filter(df, df$waiting < 50))

sparkR.session.stop()
```

## Comparison with sparklyr

|  | SparkR | sparklyr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maintained by | The Apache Spark project, inside the Spark repository[^desc] | A separate open source project (github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr)[^sparklyr] |
| Status | Deprecated since Spark 4.0.0[^jira49347] | Recommended by the SparkR startup message[^zzz] |
| Installation | Ships with the Spark distribution; not maintained on CRAN[^discuss] | `install.packages("sparklyr")` from CRAN[^sparklyr] |
| API style | Its own functions over `SparkDataFrame` (`filter`, `select`, `agg`)[^guide] | Described in the deprecation proposal as more idiomatic R[^discuss] |
| Spark Connect | Not a Spark Connect client; connects through the R backend in the driver | `spark_connect(method = "spark_connect")`[^sparklyr] |

# Stream processing

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Streaming, unbounded data processing</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering, distributed systems</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Unbounded input, event time, windows, state, [Watermarks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), triggers, checkpoints</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), Kafka Streams ([Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka))</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse), [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming guides, the Apache Flink 2.3 documentation, the Apache Kafka 4.4 Streams documentation and the Dataflow Model paper (VLDB 2015)</Verified>

**Stream processing** is the continuous computation of results over data that has no defined end, in which an engine processes records as they arrive and keeps its output up to date instead of waiting for a complete dataset. The input is called an **unbounded** dataset or stream; data with a fixed start and end is **bounded**.[^flink-arch] In the open lakehouse, the term covers engines such as [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) and Kafka Streams, which read from message buses and write to tables, topics or other systems.

## Unbounded data, not a kind of engine

The Dataflow Model paper (Akidau et al., Google, published in the Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment in 2015) prefers the terms "unbounded" and "bounded" to "streaming" and "batch", because the latter imply a particular execution engine. The paper notes that unbounded data has long been processed by repeated batch runs, and that well-designed streaming systems can also process bounded data; it reserves "streaming" and "batch" for describing runtime engines.[^dataflow]

The Apache Flink documentation draws the same line: batch processing is processing of a bounded stream, where the engine may read the whole input before producing results (for example, to sort it), while an unbounded stream must be processed continuously as data arrives.[^flink-learn]

## Core ideas

### Event time and processing time

Every record has at least two times. **Event time** is when the event occurred on the device or system that produced it. **Processing time** is the clock time of the machine that handles the record.[^flink-time] Kafka Streams adds a third, **ingestion time**: when a Kafka broker stored the record in a topic partition.[^kstreams]

The Dataflow paper points out that event time for an event never changes, while the skew between event time and processing time varies constantly because of network delays, scheduling and processing time.[^dataflow] Records therefore arrive out of order, and a result grouped by event time is never certain to be complete. A [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) is the engine's estimate of how far event time has progressed, and it lets the engine decide when a result is final.

### Windows

Aggregations over an unbounded stream need finite groups, called **windows**. Three types are common across engines:[^dataflow][^ss-apis][^flink-time]

| Window | Definition | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tumbling (fixed) | Fixed size, non-overlapping, contiguous intervals; each record belongs to one window | Counts per 5-minute interval |
| Sliding | Fixed size with a slide shorter than the size, so windows overlap and a record can belong to several | 10-minute windows starting every 5 minutes |
| Session | Variable size; a window grows while records keep arriving within a gap duration, and closes after a gap with no input | One window per user visit, closed after 30 idle minutes |

In PySpark the three types map to two functions: `window()` for tumbling and sliding windows and `session_window()` for session windows.[^ss-apis]

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import window, session_window

events.groupBy(window("ts", "5 minutes"))                 # tumbling
events.groupBy(window("ts", "10 minutes", "5 minutes"))   # sliding
events.groupBy("user", session_window("ts", "30 minutes")) # session
```

### State

Aggregations, joins and deduplication must remember earlier records, so the engine keeps **state** between inputs. Structured Streaming keeps it in a state store, with an optional RocksDB-based provider.[^ss-apis] Flink keeps task state in memory and moves large state to on-disk structures.[^flink-arch] State grows without bound unless something says when old entries can be dropped; in event-time queries that signal is the watermark.[^ss-apis]

### Triggers, latency and throughput

A **trigger** decides when an engine computes and emits results. Engines that group records into small batches gain throughput and simpler fault tolerance, but each batch adds scheduling overhead that sets a floor on latency. Engines that keep long-lived tasks and handle each record as it arrives reach lower latency.[^ss-rtm]

## Execution models

<Hatnote>Main article: [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Hatnote>

Two execution models are common:

- **Micro-batch**: the engine runs the query as a series of small batch jobs. This is the default in [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), with end-to-end latencies as low as about 100 milliseconds and exactly-once guarantees.[^ss-index]
- **Continuous or record-at-a-time**: long-running operators process each record as it arrives. Kafka Streams describes its processing as one record at a time, with millisecond latency.[^kstreams] Flink processes unbounded streams continuously and keeps state local to each task for low latency.[^flink-arch]

Spark offers three modes on the same DataFrame API. The Spark 4.3 documentation compares them as follows:[^ss-rtm]

| Spark mode | Typical latency | Processing guarantee | Supported queries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Micro-batch (default) | About 100 ms | Exactly-once | All streaming operations |
| Real-time Mode (Spark 4.1.0 and later) | Millisecond scale | Exactly-once | Stateless queries; since Spark 4.3.0 also deduplication, aggregation and JVM `transformWithState` |
| Continuous Processing (experimental) | About 1 ms | At-least-once | Map-like operations only; the documentation calls it legacy and points to Real-time Mode |

In Real-time Mode, the trigger duration (default 5 minutes) is mainly a checkpoint interval, not a latency target; records are processed and emitted as they arrive.[^ss-rtm]

## Comparison with batch processing

|  | Batch processing | Stream processing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | Bounded; all data present at start | Unbounded; data keeps arriving |
| Completeness | Known when the job starts | Estimated, usually with a watermark |
| Output | Produced once, at the end | Produced incrementally and updated |
| Failure recovery | Rerun the job | Restart from a checkpoint and replay the source |

The boundary is not strict. Structured Streaming's available-now trigger processes all data present at start and then stops, which runs a streaming query as an incremental batch job.[^ss-apis] In a [streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse), the same table is written by a stream and read by batch queries.

# Streaming lakehouse

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Real-time lakehouse, streaming into the lakehouse</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering, [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Streaming writers, [Open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), incremental and change-data reads, table maintenance</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Paimon](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Paimon), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Spark and Flink documentation, the Delta Lake streaming, change data feed and optimization documentation, the Apache Hudi 1.2.1 documentation, the Apache Paimon 1.4 documentation and 2024 graduation announcement, the Apache Fluss 0.9 documentation and the Spark 4.3.0 Declarative Pipelines guide</Verified>

A **streaming lakehouse** is a data architecture in which streaming jobs write directly into tables in an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), so that the same tables serve both streaming readers, which consume new changes incrementally, and batch readers, which query a consistent snapshot. It applies the [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse) idea to continuously arriving data: instead of keeping a separate real-time store next to the lake, the table itself is the hand-off point between pipeline stages.

## Terminology

The term is used loosely and has no single defining paper or specification. Some projects use it as a name for their own design:

- [Apache Paimon](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Paimon), formerly Flink Table Store, describes itself as "a lake format for building Lakehouse Architecture for both streaming and batch operations".[^paimon-tlp][^paimon-docs] The Apache Software Foundation's announcement of Paimon's graduation to a top-level project, on 16 April 2024, calls it "a streaming data lake platform" and a format that enables real-time lakehouse architectures.[^paimon-tlp]
- Apache Fluss, a streaming storage project (incubating at its 0.9 release), uses "Streaming Lakehouse" as the name of the setup in which its tiering service moves table data into Paimon or Iceberg, with recent data held in Fluss and historical data in the lake table, and queries combining both.[^fluss]

[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) document the same pattern (streaming writes and incremental reads on one table) without using the name. This page uses "streaming lakehouse" for the general pattern, not for any one product.

## How it works

A streaming lakehouse has three moving parts.

### Streaming writes

A streaming engine writes each micro-batch or checkpoint interval as one atomic commit to the table. [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) can write to Iceberg tables in append or complete output mode, to Delta tables, and to Hudi tables.[^iceberg-ss][^delta-stream][^hudi-ss] The Iceberg Flink sink commits to the table after each successful Flink checkpoint and supports upserts on tables with a primary key or identifier fields.[^iceberg-flink] Because each commit is atomic, batch readers never see a half-written batch, and the sink can be part of an [exactly-once](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics) pipeline.[^delta-stream]

### Incremental and change-data reads

Downstream jobs read only what changed since their last position, which turns each table into a source for the next stage, as in a [medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture). What a reader can see differs by format:

| Format | Incremental read | Updates and deletes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) | Spark streaming reads start from a timestamp (`stream-from-timestamp`); Flink streaming reads start from a snapshot and poll for new ones[^iceberg-ss][^iceberg-flinkq] | Spark streaming reads only append snapshots; overwrite and delete snapshots raise an error unless skipped with `streaming-skip-overwrite-snapshots` or `streaming-skip-delete-snapshots`[^iceberg-ss] |
| [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) | A streaming read processes the existing table and then new data[^delta-stream] | Plain streaming reads fail on non-append commits unless `skipChangeCommits` is set; the change data feed (`readChangeFeed`) returns row-level inserts, updates and deletes[^delta-stream][^delta-cdf] |
| [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) | Incremental queries return data written since an instant on the table's timeline[^hudi-types] | Incremental CDC queries return inserts, updates and deletes with before and after images[^hudi-types] |
| [Apache Paimon](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Paimon) | Streaming updates on an LSM-tree structure, typically written with Flink[^paimon-docs] | Changelog producers generate a complete changelog for merge engines[^paimon-docs] |

The Delta change data feed is enabled with the table property `delta.enableChangeDataFeed` and adds the columns `_change_type` (`insert`, `update_preimage`, `update_postimage` or `delete`), `_commit_version` and `_commit_timestamp`. Only changes made after it is enabled are recorded.[^delta-cdf]

### Declarative streaming tables

[Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) (SDP) expresses the pattern declaratively. An SDP **streaming table** is a table filled by one or more streaming flows that process only new data, and it can read from any source that `spark.readStream` supports, including Kafka.[^sdp] In Spark 4.3, **Auto CDC** applies a stream of change events to a target streaming table by key and sequence value, handling out-of-order and duplicate events.[^sdp]

```sql
CREATE STREAMING TABLE orders
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM orders_source;
```

## Example

This PySpark sketch writes a Kafka topic into an Iceberg table once a minute, then reads the same table as a batch snapshot and as an incremental stream. It assumes the Iceberg Spark runtime and Kafka connector are on the classpath and that a catalog named `lake` is configured.

```python
orders = (
    spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "orders")
    .load()
    .selectExpr("CAST(key AS STRING) AS order_id",
                "CAST(value AS STRING) AS payload",
                "timestamp")
)

(orders.writeStream.format("iceberg")
    .outputMode("append")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")          # one commit per minute
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/bronze_orders")
    .toTable("lake.bronze.orders"))

spark.table("lake.bronze.orders").count()        # batch reader: a snapshot
spark.readStream.format("iceberg").load("lake.bronze.orders")  # streaming reader
```

## Limits

### Latency is bounded by commit frequency

Readers see new data only after it is committed, so freshness is set by how often the writer commits, not by how fast the engine processes records. Iceberg recommends a trigger interval of at least 1 minute for streaming writes, because frequent commits create many data files, manifests and snapshots.[^iceberg-ss] With Flink, Iceberg commits follow checkpoints, so the checkpoint interval is also the commit interval.[^iceberg-flink] Systems such as Fluss address this by keeping the most recent data in a separate low-latency store and combining it with the lake table at query time.[^fluss]

### Small files and metadata growth

<Hatnote>See also: [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Hatnote>

Each streaming commit usually writes small files. Iceberg's documentation states that streaming writes typically produce small amounts of data per commit, leading to many small files, and recommends compacting data files (`rewrite_data_files`), expiring old snapshots and rewriting manifests (`rewrite_manifests`) on tables written by streams.[^iceberg-ss] Delta Lake offers `OPTIMIZE` to coalesce small files, and since Delta 3.1.0, auto compaction and optimized writes.[^delta-opt] In Hudi, merge-on-read tables lower write latency for near real-time availability, at the cost of query performance until log files are compacted.[^hudi-types] See [Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read).

### Updates downstream

Append-only incremental reads are the simplest case. When an upstream table receives updates or deletes, downstream streams need a change feed (Delta, Hudi, Paimon) or must skip those commits and lose the changes, as with Iceberg's and Delta's skip options.[^iceberg-ss][^delta-stream]

# Structured Streaming

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 2.0.0 (2016-07-26, experimental)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Java, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Stream processing engine</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/streaming/index.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark](https://github.com/apache/spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming guides (overview, APIs, Real-time Mode, transformWithState) and the Spark 2.0.0, 2.2.0, 4.0.0, 4.1.0 and 4.3.0 release notes</Verified>

**Structured Streaming** is the stream processing engine of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), built on the Spark SQL engine, in which a streaming computation is written with the same DataFrame and Dataset operations as a batch computation on static data.[^overview] Spark runs the query incrementally as new data arrives and keeps the result up to date. Through checkpointing and write-ahead logs, Structured Streaming provides end-to-end exactly-once guarantees with sources and sinks that support them.[^overview]

## Programming model

Structured Streaming treats a live data stream as a table that grows as new rows arrive. A streaming query is a query on that input table, and its output is a result table that Spark updates each time it processes new data.[^start]

The **output mode** says what part of the result table is written to the sink after each update:[^start]

- **Append**: only rows added since the last trigger. It applies to queries whose existing result rows never change.
- **Complete**: the entire result table.
- **Update**: only rows that changed since the last trigger (available since Spark 2.1.1). Without aggregations it behaves like append mode.

Streaming queries can aggregate over event-time windows, including tumbling, sliding and session windows. A **watermark** tells Spark how late data may arrive, so that it can finalize old windows and drop their state. Structured Streaming also supports stream-static joins, stream-stream joins and deduplication.[^apis]

The following PySpark example counts rows from the built-in `rate` test source in 30-second event-time windows and prints finished windows to the console. It runs on Spark 4.3.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import window

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("rate-counts").getOrCreate()

events = spark.readStream.format("rate").option("rowsPerSecond", 10).load()

counts = (
    events.withWatermark("timestamp", "1 minute")
    .groupBy(window("timestamp", "30 seconds"))
    .count()
)

query = (
    counts.writeStream.outputMode("append")
    .format("console")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/rate-counts-checkpoint")
    .start()
)
query.awaitTermination()
```

## Sources, sinks and state

Built-in sources include files, Apache Kafka, a socket source for testing and rate sources that generate test data.[^apis] Built-in sinks include files, Kafka, `foreach`, `foreachBatch`, and console and memory sinks for debugging.[^apis] Connectors for [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) let their tables serve as streaming sources and sinks.[^n1][^n2]

Stateful operators such as aggregations, joins and deduplication keep state between batches in a **state store**. Since Spark 3.2, Spark includes a RocksDB-based state store provider that keeps state in native memory and on local disk instead of the JVM heap.[^apis]

`transformWithState`, available since Spark 4.0, is the operator for arbitrary stateful processing. It replaces the older `mapGroupsWithState` and `flatMapGroupsWithState` APIs in Scala and `applyInPandasWithState` in Python, and adds features such as timers and time-to-live (TTL) eviction of state. It is available in Scala, Java and Python.[^tws]

## Execution modes and triggers

By default, Structured Streaming runs a query as a series of small batch jobs (**micro-batches**), with end-to-end latencies as low as about 100 milliseconds.[^overview] The **trigger** controls timing:[^apis]

| Trigger | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Unspecified (default) | Starts the next micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes. |
| Fixed interval (`processingTime`) | Starts micro-batches at a set interval; skips a batch when there is no new data. |
| Available-now (`availableNow`) | Processes all data available at start, possibly in several micro-batches, then stops. |
| One-time | Processes available data in one micro-batch, then stops. Deprecated in favour of available-now. |
| Continuous | Experimental low-latency mode, added in Spark 2.3, with at-least-once guarantees.[^overview] |
| Real-time | Real-time Mode, added in Spark 4.1.0 (see below). |

**Real-time Mode** runs long-lived tasks, one per input partition, that process records as they arrive instead of waiting for a batch boundary. The Spark documentation states that this lowers end-to-end latency from the micro-batch floor to roughly the time needed to process and send one record. The trigger's duration (default 5 minutes) then mainly sets how often the query checkpoints.[^rtm] Spark 4.1.0 supported stateless queries in this mode.[^r410] Spark 4.3.0 added streaming aggregation, `dropDuplicates` and the Scala and Java `transformWithState` operator, using a pipelined shuffle; stream-stream joins and `flatMapGroupsWithState` are not yet supported in this mode.[^rtm][^r430] In PySpark, the mode is enabled with `.trigger(realTime="5 minutes")`.[^rtm]

## History

Spark 2.0.0 shipped the first, experimental release of Structured Streaming as a higher-level streaming API on Spark SQL and the Catalyst optimizer.[^n3] Spark 2.2.0 removed the experimental label and declared the APIs generally available (SPARK-20844).[^n4] Spark 4.0.0 added the Arbitrary State API v2 (`transformWithState`) and a State Data Source for reading state when debugging.[^n5] Real-time Mode followed in 4.1.0 (SPARK-53736) and gained stateful queries in 4.3.0.[^r410][^r430]

The older Spark Streaming API, based on discretized streams (DStreams), is described in the Spark 4.3 documentation as the previous generation of Spark's streaming engine; it receives no further updates, and the documentation directs new work to Structured Streaming.[^n6]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Structured Streaming typically ingests events from a message bus into bronze tables and keeps downstream tables current. [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) builds on it: SDP streaming tables are filled by Structured Streaming flows, and SDP can read from any source that `spark.readStream` supports.[^n7]

# transformWithState

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState

<Infobox type="concept" name="transformWithState">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Arbitrary State API v2, TWS</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Stateful processor, state variables (value, list, map), timers, TTL, time mode, output mode, optional initial state</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 4.0 and later (Scala, Java, Python)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.0.0, v4.1.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (KeyValueGroupedDataset.scala, StatefulProcessor.scala, TransformWithStateExecBase.scala, python/pyspark/sql/pandas/group_ops.py, python/pyspark/sql/connect/group.py, docs/streaming/structured-streaming-transform-with-state.md), the Spark 4.0.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, and SPARK-46815, SPARK-50770, SPARK-50855, SPARK-50856, SPARK-51814 and SPARK-51827</Verified>

<Status level="active" since="Apache Spark 4.0.0">The current operator for arbitrary stateful processing in Structured Streaming. Its public interfaces (`StatefulProcessor`, `TimeMode`) carry the `@Evolving` annotation at v4.3.0, not `@Experimental`.[^jira46815]</Status>

In [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), **transformWithState** is the operator for arbitrary stateful processing: user code, written as a stateful processor class, receives the rows for each grouping key, keeps any number of typed state variables for that key across micro-batches, registers timers and emits zero or more output rows.[^guide] It was added in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 4.0.0 as the "Arbitrary State API v2".[^r400] The Spark documentation calls it the next-generation replacement for [mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState) in Scala and Java and for `applyInPandasWithState` in Python; those older operators are still supported and are not deprecated.[^guide]

## What transformWithState is for

Built-in stateful operators such as streaming aggregation, deduplication and stream-stream joins cover common patterns, and Spark manages their state. Some logic does not fit them: sessionization with custom rules, downtime detection, fraud scoring over a user's history, or emitting an alert when nothing has arrived for a key. For these, Structured Streaming offers arbitrary stateful operators, where user code decides what to store, when to emit and when to forget.[^ssguide] transformWithState is the second generation of that API. The guide says that since Spark 4.0 users are encouraged to build complex stateful applications on it rather than on the older operators.[^ssguide]

## How it works

A query groups a streaming Dataset or DataFrame by key and passes a **stateful processor** to `transformWithState`. The processor is a class that extends `StatefulProcessor` and implements these methods:[^guide][^sp]
- `init`, called once to declare state variables through the processor's handle.
- `handleInputRows`, called with the key and an iterator of that key's new rows; it returns output rows.
- `handleExpiredTimer`, called once for each timer that has fired; by default it returns nothing.
- `handleInitialState`, available on `StatefulProcessorWithInitialState`, called once per key of an optional initial-state DataFrame before any input is processed.
- `close`, for cleanup.

### State variables

State is declared as named variables, not as a single object per key. There are three types: **ValueState** (one value), **ListState** (appends are cheap) and **MapState** (point lookups by a user key are cheap). A processor can declare several of each, and each has its own encoder.[^guide] Variables can be added between runs of the same query, and removed with `deleteIfExists` in `init`. With the Avro state encoding (`spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.encodingFormat` set to `avro`), the schema of a variable's value can evolve by adding, removing, reordering or widening fields.[^guide]

### Timers and TTL

The time mode is chosen per query: `TimeMode.None()`, `TimeMode.ProcessingTime()` or `TimeMode.EventTime()`.[^timemode] In processing-time or event-time mode, the processor can register, list and delete any number of timers per key; timers are checkpointed and can fire after a restart.[^guide] In event-time mode, timers fire as the [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) passes them.

Each state variable can have a time-to-live (TTL) through `TTLConfig`. Values are not returned after the TTL has passed and are eventually removed; every update resets the TTL. TTL works only with `TimeMode.ProcessingTime`.[^guide][^n1]

### State store requirement

transformWithState runs only on the RocksDB [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store). In a streaming query, the operator checks `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass` and fails with the error `STORE_BACKEND_NOT_SUPPORTED_FOR_TWS` unless it is `RocksDBStateStoreProvider`.[^base] The default provider in Spark 4.3.0 is still the HDFS-backed state store, so the setting must be changed before the query first starts; the provider cannot be changed between restarts of a query.[^n2] The operator stores its several variables as column families in one RocksDB instance.[^r400]

### Debugging and testing

The state data source can read a transformWithState query's state one variable at a time (option `stateVarName`) and list registered timers (option `readRegisteredTimers`). `TwsTester`, in Scala and Python, runs a stateful processor without a streaming query for unit tests; it does not model TTL or automatic watermark advancement.[^guide]

## Language and Spark Connect support

| API | Language | Data passed to the processor | Added in | Spark Connect support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `KeyValueGroupedDataset.transformWithState` | Scala, Java | Typed objects (encoders) | 4.0.0[^r400][^jira50770] | 4.1.0[^jira50855] |
| `GroupedData.transformWithStateInPandas` | Python | pandas DataFrames | 4.0.0[^groupops] | 4.1.0[^jira50856] |
| `GroupedData.transformWithState` | Python | `Row` objects | 4.1.0[^jira51814] | 4.1.0[^jira51827] |

In Spark 4.0.0 the [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) Scala client declared `transformWithState` but threw `UnsupportedOperationException`, and the Python Connect client had no `transformWithStateInPandas`; both work over Connect from 4.1.0.[^n3][^r410] The guide suggests the pandas variant for most Python users and the Row variant for high key cardinality, where conversion to pandas costs more.[^guide]

From Spark 4.3.0 the Scala and Java API can run with the real-time trigger (SPARK-57228); the two Python APIs are not supported in Real-time Mode.[^guide][^n4] transformWithState also runs in batch queries (SPARK-46865 for Scala, SPARK-50428 for Python).[^r400]

## Comparison with mapGroupsWithState

<Hatnote>Main article: [mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState)</Hatnote>

|  | transformWithState | mapGroupsWithState / flatMapGroupsWithState |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Added in | Spark 4.0.0[^r400] | Spark 2.2.0[^r220] |
| User code | A class with `init`, `handleInputRows`, `handleExpiredTimer` and other methods[^sp] | One function of key, values and a `GroupState`[^gs] |
| State per key | Any number of named value, list and map variables[^guide] | One state object[^gs] |
| Timers | Many timers per key, listed and deleted by the processor[^guide] | One timeout per key[^gs] |
| Automatic expiry | TTL per state variable (processing time)[^guide] | None; the function removes state itself, usually on timeout |
| State schema evolution | Supported for values with Avro encoding[^guide] | Not offered |
| State store | RocksDB only[^base] | HDFS-backed (default) or RocksDB |
| Python API | `transformWithStateInPandas` (4.0.0), `transformWithState` (4.1.0)[^groupops] | `applyInPandasWithState` (3.4.0)[^groupops] |
| Deprecated? | No | No; see [mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState) |

## Example

A running count per word in Scala, for Spark 4.0 or later. `words` is a streaming `Dataset[String]` and `spark.implicits._` is imported.

```scala
import org.apache.spark.sql.Encoders
import org.apache.spark.sql.streaming._

class RunningCount extends StatefulProcessor[String, String, (String, Long)] {
  @transient private var count: ValueState[Long] = _

  override def init(outputMode: OutputMode, timeMode: TimeMode): Unit = {
    count = getHandle.getValueState[Long]("count", Encoders.scalaLong, TTLConfig.NONE)
  }

  override def handleInputRows(
      key: String,
      rows: Iterator[String],
      timerValues: TimerValues): Iterator[(String, Long)] = {
    val updated = (if (count.exists()) count.get() else 0L) + rows.size
    count.update(updated)
    Iterator((key, updated))
  }
}

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
  "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")

val counts = words
  .groupByKey(identity)
  .transformWithState(new RunningCount, TimeMode.None(), OutputMode.Update())
```

# Trigger (Structured Streaming)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trigger_(Structured_Streaming)

<Infobox type="concept" name="Trigger">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Streaming trigger, trigger policy</Field>
  <Field name="field">Stream processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Unspecified (default), processing time, once (deprecated), available now, continuous (experimental), real time</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v2.0.0, v2.2.0, v3.3.0, v3.4.0 and v4.0.0 to v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (Trigger.java, Triggers.scala, python/pyspark/sql/streaming/readwriter.py, docs/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.md, docs/streaming/performance-tips.md, docs/streaming/real-time-mode.md), the Spark 3.4.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, SPARK-39805, SPARK-53737 and SPARK-57281</Verified>

In [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), a **trigger** is the setting on a streaming query that decides when the query processes data and which execution mode runs it: micro-batches as fast as possible, micro-batches on a fixed interval, all available data and then stop, or one of the low-latency modes.[^ssguide] The trigger is set with `DataStreamWriter.trigger()`, and a query can have only one.[^pyrw] Of the trigger types, **once** is deprecated since Spark 3.4.0 in favor of **available now**, and **continuous** is still experimental; the **real-time** trigger was added in Spark 4.1.0.[^triggerjava][^perf][^jira53737]

## Trigger types and status

| Trigger | Scala/Java | Python keyword | Added | Status in Spark 4.3.0 | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unspecified (default) | none | none | Spark 2.0.0[^pyrw] | Active | Starts each micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes; the same as a processing-time trigger of 0 seconds[^ssguide][^pyrw] |
| Processing time | `Trigger.ProcessingTime(interval)` | `processingTime` | Spark 2.2.0 for `Trigger.ProcessingTime`[^triggerjava] | Active | Starts micro-batches at a fixed interval[^ssguide] |
| Once | `Trigger.Once()` | `once` | Spark 2.2.0[^triggerjava] | **Deprecated** since Spark 3.4.0[^triggerjava][^r340] | Processes all available data in a single micro-batch, then stops[^triggerjava] |
| Available now | `Trigger.AvailableNow()` | `availableNow` | Spark 3.3.0[^triggerjava] | Active; the replacement for once | Processes all available data in one or more micro-batches, then stops[^ssguide] |
| Continuous | `Trigger.Continuous(interval)` | `continuous` | Spark 2.3.0[^triggerjava] | **Experimental**[^perf] | Runs the continuous processing engine with the given checkpoint interval; at-least-once[^perf] |
| Real time | `Trigger.RealTime(duration)` | `realTime` (from Spark 4.2.0)[^r420] | Spark 4.1.0[^jira53737] | Active; see [Real-time trigger](#real-time-trigger) | Runs Real-time Mode with long-running batches; the duration is mainly a checkpoint interval[^rtm] |

## Processing-time and default triggers

With no trigger set, Structured Streaming runs in micro-batch mode and starts the next micro-batch as soon as the previous one completes.[^ssguide] A processing-time trigger adds a fixed interval. If a micro-batch finishes early, the engine waits for the interval to end; if it runs past the interval, the next micro-batch starts as soon as it completes, without waiting for the next boundary. If no new data has arrived, no micro-batch starts.[^ssguide]

Triggers have been part of Structured Streaming since Spark 2.0.0.[^pyrw] Spark 2.2.0 added the `Trigger.ProcessingTime` factory methods and deprecated the older `ProcessingTime` class in their favor.[^triggerjava][^n1]

## Once and available now

**Trigger.Once** runs one micro-batch over all available data and stops the query. The programming guide describes its use for clusters that start on a schedule, process what arrived since the last run and shut down.[^ssguide] Trigger.Once is deprecated as of Spark 3.4.0 (SPARK-39805): the Java API carries `@Deprecated(since = "3.4.0")` and points to `AvailableNow()`.[^triggerjava][^r340] It has not been removed; it is still in the Spark 4.3.0 API.[^triggerjava]

**Trigger.AvailableNow**, added in Spark 3.3.0, has the same goal but can split the work into several micro-batches according to source options such as `maxFilesPerTrigger`.[^triggerjava][^ssguide] The guide gives these reasons to prefer it over Once:[^ssguide]
- All data available when the query starts is processed before it stops, including batches left uncommitted by an earlier run.
- The [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) advances after each batch, and a final no-data batch runs if the last batch moved the watermark, which keeps state small for stateful operators.

If any source in the query does not support AvailableNow, Spark falls back to a single micro-batch, as with Once.[^ssguide]

## Continuous trigger

The continuous trigger runs **continuous processing**, an execution mode introduced in Spark 2.3 that the Spark 4.3.0 documentation still labels experimental. It aims at end-to-end latency near 1 millisecond with at-least-once guarantees, compared with about 100 milliseconds and exactly-once for the micro-batch engine.[^perf] The argument is a checkpoint interval, not a batch interval. Continuous processing supports only map-like operations (projections and selections), no aggregations, and a small set of sources and sinks such as Kafka and the rate source.[^perf] The Real-time Mode documentation describes continuous processing as legacy and recommends Real-time Mode for new low-latency workloads.[^rtm]

## Real-time trigger

The real-time trigger enables **Real-time Mode**, added in Spark 4.1.0 (SPARK-53737, part of the SPARK-53736 SPIP) with support for stateless Scala queries.[^jira53737][^n2] Spark 4.2.0 added the `realTime` keyword to PySpark (SPARK-54660).[^r420] Spark 4.3.0 added a first set of stateful queries: streaming deduplication, streaming aggregation and the JVM `transformWithState` operator.[^r430][^rtm]

Real-time Mode launches long-running tasks instead of one job per micro-batch, so records are processed and emitted as they arrive. The duration passed to the trigger (default 5 minutes) is mainly the checkpoint interval; it must be at least `spark.sql.streaming.realTimeMode.minBatchDuration`, which defaults to 5 seconds. A real-time query must use the `update` output mode. The Kafka source supports Real-time Mode, and supported sinks include Kafka, console and memory.[^rtm]

In Spark 4.1.0 the internal `RealTimeTrigger` class carried the `@Experimental` annotation; the public `Trigger.RealTime` methods did not.[^n3] SPARK-57281 removed the annotation. Its JIRA fix version is 4.3.0 and the Spark 4.3.0 release notes list it, although the change is also present at the v4.2.0 tag.[^n4][^r430]

## Example

The following PySpark code, valid for Spark 4.3, runs a streaming query from JSON files into Parquet with the available-now trigger: it processes every file present at start, in one or more micro-batches, and then stops. Replacing `availableNow=True` with `processingTime="1 minute"` keeps the query running and starts a micro-batch every minute.

```python
query = (spark.readStream.format("json").schema("id LONG, msg STRING")
         .option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 100)
         .load("/data/in")
         .writeStream.format("parquet")
         .option("path", "/data/out")
         .option("checkpointLocation", "/data/chk")
         .trigger(availableNow=True)
         .start())
query.awaitTermination()
```

The Scala equivalent of the real-time trigger, for a supported query with a Kafka source and sink, is `.outputMode("update").trigger(Trigger.RealTime("5 minutes"))`.[^rtm]

# Trino

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Trino Software Foundation and contributors</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2019 (as PrestoSQL); renamed Trino in December 2020</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">484</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-15</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">Distributed SQL query engine</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[trino.io](https://trino.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/trinodb/trino](https://github.com/trinodb/trino)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Trino release notes (release 484) and the Trino 484 documentation</Verified>

**Trino** is an open source distributed SQL query engine for analytical queries over large datasets. It does not store data itself; it queries data where it lives, through connectors for data lakes, [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), relational databases and other systems.[^usecases][^concepts] Trino was known as PrestoSQL until December 2020, and it is supported by the Trino Software Foundation.[^rename]

## History

Dain Sundstrom, David Phillips and Martin Traverso joined the Facebook data infrastructure team in 2012 and created Presto there, to run low-latency interactive queries against the company's large Hadoop data warehouse.[^rename]

According to the creators, it became clear in 2018 that Facebook management wanted tighter control over the project. In January 2019 they started the Presto Software Foundation as an independent entity to oversee the software and its community, and the project continued under the name PrestoSQL. In September 2019, Facebook established a separate Presto Foundation at the Linux Foundation.[^rename]

On 27 December 2020, the creators announced that PrestoSQL was being renamed Trino. The announcement gives the reason as Facebook's application for a trademark on the name "Presto" and its enforcement, after attempts to agree on terms with Facebook and the Linux Foundation failed.[^rename]

Trino releases are numbered with a single integer. Release 484, the latest at the time of writing, is dated 15 October 2026 in the release notes.[^release] Trino is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.[^rename]

## Architecture

A Trino cluster has one coordinator and zero or more workers. Users connect to the coordinator with their SQL client. The coordinator parses SQL statements, plans queries and manages the workers. Workers execute tasks and process data, fetching it from connectors and exchanging intermediate results with each other.[^concepts]

A query runs as a hierarchy of stages that the coordinator builds as a distributed plan. Each stage runs as a set of tasks on workers, and tasks process splits, which are sections of a larger dataset.[^concepts]

A connector adapts Trino to a data source, much like a database driver, by implementing Trino's service provider interface. A catalog is a set of configuration properties that uses a connector to reach one specific data source; the catalog name comes from the name of its properties file.[^concepts]

## What Trino is not

The Trino documentation states that Trino is not a general-purpose relational database and is not a replacement for databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL or Oracle. It was not designed for online transaction processing (OLTP). It targets analytical workloads such as aggregating large datasets and producing reports.[^usecases]

## Lakehouse connectors

Trino's connector list includes connectors for [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) and Hive, as well as connectors for relational databases, Kafka and other systems.[^n1]

The Iceberg connector reads and writes data files in Avro, ORC and [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) format, with Parquet as the default. It supports `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and `MERGE` statements; row-level deletes need tables that use version 2 of the Iceberg specification.[^iceberg]

The Iceberg connector supports table maintenance through `ALTER TABLE EXECUTE`, with procedures including `optimize`, `expire_snapshots` and `remove_orphan_files`. It exposes metadata tables such as `$snapshots`, `$history` and `$files`, and it supports time travel by snapshot ID, timestamp, branch or tag:[^iceberg]

```sql
SELECT *
FROM example.testdb.customer_orders
FOR VERSION AS OF 8954597067493422955;
```

## Catalog support

The Iceberg connector needs a metastore or catalog. The property `iceberg.catalog.type` accepts the values `hive_metastore`, `glue`, `jdbc`, `rest`, `nessie` and `snowflake`.[^metastores]

With the `rest` type, Trino connects to an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) at the URI set in `iceberg.rest-catalog.uri`. The property `iceberg.rest-catalog.vended-credentials-enabled` controls whether Trino uses storage credentials supplied by the REST catalog; it defaults to false.[^metastores] Through this connector type Trino can use REST catalogs such as [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), whose site lists Trino among compatible engines, and the open source [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), whose documentation gives a Trino configuration for its Iceberg REST endpoint.[^n2][^n3]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Trino is a distributed engine for interactive SQL over shared tables. A single Trino cluster can define many catalogs with different or identical connectors, and one SQL query can read from more than one of them, so tables from different systems can be queried together.[^concepts]

[^n3]: [Unity Catalog Trino integration](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/main/docs/integrations/unity-catalog-trino.md). *Unity Catalog project*. Retrieved 2026-11-22.

# Unity Catalog

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Unity Catalog community, hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2024-07-09 (v0.1.0)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">0.7.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-13</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[unitycatalog.io](https://unitycatalog.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Unity Catalog v0.7.0 GitHub release, unitycatalog.io documentation and the LF AI & Data announcement</Verified>

**Unity Catalog** is an open source [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) for tables, files, functions and machine learning models in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse). It records which data and AI assets exist, where their data is stored and who can use them, and query engines reach it through open REST APIs.[^what] The project is hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation, part of the Linux Foundation, as a sandbox project.[^readme] This article covers the open source project (sometimes called Unity Catalog OSS), not the managed service of the same name.

## History

Databricks developed Unity Catalog and introduced it in 2021 as part of its commercial platform.[^lfai] On 13 June 2024, Databricks announced that it was releasing Unity Catalog as open source, with the server under the Apache License 2.0 and the API defined by an OpenAPI specification.[^dbblog]

The LF AI & Data Foundation announced Unity Catalog as its newest sandbox project in June 2024, stating that Databricks had open sourced the project and donated it to the foundation.[^lfai] The first tagged release, v0.1.0, was published on GitHub on 9 July 2024.[^n1]

The open source documentation describes Databricks Unity Catalog as a managed service that shares the same API lineage and has a larger feature set. The project documentation covers only the open source server.[^what]

## Data model

Unity Catalog organizes assets in a three-level namespace. A catalog is the top level, a schema belongs to one catalog, and every table has a three-part name of the form `catalog.schema.table`.[^quickstart]

The assets that Unity Catalog governs are:[^what]
- **Tables**: [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) tables, tables in other formats registered as external tables, and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables. For managed Delta tables, the catalog allocates storage and coordinates commits.
- **Views and metric views**: stored SQL or YAML definitions that an engine runs.
- **Volumes**: governed directories for non-tabular files.
- **Functions**: registered Python or SQL functions, which run in the caller's environment.
- **Registered models**: MLflow models and their versions.

## APIs

Unity Catalog exposes three REST interfaces. The Unity Catalog REST API manages catalogs, schemas, tables, volumes and other objects. The Delta API serves catalog-managed Delta tables. The Iceberg REST Catalog API serves Iceberg clients.[^what]

The Delta API was added in version 0.5.0. It lets Delta clients create, load, list, alter, rename and delete catalog-managed Delta tables, and it validates commits on the server before they land.[^n2]

Unity Catalog implements the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification at the path `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg`. Through this endpoint the server lists Iceberg tables, and lists Delta tables only when they carry UniForm Iceberg metadata.[^irc] Version 0.7.0 extended this endpoint so that any engine that supports the Iceberg REST protocol can create, write, read, rename and drop Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog.[^rel070] The project documentation shows [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), PyIceberg and DataFusion as clients of this endpoint.[^irc]

## Access control and credential vending

When authentication and authorization are enabled, the Unity Catalog server validates tokens from an external identity provider, maps them to known users, and checks ownership and privileges such as `USE_CATALOG`, `SELECT` and `MODIFY` on each request.[^what]

Unity Catalog uses credential vending to give engines access to storage. The server holds the storage identity. After an authorization check, it returns a short-lived credential that is limited to one location and one kind of access, and the client then reads and writes data directly in object storage.[^vend]

The documentation describes per-cloud mechanisms: an AWS STS session policy for Amazon S3, a user-delegation SAS token for Azure Data Lake Storage, and a downscoped Google STS token for Google Cloud Storage. Credentials cannot be recalled once issued, so revoking a grant blocks only new credentials. Access is all-or-nothing per location, so row and column filtering must be enforced by the engine.[^vend]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Unity Catalog acts as the shared catalog that several engines use for the same tables. Delta clients can use the Delta API, and Iceberg clients can use the Iceberg REST endpoint without a Unity Catalog connector.[^what][^rel070] The project documentation also includes guides for connecting Apache Spark and DuckDB.[^n3][^n4]
